text: A groom tells the mute Ivan-tsarevich that his mother will soon bear a daughter, a witch who will eat everyone, and tells him to ask his father for the best horse and flee
Ivan speaks to his father for the first time in his life, asking for a horse
The overjoyed tsar has the best horse saddled for him
Ivan rides off wherever his eyes lead him
Ivan asks two old seamstresses to take him in; they refuse, saying they will die when they finish their chest of needles and thread
Weeping, Ivan rides on and asks Vertodub to take him in; Vertodub refuses, saying he will die when he has uprooted the last oaks
Ivan rides on and asks Vertogor; Vertogor refuses, saying he will die when he has turned the last mountains
Ivan comes to the Sun's Sister, who takes him in and cares for him like her own son
Ivan climbs a high mountain, sees that everything at his home has been eaten and only the walls remain, and weeps
The Sun's Sister asks why he has been crying, and he lies that the wind blew in his eyes
When it happens again, the Sun's Sister forbids the wind to blow
The third time Ivan confesses everything and begs to be let go home
The Sun's Sister refuses, but at last lets him go and gives him a brush, a comb and two apples of youth
At Vertogor, who has one mountain left, Ivan throws the brush and countless mountains rise; Vertogor gladly sets to work
At Vertodub, who has three oaks left, Ivan throws the comb and oak forests rise; Vertodub thanks him
Ivan gives the old women an apple each; they eat them and become young
The old women give him a kerchief that makes a lake when waved
Ivan arrives home; his sister greets him and tells him to play the gusli while she cooks dinner
A mouse warns Ivan to flee because his sister has gone to sharpen her teeth
Ivan mounts his horse and gallops back, while the mouse runs over the strings to keep the gusli sounding
The witch sharpens her teeth, finds the room empty, and in a rage gives chase
Ivan waves the kerchief and a deep lake appears; while the witch swims across, he gets far ahead
Vertodub throws uprooted oaks across the road; the witch gnaws her way through
Vertogor turns a mountain onto the road and sets another on it; the witch climbs over
The witch catches sight of Ivan and cries that he will not escape her now
Ivan reaches the Sun's Sister's tower and calls to the Sun to open the window; she opens it and he leaps in with his horse
The witch demands that her brother be handed over; the Sun's Sister refuses
The witch proposes that she and Ivan be weighed: if she is heavier she eats him, if he is heavier he kills her
Ivan sits on the scales; as the witch steps on, he is flung up into the sky to the Sun's Sister's tower, and the witch stays on earth
The old woman tells the old man they will marry off her stepdaughter Marfusha, and orders him to drive her off next morning
Marfusha, glad to be going on a visit, rises early, packs and dresses
At breakfast the old woman tells the old man to take Marfusha to the great pine in the forest and give her to Morozko; the girl wails
The old man drives Marfusha into the forest, leaves her under the pine with her box, tells her to be kind to her groom, and drives home
Morozko comes down the pine and three times asks the freezing girl if she is warm; each time she answers kindly that she is
Morozko takes pity on her and wraps her in furs and blankets
Next morning the old woman sends the old man to wake the newlyweds
The old man finds his daughter alive, with a fine fur coat, a veil and a box of rich gifts, and brings her home
The girl bows at her stepmother's feet; the old woman is amazed to see her alive and rich
The old woman tells the old man to take her own daughters to the groom too
She feeds and dresses her daughters, and the old man leaves them under the same pine
The two daughters, growing cold, quarrel over which of them the groom will take
Morozko comes and three times asks if they are warm; they answer rudely and curse him
The daughters freeze stiff
Next morning the old woman sends the old man for them; he finds them dead and brings them home under a mat
The old woman finds her daughters dead and berates the old man; he answers that her greed was to blame
The old woman makes peace with her stepdaughter
A neighbour woos Marfusha; they marry and she lives happily
The stepmother nags the old man to take his daughter to a dugout in the forest to spin
The man takes his daughter to the dugout, gives her flint, tinder and a bag of groats, and tells her to keep the fire, cook and spin
At night the girl lights the stove and cooks porridge
A mouse asks the girl for a spoonful of porridge, and she feeds it its fill
A bear breaks in and tells the girl to put out the lights and play blind man's buff
The mouse whispers to the girl to agree, put out the light and hide under the stove, while it runs ringing the bell
The girl does so; the bear chases the mouse, cannot catch it, and throws logs without hitting
The tired bear praises the girl's skill and promises to send her a herd of horses and a cartload of goods in the morning
The wife sends the old man to see what his daughter has spun
The little dog barks that the daughter is coming with horses and goods; the woman calls it a liar
The old man and his daughter drive into the yard with a herd of horses and a full cart
The greedy woman demands that her own daughter be taken to the forest, boasting she will bring back twice as much
The man takes the woman's daughter Natashka to the dugout and supplies her the same way
When the mouse asks for porridge, Natashka throws a spoon at it, and the mouse runs off
Natashka eats the porridge alone, blows out the lights and lies down in a corner
At midnight the bear breaks in, finds her, and makes her run with the bell while he catches her
Her trembling hand keeps the bell ringing, and the mouse calls out that the wicked girl will not live
Next morning the woman sends the old man to the forest, boasting of the carts and herds her daughter will bring
The dog barks that the woman's daughter is rattling as bones in a box; the woman calls it a liar
The old man hands his wife the box; she opens it, sees the bones and howls
The woman, in grief and rage, dies the next day
The old man lives out his life well with his daughter and takes a noble son-in-law into the house
The little orphan Khavroshechka is taken in by heartless people, who work her to exhaustion
Khavroshechka complains to her dappled cow of her tasks; the cow has her climb in one ear and out the other, and the work is done
The puzzled stepmother sends her daughter One-Eye to find out who helps the orphan
One-Eye lies down in the sun, and Khavroshechka lulls her eye to sleep
While One-Eye sleeps, the cow weaves and bleaches the cloth
The stepmother sends Two-Eyes; Khavroshechka lulls both her eyes to sleep, and the cow does the work
On the third day the angry stepmother sends Three-Eyes and gives the orphan still more work
Khavroshechka sings two of Three-Eyes' eyes to sleep but forgets the third
The third eye sees Khavroshechka climb in one ear of the cow and out the other and gather the finished cloth
Three-Eyes tells her mother everything
The stepmother orders her husband to slaughter the cow; he objects, but she insists and he sharpens the knife
Khavroshechka runs to warn the cow
The cow tells her not to eat its meat, but to gather its bones, plant them in the garden and water them every morning
Khavroshechka does so, going hungry rather than eating the meat and watering the bones daily
An apple tree with golden leaves and silver branches grows from the bones
A rich young gentleman riding by sees the apples and promises to marry whichever girl brings him one
The three sisters rush to the tree, but the apples rise out of reach and the branches tear at them
Khavroshechka comes up, and the branches bow and the apples come down to her
The gentleman marries Khavroshechka, and she lives happily
The tsaritsa dies and the tsar marries Yagishna
Yagishna bears two daughters, one two-eyed and one three-eyed
The stepmother sends Marya-tsarevna to herd the cow Burenushka with only a dry crust of bread
Marya bows to the cow's right leg, eats, drinks and dresses finely, follows the cow all day like a lady, and in the evening brings the crust home untouched
Wondering what keeps her alive, Yagishna gives her the same crust and sends her elder daughter to watch her
Marya offers to search the sister's hair and lulls both her eyes to sleep
Marya bows to the cow, eats and dresses, and in the evening wakes her sister to go home
The sister tells her mother she saw nothing, and Yagishna scolds her
Yagishna sends her three-eyed daughter to see what Marya eats and drinks
Marya lulls two of the sister's eyes to sleep but forgets the third
The third eye watches Marya bow to the cow, eat, drink and dress
Three-Eyes tells her mother everything
Yagishna orders the old man to slaughter the cow, and he does
Marya begs the old man for a piece of gut, and he throws it to her
Marya plants the gut by the gatepost; a willow bush grows with sweet berries and singing birds
Ivan-tsarevich hears of Marya, comes to the stepmother, sets a dish on the table and promises to marry the girl who fills it with berries
Yagishna sends each of her daughters for berries, but the birds will not let them near
At last Marya is let go; the birds help fill her dish, and she sets it on the table and bows to the tsarevich
Ivan-tsarevich marries Marya
Marya bears a son
Marya goes with her husband to visit her father
The stepmother turns Marya into a goose and dresses her elder daughter up as Ivan's wife
Ivan-tsarevich returns home
The old tutor takes the baby out to the bush in the field and asks the passing geese where the baby's mother is
The mother drops from the second flock, throws off her skins, nurses the baby in tears, and says that in two days she will fly away
The false wife scolds the old man for taking the child into the field
Next morning the tutor goes again, and Ivan follows him unseen and hides in the bush
The mother drops from the flock again, throws her skins on the bush, nurses the baby, says farewell and hands him back to the tutor
Ivan burns her skins
Ivan seizes Marya; she turns into a frog, a lizard, every kind of vermin and at last a spindle
Ivan breaks the spindle in two and throws the pieces behind and before him, and Marya becomes a young woman
They go home together, and Yagishna's daughter cries out that the destroyer is coming
Ivan asks the princes and boyars which wife he should live with, and they say the first
Ivan says he will live with whichever wife jumps up onto the gate faster; the false wife climbs up, Marya does not
Ivan shoots the false wife and lives on with Marya as before
The dying merchant's wife gives her eight-year-old daughter Vasilisa a doll with her blessing, telling her to keep it hidden, feed it in trouble and ask its advice
The mother kisses her daughter and dies
The merchant marries a widow with two daughters
The stepmother and her daughters, envious of Vasilisa's beauty, torment her with every kind of work
Vasilisa secretly feeds the doll and tells it her grief; the doll comforts her and does all her work
Suitors court Vasilisa; the stepmother refuses them all, saying the younger will not marry before the elder, and takes her spite out on Vasilisa with beatings
The merchant leaves home on a long trading journey
The stepmother moves to a house by a dense forest where Baba Yaga lives
The stepmother keeps sending Vasilisa into the forest, but the doll guides her home and away from Baba Yaga's hut
One autumn the stepmother gives the three girls evening work, puts out every light but one candle, and goes to bed
On her mother's orders, one stepsister puts out the candle as if by accident
The stepsisters refuse to fetch fire and push Vasilisa out to get it from Baba Yaga
Vasilisa feeds the doll and tells it she is being sent to Baba Yaga; the doll tells her to go and keep it always with her
Vasilisa puts the doll in her pocket, crosses herself and goes into the forest
A white horseman rides past her and day breaks; then a red horseman rides past and the sun rises
After a night and a day Vasilisa reaches Baba Yaga's hut, fenced with bones and skulls, and stands rooted in terror
A black horseman rides to the gate and vanishes; night falls and the skulls' eyes light up
Baba Yaga arrives in her mortar and smells a Russian smell
Vasilisa bows and says her stepmother's daughters have sent her for fire
Baba Yaga says Vasilisa must first live and work for her, or she will eat her
Baba Yaga orders the gates open, and she and Vasilisa go in
Vasilisa serves Baba Yaga food enough for ten, which she eats, leaving the girl scraps
Baba Yaga orders her to clean the yard and hut, cook, see to the linen and pick the black seeds out of the wheat, or be eaten
Vasilisa gives the doll the scraps and begs for help; the doll tells her to sleep, as morning is wiser
In the morning Baba Yaga rides off in her mortar
Vasilisa finds all the work done, the doll picking out the last seeds, and thanks it
In the evening Vasilisa sets the table and meets Baba Yaga, who inspects everything and is vexed to find no fault
Baba Yaga calls three pairs of hands, which carry the wheat away to be ground
Baba Yaga orders the same work for the next day, and the poppy seed to be cleaned of earth
Vasilisa feeds the doll, which promises that all will be done
Next day Vasilisa and the doll do all the work at once
Baba Yaga returns, inspects it, and has the hands press oil from the poppy seed
At dinner Vasilisa asks about the white, red and black horsemen, and Baba Yaga says they are her day, her sun and her night
Vasilisa holds back from asking about the three pairs of hands
Baba Yaga asks how she manages the work, and Vasilisa answers that her mother's blessing helps her
Baba Yaga, wanting no blessed ones, pushes her out of the gate and gives her a skull with burning eyes on a stick as the fire
Vasilisa runs home by the skull's light and reaches the house the next evening
She is about to throw the skull away when it tells her to carry it to her stepmother
For the first time the stepmother and her daughters greet her kindly; they have had no fire since she left
The skull's eyes follow the stepmother and her daughters wherever they hide and burn them to coal by morning, leaving Vasilisa untouched
Vasilisa buries the skull, locks the house, goes to town and lodges with a lonely old woman
Vasilisa has the old woman buy flax and spins a yarn as fine as a hair
No reed fits the yarn, so Vasilisa asks the doll, which makes her a loom overnight from an old reed, a shuttle and horsehair
Vasilisa weaves and bleaches the linen and asks the old woman to sell it and keep the money
The old woman takes it to the palace and walks past the windows until the tsar asks what she wants
The tsar marvels at the linen; the old woman gives it to him as a gift, and he sends her off with presents
When no seamstress can be found for the shirts, the tsar summons the old woman; she says her foster daughter made the linen, and he orders the girl to sew them
The old woman tells Vasilisa, who shuts herself in and soon sews a dozen shirts
The old woman takes the shirts to the tsar, while Vasilisa dresses and waits by the window
A royal servant comes to summon the needlewoman to be rewarded by the tsar
Vasilisa appears before the tsar, who falls in love with her and says she will be his wife
The tsar and Vasilisa are married
Vasilisa's father returns, rejoices at her fortune and stays to live with her
Vasilisa takes the old woman to live with her and keeps the doll in her pocket for the rest of her life
A childless old man going for mushrooms meets an old grandfather, who tells him to collect an egg from every house and set a hen on them
The old man collects an egg from each of the forty-one houses and sets a hen on them
Forty-one boys hatch from the eggs, forty strong and one sickly
The old man names them all, and having no name left for the last, calls him Zamoryshek
The brothers mow and stack hay for a week, come home, eat and go to sleep
The old man grumbles that they have done nothing, and Zamoryshek tells him to go and look first
The old man drives to the meadow, finds forty haystacks and praises his sons
Next day he finds one stack gone and tells his sons
Zamoryshek promises to catch the thief and takes a hundred roubles from his father
Zamoryshek has a smith forge a chain; he bursts the first, the second, twice as strong, holds, and he pays
Zamoryshek sits under a haystack to keep watch
At midnight a wondrous mare comes out of the sea and starts eating the hay
Zamoryshek bridles her with the chain and mounts her; she carries him over hill and dale but cannot throw him
The mare stops and gives him her foals
The mare neighs by the sea, and forty-one stallions come out onto the shore
In the morning Zamoryshek drives the herd home to his father's yard
Zamoryshek proposes that the brothers, each now with a horse, ride off to seek brides
Their parents bless them and the brothers set out
After long travels they find a white stone palace with forty-one iron posts and tie their horses to them
Baba Yaga scolds them for tying up their horses; they tell her to feed them and give them a bath before asking questions
Baba Yaga feeds and bathes them and asks their business; they say they seek brides
Baba Yaga brings out her forty-one daughters; the brothers are betrothed to them and the weddings are feasted
Zamoryshek goes to see his horse, which warns him that the brothers must dress their wives in their clothes and wear the wives' clothes
Zamoryshek tells his brothers; they change clothes with their wives and go to bed, but Zamoryshek stays awake
At midnight Baba Yaga orders her servants to cut off the guests' heads
The servants cut off the heads of Baba Yaga's daughters
Zamoryshek wakes his brothers; they set the heads on the iron spikes round the wall, saddle their horses and ride off
In the morning Baba Yaga sees the heads, rages, and gives chase with her fiery shield, burning on all sides
Trapped at the sea, Zamoryshek waves a kerchief he took from Baba Yaga, and a bridge spans the sea; the brothers cross
Zamoryshek waves the kerchief the other way, the bridge vanishes, Baba Yaga turns back, and the brothers ride home
The cat and the sparrow go to chop wood, telling the zhikhar to keep house and say nothing if Baba Yaga comes to count the spoons
Baba Yaga comes and counts the spoons
The zhikhar cannot hold back and shouts at her not to touch his spoon
Baba Yaga seizes the zhikhar and rides off with him in her mortar
The zhikhar cries out for the cat and the sparrow
They come running; the cat scratches and the sparrow pecks Baba Yaga, and they take the zhikhar back
Next day they go for wood again, warning the zhikhar to say nothing because they will be far away
Baba Yaga counts the spoons again and the zhikhar shouts at her not to touch his
Baba Yaga drags him off; he cries out, and the cat and sparrow come and rescue him again
On the third day they go for wood, warning him once more
Baba Yaga counts the spoons twice, and the zhikhar keeps silent
At the third count the zhikhar cannot bear it and curses her for touching his spoon
Baba Yaga drags him off; he cries for help, but his brothers do not hear
Baba Yaga brings him home, puts him under the stove-bench, heats the oven and tells her eldest daughter to roast him for dinner while she goes to Rus
The daughter tells him to lie on the roasting pan; he sets one foot against the ceiling and the other against the oven top
She says that is wrong, he asks her to show him, and she lies down on the pan
The zhikhar shoves her into the oven with the oven fork and goes back to wait under the bench
Baba Yaga runs in, gloating over the zhikhar's bones; he answers that she may gloat over her daughter's
Baba Yaga finds her daughter roasted, vows he will not escape, and orders her middle daughter to roast him
The zhikhar tricks the middle daughter the same way, shoves her into the oven, and mocks Baba Yaga again
Baba Yaga orders her youngest daughter to roast him, but he roasts her too
Baba Yaga heats the oven herself and tells him to lie on the pan; he braces his feet again and pretends not to know how
Baba Yaga lies down on the pan to show him, and he shoves her into the oven
The zhikhar runs home and tells his brothers what he has done to Baba Yaga
Ivashko begs his parents to let him go fishing; they fear he will drown, but he insists
His mother dresses him in a white shirt and red belt and lets him go
Ivashko gets into his boat and speaks to it; it carries him far out and he fishes
His mother comes to the shore and calls him; he answers and the boat brings him to shore
The mother takes the fish, feeds him, changes his shirt and belt, and lets him go fishing again
Ivashko sails far out again and fishes
His father comes to the shore and calls him; he answers and the boat brings him in
The father takes the fish, feeds him, changes his shirt and belt, and lets him go again
A witch who has overheard comes to the shore and calls him in a hoarse voice; Ivashko knows it is not his mother's voice and sings back
The witch makes a smith, on threat of eating him, forge her a thin voice like Ivashko's mother's
At night the witch sings to Ivashko in the mother's voice, and he sails to shore
The witch takes the fish, seizes Ivashko and carries him home
The witch tells her daughter Alyonka to heat the oven and roast Ivashko while she gathers her guests
Alyonka heats the oven and tells Ivashko to sit on the shovel
Ivashko says he is too small to know how and asks her to show him
As soon as Alyonka sits on the shovel, Ivashko shoves her into the oven and shuts the damper
Ivashko leaves the hut, locks the door and climbs a tall oak
The witch comes with her guests, finds the door locked, curses Alyonka, climbs in the window and lets the guests in
The witch takes the roasted Alyonka from the oven, and she and her guests eat and drink and go out to roll on the grass
The witch chants that she will roll about, full of Ivashko's flesh, and Ivashko answers from the oak that she is full of Alyonka's
When she hears it a second time, the witch looks up and sees Ivashko
The witch gnaws at the oak until she breaks her two front teeth, then has the smith, under threat, forge her iron ones
The witch gnaws through the oak, but as it falls Ivashko jumps to the next one
The witch gnaws the second oak until she breaks two lower teeth, and the smith forges her two more
The witch goes back to gnawing the oak
Ivashko asks a passing flock of geese-swans to take him; they say the middle flock will take him
He asks the second flock; they say the hindmost will take him
He asks the third flock, which picks him up, carries him home and sets him in the loft
Next morning the mother bakes pancakes, longing to see her son; the father says he dreamt the geese-swans brought him home
As the mother shares the pancakes between herself and the old man, Ivashko calls out from the loft that there are none for him
The old man climbs into the loft and brings Ivashko down
The parents rejoice, ask him about everything, and they all live happily together
The mother tells her daughter to look after her little brother and not leave the yard, promising her presents
The parents go off to work
The girl forgets, sets her brother on the grass under the window and runs off to play in the street
Geese-swans swoop down and carry the boy off
The girl comes back, finds him gone, and searches, calls and weeps for him
Running into the field, she sees the geese-swans vanish beyond the dark forest, guesses they have her brother, and chases them
She asks a stove where the geese flew; it asks her to eat its rye pie, she scorns it, and it does not tell
She asks an apple tree; it asks her to eat its wild apple, she scorns it
She asks a river of milk with banks of kissel; it asks her to eat its kissel, she scorns it
She meets a hedgehog and asks it, and it points the way
She comes to a hut on chicken legs where Baba Yaga sits and her brother plays with golden apples on a bench
She creeps up, snatches her brother and runs off with him
The geese-swans fly after her
She begs the milk river to hide her; she eats its kissel, it hides her under the bank, the geese fly past, and she thanks it
The geese turn back toward her; she begs the apple tree to hide her, eats its wild apple, and it covers her with branches and leaves
The geese see her and chase her, beating at her with their wings, almost tearing the boy from her arms
She begs the stove to hide her, eats its rye pie and climbs into its mouth; the geese fly about crying and leave with nothing
She runs home with her brother just before her father and mother return
A wicked witch, wanting to ruin an old princess's son and daughter, comes to the mother in the shape of a fox and gives her a ring: the son must wear it and marry the girl it fits
The old princess believes her and, dying, bids her son marry the girl the ring fits
The son grows up and seeks a bride through villages and towns, but the ring fits no girl, and he comes home brooding
His sister asks why he grieves, and he tells her
The sister tries the ring on, and it fits her as if made for her
The brother declares she will be his wife; she protests that it is a sin, but he orders preparations for the wedding
The sister goes out and sits weeping on the threshold
She calls in some passing old women, feeds them, and tells them her grief
The old women tell her to make four dolls and set them in the four corners, to go to the wedding but not to hurry to the bedchamber
The brother and sister are married
Three times the brother calls Katerina to bed and she delays, taking off her earrings, belt and shoes, while the dolls cuckoo and the earth opens and swallows her
The brother, angry, bursts open the door and finds only the dolls cuckooing for the earth to swallow his sister
He chops off the dolls' heads with an axe and throws them into the stove
Walking underground, the sister comes to a hut on chicken legs and bids it turn round to her
A girl embroidering a towel inside welcomes her, warning that her mother is a witch
They embroider together; before the witch returns, the daughter turns the guest into a needle and hides her in a broom
The witch smells a Russian; the daughter says only old passers-by came for water, and the witch tells her to keep everyone in future and flies off
The witch returns and smells a Russian again; the daughter says old men came to warm their hands, and the hungry witch scolds her and flies off
The girls hurry to finish the towel and plot how to escape
The witch surprises them, and the daughter presents the girl to her
The witch has the oven heated hot
The witch tells the guest to sit on the shovel; twice the girl puts one foot in the oven and the other outside, and the witch pulls her back
The witch sits on the shovel to show her, and the girls shove her into the oven and seal it up
The girls run off with the embroidered towel, a brush and a comb
The witch breaks out, sees them and gives chase
They throw the brush and thick reeds grow; the witch claws a path through
They throw the comb and a dark oak forest grows; the witch gnaws and tears a way through
They throw the towel and a sea of fire spreads; the witch tries to fly over, falls into the fire and burns
As the girls sit resting, a man asks who they are and tells his master that one of the two look-alike beauties must be his sister
The master invites them in but cannot tell which is his sister, and she in her anger will not say
The servant proposes to fill a sheep's bladder with blood, put it under the master's arm and stab it
The servant stabs the bladder, the brother falls, and his sister rushes to embrace him, weeping
The brother springs up unharmed, embraces his sister and marries her to a good man
He marries her companion, whom the ring also fits, and they all live happily
Two poor peasants, one who lives by falsehood and one who lives by truth, argue which is the better way to live, and neither wins
They set out along the road, agreeing to put the question to the first three people they meet
A ploughing serf tells them that living by falsehood is easier, and the false man claims he is right
A merchant in a covered cart gives the same answer
A priest gives the same answer; the false man claims victory, but the true man says he will not live by falsehood
The true man asks the false man for a piece of bread; the false man demands an eye in return, puts it out, and gives him a little bread
When the true man begs again, the false man puts out his other eye for a little bread and leaves him blind on the road
The blind man gropes along, loses his way, and prays to God
A voice tells him to follow a path in the forest to a spring, bathe his eyes, then climb a great oak and listen to the devils at night
He finds the path and the spring, washes his eyes with its water, and sees again
He goes up the stream to the great oak, climbs it and waits for night
Devils gather under the oak, and one tells how he has tormented a tsarevna for ten years and can be driven out only by the icon on a rich merchant's gate
In the morning the true man finds the merchant and offers to work a year for the icon
After a year the merchant offers money instead and makes him work another year
After the second year the merchant again holds back the icon and makes him work a third
After the third year the merchant gives him the icon, feeds him and rewards him with a little money
The true man goes to the tsar and says he can cure the tsarevna
He prays, dips the icon three times in water, hangs it on the tsarevna and has her wash in the water; the devil flies out of her and she is well
All rejoice and offer him land and wages, but he refuses everything
The tsarevna says she will marry him, the tsar agrees, and they are wed
Living at court, he asks to visit his poor old mother, and the tsarevna goes with him
Near his home they meet the false man; the true man greets him by name and reveals who he is
The true man forgives him and tells him how to find his own fortune at the spring and the oak
The false man does all he was told, climbs the oak and waits for night
The devils gather, smell him in the oak, and tear him to pieces
A cunning prisoner with iron hands, cast-iron head and copper body, long held by a tsar, begs the tsar's little son Ivan for a drink
Ivan, knowing nothing, gives him water, and the prisoner vanishes from the jail
The tsar has Ivan banished from the kingdom, and he goes wherever his eyes lead
Ivan comes to another tsar and asks for service, and is made a stable boy
Ivan only sleeps in the stable instead of tending the horses, and the head groom beats him more than once; Ivan endures it
A tsar refused the hand of the princess declares war
The tsar goes off with his army, leaving his daughter Marfa-tsarevna to rule
Marfa, who has noticed Ivan is of no common birth, sends him to be a governor
Out hunting, Ivan meets the iron-handed man, who greets him and invites him home
The man's youngest daughter brings Ivan a half-bucket cup of wine; he says he cannot drink it, but at the old man's bidding drains it in one draught
The old man takes him to a stone of five hundred poods and tells him to lift it, and Ivan throws it easily
The middle daughter brings a bucket of wine; Ivan drains it and throws a stone of a thousand poods
The eldest daughter brings a bucket and a half; Ivan drains it and lightly throws a stone of fifteen hundred poods
The old man gives Ivan a self-spreading tablecloth and tells him to strengthen his porch, chairs and floors, since nothing will now bear his weight
Ivan comes home from the hunt on foot leading his horse, and people laugh
Ivan has his floors propped and chairs remade, sends away his cooks and maids, and lives alone, fed by the tablecloth
The tsar returns from the war, removes Ivan as governor and makes him a stable boy again
The head groom strikes Ivan, and Ivan strikes back and knocks his head off
Brought before the tsar, Ivan says the groom struck first; the other grooms agree, and Ivan is only moved to be a soldier

A man as small as a fingernail with a beard as long as an elbow brings the tsar a letter from the Water King: Marfa must be brought to an island for his son, guarded by a three-headed dragon, or the kingdom will be burnt
The tsar writes back agreeing, takes counsel, and proclaims that whoever saves Marfa from the dragon shall marry her
A gentleman comes forward, takes a company of soldiers, brings Marfa to the island, leaves her in a hut and waits outside
Ivan learns of it, goes to the island, tells the weeping Marfa not to cry, lays his head in her lap and sleeps
The dragon comes out with a flood of water, and the gentleman orders his soldiers up into the trees
Marfa wakes Ivan, who cuts off all three of the dragon's heads at one stroke and leaves
The gentleman takes Marfa home to her father
The little man brings a second letter demanding Marfa for a six-headed dragon; the tsar agrees and proclaims again
The same gentleman offers to save her again with one company of soldiers
Ivan, grateful for her kindness, goes to the hut, where Marfa is glad to see him, and falls asleep
The six-headed dragon comes; Marfa wakes Ivan, who fights it, cuts off all six heads, throws them in the water and leaves
The gentleman tells the tsar he saved Marfa and frightens her into silence; he presses for the wedding, but Marfa asks for time to recover
A third letter demands Marfa for a nine-headed dragon; the tsar agrees, and the gentleman takes her to the island again
Ivan comes; Marfa asks who he is, but he says nothing and falls asleep
The nine-headed dragon comes out, and the gentleman orders the soldiers into the trees
Marfa cannot wake Ivan, so she cuts his cheek with a penknife; he wakes and fights the dragon
The dragon begins to overpower Ivan; the iron-handed man appears, and together they cut off all its heads and throw them in the water
The gentleman presses the tsar for the wedding, and Marfa again asks for time
The little man brings a letter in which the Water King demands the guilty one; the gentleman is sent by ship, and Ivan, serving in the fleet, is aboard
Passing ships cry out for the guilty one; Ivan points to the gentleman, and they beat him half to death
The Water King orders the guilty one put into a red-hot bathhouse, and the gentleman is terrified
Ivan sends a man who has entered his service into the bathhouse, and he comes back unharmed
The Water King summons the guilty one, berates and beats the gentleman, and drives him away
Back home the gentleman grows proud and presses the tsar, who betroths Marfa to him and sets the wedding day
Marfa asks her father to assemble all the soldiers for her to inspect
She finds Ivan by the scar on his cheek and leads him to her father as the one who saved her
The soldiers confirm that the gentleman sat in the trees
The gentleman is stripped of rank and exiled
Ivan marries Marfa
Something starts eating a farmer's wheat; he sends his eldest son to guard it, but the son falls asleep before dawn and the wheat is eaten
The second son guards the next night, also falls asleep, and the wheat is eaten
The third son, the fool, sleeps in the evening, wakes before dawn, catches the bird that comes, puts it in a sack and goes back to sleep
The elder brothers find the wheat whole, hear the fool's story, take the bird from him and tell their father they caught it
The father takes the bird to the king, who pays him, has it locked in a cellar and gives the key to the queen
The bird speaks to the little prince and begs him to free it, telling him to coax his mother and steal the key from her neck
The prince fondles his mother, steals the key and lets the bird out
The bird, who is the Brass Old Man, promises to come and do whatever the prince needs whenever he calls
The king invites guests to see the bird, and they find the cellar empty
The queen swears she did not free it but is condemned to death; she remembers her son fondling her and says he must have stolen the keys
Some guests would hang the boy, others drown him, but one proposes to sew him a pigskin coat and turn him out into the world, and all agree
The weeping mother sews a hundred thousand in money into the pigskin coat and sends him off
The prince walks off weeping, climbs a hill and calls the Brass Old Man, who comes and hears his story
The old man tells him to go over the sea to a king and become his kitchen boy, and when war comes to get leave to watch it and call him
The prince goes over the sea and asks the king to take him as a kitchen boy; the king agrees
In the third year war breaks out and the king rides off with his army
The kitchen boy pays the cook five roubles for leave to watch the war, goes out of the gate and calls the old man
The old man gives him a horse, officer's clothes, a sword and a silver apple, telling him to refuse the king's invitation and give the apple to the princess for a night on her threshold
The prince destroys the whole enemy army and refuses the king's invitation to the palace
Back in his pigskin, he rolls the silver apple in the kitchen; the princess begs to buy it, and he asks only to spend the night on her threshold, which she grants
He spends the night on the threshold of her room and goes back to the kitchen
Two years later war comes again; the kitchen boy gets leave and calls the old man, who gives him a horse, officer's clothes and a golden apple
The prince again destroys the enemy army and refuses the king's invitation
The princess begs for the golden apple, and in return lets him spend the night beside her bed
Three years later war comes once more; the old man gives him a better horse and an apple like the sun, foretelling that he will be wounded
The prince cuts down the whole enemy army but is wounded in the arm by a sabre
The king binds the wound with his own kerchief, gives him his ring as a keepsake and invites him to the palace, but the prince refuses and gallops off behind a hill
Back in the kitchen in his pigskin, he tells the others about the unknown lord who beat the enemy
The princess sees the shining apple and offers any money for it; he asks to spend the night on her bed, she agrees, and he sleeps there
Waking at noon, the prince sends for the king
The king comes, passes strange guards, and is welcomed by the prince, whom he recognises by the kerchief and ring as the victor of the three wars
The king embraces him and leads him to his daughter, who has long loved him, and they are betrothed
At the betrothal the prince tells the story of his banishment and the Brass Old Man
Three weeks later they hold a grand wedding
They visit the prince's parents, who had thought him lost and rejoice, and he tells his mother everything
Both sets of parents die and leave their kingdoms to the couple, and the Brass Old Man helps them till his death
A rich merchant selling goods to a tsar hears him complain that he can find no bride, and boasts of his beautiful daughter, who knows whatever anyone thinks
The tsar at once sends gendarmes with a letter ordering the merchant's daughter to come and be married
The daughter weeps and makes ready, and she and her maid, who looks exactly like her, dress alike and set off to the tsar
The spiteful maid invites her to walk on an island, puts her to sleep with a potion, cuts out her eyes and puts them in her pocket
The maid tells the gendarmes that her servant has wandered off to the sea, and they say they need only her
They reach the tsar, and he marries the maid
The tsar begins to think the merchant deceived him, since his wife is witless and can do nothing
The blind daughter comes to, hears an old man herding cattle, and asks him to take her in; he does
She has him drive the cattle off and sends him to buy velvet and silk on credit; only a poor shop will give it
She sends him to sleep and through the night sews a wonderful crown from the velvet and silk
In the morning she sends him to the tsar with the crown, telling him to ask for nothing but an eye
At the palace all marvel at the crown; the old man asks only for an eye, and the angry tsar threatens him with prison, then orders an eye cut from a captive soldier
The tsaritsa runs out and gives the tsar an eye, he thanks her, and gives it to the old man
The old man brings the eye home; the girl goes out at dawn, spits on it, puts it in and can see
She sends him to pay the debt and buy velvet and gold, sews a second crown, and sends him to ask again for an eye and to say God gave it to him
The tsar must have the crown; the tsaritsa gives him the other eye, and the old man, asked where he gets the crowns, says God gave them
The old man brings the eye home and the girl puts it in and sees with both eyes
After a night in the hut she suddenly finds herself in a glass house and holds festivities
The tsar comes to see the marvel; she welcomes and feasts him, and he invites her to visit him
The tsar praises the girl to his tsaritsa, who guesses it is the girl whose eyes she cut out
The tsar visits the girl again and invites her, to the tsaritsa's vexation
Before setting out, the girl gives the old man a chest of money that never empties and tells him she will be killed and cut to pieces, and that he must gather and bury her
The gendarmes take her to the palace, where the tsaritsa will not look at her
The tsaritsa orders the gendarmes to cut the girl to pieces on the way home and bring her her heart
The girl, knowing their purpose, tells them to cut her quickly; they cut her up, bury her in a dung heap and take her heart to the tsaritsa
The tsaritsa rolls the heart into an egg and puts it in her pocket
The old man wakes in his hut, weeps, makes a coffin, digs up all her pieces and buries them
The tsar rides to visit the girl, finds only a garden grown over her grave, and tells the tsaritsa
The tsaritsa orders the gendarmes to cut down the garden, and it turns to stone
The tsar goes to see the garden, finds a lovely little boy in it and takes him to the palace
The boy screams until the tsaritsa gives him the egg rolled from the heart; then he quiets and runs about
The boy runs out to the garden with the tsar following, and there the tsar finds the girl
The girl tells him she is his bride, the merchant's daughter, and his tsaritsa is her maid
At the palace the tsaritsa falls at her feet and begs forgiveness, but the girl reminds her she showed no mercy
The tsar has the gendarmes cut out the tsaritsa's eyes and tie her to horses, which drag her to pieces over the fields
The tsar and his young tsaritsa live happily
The old man and woman decide to marry their sons and send the eldest, Egorushko, to look for a bride
Egorushko walks a long time but finds no girl to his liking
Egorushko meets a three-headed dragon, who offers to lead him to a bride
The dragon brings him to a great stone and tells him to turn it over
Egorushko cannot move the stone, and the dragon tells him he gets no bride
Egorushko goes home and tells his parents everything
The parents send the middle son, Misha, and the same thing happens to him
Ivashko asks to go himself, and after refusing at first his parents let him
Ivashko meets the three-headed dragon, who offers to show him the way
Ivashko throws the stone from its place, uncovering a hole into the earth with straps beside it
The dragon tells him of three kingdoms below, and Ivashko is let down on the straps
Ivashko reaches the copper kingdom, where the maiden questions him and he rebukes her for not feeding him first
The maiden feeds him and he asks her to marry him
She refuses, sends him on to a fairer maiden in the silver kingdom and gives him a silver ring
In the silver kingdom the maiden questions him, he rebukes her, she feeds him and he asks her to marry him
She sends him on to the golden kingdom and gives him a gold ring
In the golden kingdom the maiden questions him, he rebukes her, she feeds him and he asks her to marry him
The golden maiden agrees, gives him a golden ball, and they set off together
On the way back they take along the maidens of the silver and copper kingdoms
They reach the hole, where Ivashko's elder brothers stand ready to climb down to look for him
Ivashko sends the three maidens up on the straps one after another, and the brothers haul them up
Ivashko sits on the straps himself, and the brothers, seeing it is him, cut the straps so as to keep the maidens
Ivashko falls back down
Ivashko weeps and walks on
Ivashko meets a tiny old man on a stump and tells him what has happened
The old man tells him to go to a hut and ask the long man lying there how to get out to Rus'
Ivashko reaches the hut and begs the mighty Idolishche not to destroy him but to tell him the way to Rus'
Idolishche sends him to Baba Yaga, who has an eagle that can carry him out
Ivashko reaches Baba Yaga's hut and asks her for the eagle
Baba Yaga tells him how to get the eagle and to feed it beef whenever it looks round
Ivashko does all she says, mounts the eagle and flies, feeding it meat each time it looks round
The meat runs out, and the eagle tears a piece of flesh from Ivashko's nape and eats it
The eagle carries Ivashko up through the hole to Rus'
The eagle spits out the flesh and tells Ivashko to put it back; he does, and his nape heals
Ivashko comes home, takes the golden maiden from his brothers, and they live together
A Black Sea dragon takes to flying into the tsar's garden
The dragon carries off the tsar's three daughters when they stay late in the garden
The tsar sends maids to look for them in the garden, but they do not find them
The tsar raises an alarm and promises as much money as anyone wants to whoever finds his daughters
A drunken soldier, Frolka the Sitter and Yeryoma come forward, agree terms with the tsar and set out
In a dense forest sleep overcomes them, but Frolka takes snuff and rouses the others to go on
They reach the house of a five-headed dragon, and Frolka breaks the door in with one knock
A maiden comes out and warns them the dragon will eat them, and Frolka boasts that they will eat him
The dragon flies in, Frolka answers his taunt and chooses to fight rather than make peace
Frolka cuts off all five heads at one stroke, puts them under a stone and buries the body
The maiden, a tsar's daughter, asks to go with them, feeds them and begs them to free her sisters
Frolka promises, and she tells them where her sisters are held
They reach the middle sister's palace, and Frolka knocks the iron gates open
A seven-headed dragon flies in, and Frolka cuts off all seven heads at one stroke and disposes of them
They find the middle princess, who treats them and begs them to rescue her youngest sister
At a steep ravine two chained lions roar so that Frolka's comrades fall in fright, but Frolka stays standing and leads them on
An old man meets them, warns them of the twelve-headed dragon, and on hearing their purpose offers to lead them in
The old man strokes the lions, and Frolka and his comrades slip into the yard
The old man takes them to the youngest princess, who treats them and makes ready to leave
As they leave, the twelve-headed dragon flies at them; the princess runs back inside and Frolka fights it
Frolka defeats the dragon, cuts off all twelve heads and throws them into the ravine
They feast, then fetch the other princesses and all return home
The tsar rejoices, opens his treasury and tells them to take as much money as they like
Frolka pours silver into his big hat, but it tears and the silver falls through into the mud
While there is money left, Yeryoma fills his basket and the soldier his knapsack, and they go home
Frolka stays by the treasury, filling his hat to this day
A great beast called Norka takes to raiding the tsar's menagerie, eating animals every night
The tsar cannot destroy it and promises half his kingdom to whichever son kills it
The eldest son sets out armed at night but spends the night drinking in a tavern
The middle son does the same, and the tsar scolds them
The youngest son, the fool whom all laugh at, takes weapons and keeps watch in the menagerie sitting on prickly turf to stay awake
After midnight Norka leaps the fence into the menagerie; the tsarevich goes at it and it flees
The tsarevich takes the best stallion from the stable, overtakes the beast and fights it, giving it three wounds
Both exhausted, they lie down to rest, and while the tsarevich sleeps the beast runs off
The horse wakes the tsarevich; twice more he overtakes the beast, gives it three wounds and loses it while resting
The fourth time, the beast reaches a white stone, lifts it and goes down to the other world, saying he will beat it only if he comes there
The tsarevich tells his father everything and asks for a leather rope long enough to reach the other world, and the tsar has it made
The tsarevich takes his brothers, servants and a year's supplies to the stone, where they build a palace and live
Neither brother can move the stone, but the youngest hurls it far away
Neither brother will go down after the beast; the youngest mocks them as cowards and tells them to lower him and to pull when the rope shakes
The brothers lower him into the other world
Below, a richly harnessed horse greets Ivan-tsarevich as long awaited, and he rides off on it
He reaches a copper palace, eats a meal laid ready and lies down to rest
A beautiful maiden comes and bids whoever is in her house to show himself; he comes out, and she rejoices and names him her husband
He tells her his purpose, and she says the beast is her brother, now at her middle sister's, and that she has healed his wounds
They feast, and he rides on to the second sister's silver palace, where he is entertained and told Norka is now at the youngest sister's
At the golden palace the youngest sister tells him Norka sleeps on the blue sea, gives him strong water and a sword-kladenets, and tells him to cut off the head at one blow
He finds Norka asleep on a stone in the middle of the sea and cuts off its head, which cries that it is lost and falls into the sea
He goes back and takes all three sisters with him, since they love him and will not part from him
Each sister turns her palace into an egg, teaches him how to turn an egg into a palace and back, and gives him the eggs
At the rope he seats the maidens and tugs it, and the brothers haul them up
Seeing the beauties, the brothers plot to cut the rope so that their brother is killed and cannot take the brides
The tsarevich guesses their plan and sends up a stone instead; the brothers haul it high and cut the rope, and the stone smashes
The tsarevich weeps and walks on
In a storm he shelters under a tree and covers the soaked fledglings in it with his clothes
The huge mother bird arrives, thanks him and offers him anything he asks; he asks to be carried out to this world
She tells him to make a big bin and fill it with game and water to feed her, and he does
She flies him out with the bin, takes her leave and flies away
Ragged and changed past recognition, the tsarevich hires himself out as a tailor's lad
The tailor tells him the two tsareviches are to marry brides from the other world who demand dresses like those they had there, made without measuring, and no master will take the work
The tsarevich sends the tailor to the tsar to take on the work, promising to answer for it, and the tsar gives the tailor money
At night the tsarevich goes out to the field, turns the eggs into palaces, takes dresses from them, turns the palaces back into eggs and hangs the dresses up at home
The tailor takes the dresses to the tsar, and the princesses recognise them, guess the tsarevich is alive, and keep silent
The tsarevich leaves the tailor and goes from master to master, a shoemaker and the rest, each of whom he sends to the tsar and who grows rich by him
The princesses get all they asked for but weep that the tsarevich does not come, and must go to their weddings
The youngest bride asks the tsar's leave to give alms to the beggars herself, and he grants it
Giving alms, she sees on a beggar the ring she gave the tsarevich and her sisters' rings, and recognises him
She leads him to the tsar and tells him this is their rescuer and that the brothers threatened to kill them if they told
The tsar, angered, punishes his elder sons
Three weddings are celebrated
The father sends his two sons to plough and tells them their sister will bring their dinner
The sister says she does not know the way, and the brothers tell her to follow the road where wood shavings lie
The brothers drive off, cutting shavings along the road
A dragon gathers up the shavings and scatters them along the road to his lair
The mother sends the daughter with the dinner, and she follows the shavings to the dragon's lair
The dragon seizes her and throws her into his lair
The brothers wait for dinner, then unyoke the oxen and go home, and learn that the sister was sent long ago
Next morning she is still missing, and the brothers set out to look for her
A cowherd tells them that if they want to win back their sister they must eat his biggest ox; they refuse and go on
A shepherd tells them to eat his biggest ram; they refuse and go on
A swineherd tells them to eat his biggest boar; they refuse and go on
The dragon tells them to eat twelve oxen, twelve rams and twelve boars if they want their sister; they eat a little and stop
The dragon puts the brothers under a stone
The weeping mother goes for water, and a pea rolls into her bucket unseen
At home she finds the pea and eats it, and from it a son is born, named Pokotygoroshko, who grows by the minute
At supper Pokotygoroshko asks whether she had other children, and she tells him of the lost daughter and sons
Pokotygoroshko decides to go after them, has a smith make him a great mace, pays him and sets out
The cowherd tells him to eat the biggest ox; he eats it, thanks him and goes on
The shepherd tells him to eat the biggest ram; he eats it, thanks him and goes on
The swineherd tells him to eat the biggest boar; he eats it, thanks him and goes on
At the dragon's house he greets his sister at the well, and she doubts he is her brother
The dragon comes out and tells him to eat twelve oxen, twelve rams and twelve boars, and he eats them all
The dragon asks whether they will fight or make peace, and Pokotygoroshko chooses to fight
Each blows on a threshing floor: the dragon's turns to cast iron, Pokotygoroshko's to copper
Pokotygoroshko strikes the dragon knee-deep into the ground with his mace, and kills him with a second blow
He hacks the dragon to pieces and winnows the ashes
He rolls the stone off his brothers and takes them and his sister home, and the parents rejoice
Ivan the fool, called Popyalov, after lying twelve years in the ashes, gets up and shakes six poods of ash off himself
A dragon has made it always night, with no day, in the kingdom where Ivan lives
Ivan offers to destroy the dragon and has his father make him a five-pood mace
Ivan throws the mace into the sky; next day it falls on his forehead and breaks in two
He has a ten-pood mace made and throws it up; it flies three days and breaks in three on his knee
He has a fifteen-pood mace made and throws it up; it flies six days and strikes his forehead, which gives way, and he says this mace will hold out against the dragon
Ivan rides out with his brothers to kill the dragon, and they stop at the dragon's hut on a hen's leg
Ivan hangs up his gloves and tells his brothers to run to his help if blood drips from them
Ivan sits under the bridge; a three-headed dragon rides up, and his horse stumbles and says it is because Ivan Popyalov sits under the bridge
The dragon calls Ivan out to try his strength; they fight, and Ivan kills him and sits under the bridge again
A six-headed dragon rides up, and Ivan kills him too
A twelve-headed dragon rides up; Ivan fights him and knocks off nine heads, and the dragon's strength gives out
A raven flies by crying "Blood!"; the dragon tells it to fly to his wife so she will eat Ivan, but Ivan tells it to fly to his brothers, promising it meat
The raven obeys Ivan and caws over the brothers, who wake and run to help him
They kill the dragon, take his head to his hut and break it open, and daylight comes over the whole kingdom
Riding home, Ivan finds he has forgotten his gloves, tells his brothers to wait and turns back for them
At the hut he finds the dragon's wife and daughters talking, turns himself into a cat and mews at the door, and they let him in
Ivan hears everything they say, snatches his gloves, runs back to his brothers, and they ride on
They come to a green meadow with silk cushions; the brothers want to rest there, but Ivan strikes the cushions with his mace and blood flows from them
They come to an apple tree with gold and silver apples; the brothers want to eat, but Ivan strikes the tree and blood flows from it
They come to a spring; the brothers want to drink, but Ivan strikes it and its water turns to blood, killing the last of the dragon's daughters
The dragon's wife flies after them with her jaws open from sky to earth to swallow Ivan, and Ivan and his brothers throw her three poods of salt
She swallows the salt thinking it is Ivan, tastes it, sees it is not, and chases them again
Ivan gallops off and hides in the smithy of Kuzma and Demyan behind twelve doors
The dragon's wife demands Ivan, and the smiths tell her to lick through the twelve doors and take him
She licks through the doors, and when she pushes her tongue into the smithy the smiths seize it with red-hot tongs and beat her to death with hammers
They burn her and scatter her ashes on the wind
Ivan and his brothers go home and live and feast
A childless king sends far and wide for anyone who can help his queen conceive, feasts those who come and questions them
No one can say, but a peasant's son takes it on, and the king gives him a handful of gold and three days
Not knowing what to say, the peasant's son meets an old woman, rebuffs her, then tells her his trouble
The old woman tells him the queen will conceive if she eats the golden-winged pike from the sea under the palace, caught in three silk nets
The peasant's son casts the nets; twice the pike tears them, but he ties them with his belt and kerchief and catches it the third time
He brings the pike to the king, who has it cooked for the queen
A cow drinks the slops from cleaning the pike, and a kitchen maid tastes a fin on the way to the queen
The cow, the maid and the queen all conceive in the same hour
The cow, the maid and the queen each give birth to a son, all three alike
The boys grow by the hour, feel their mighty strength and ask the king's leave to go walking in the town, which he gives with money
Ivan-tsarevich proposes that whoever throws a glass ball highest shall be eldest; Burya-bogatyr Ivan the cow's son throws his out of sight and claims to be eldest
Ivan-tsarevich is angry that a cow's son should be eldest
At the Black Sea, whoever can quiet a clucking sea-serpent is to be eldest; the two Ivans fail, but Burya shouts and throws his cane and the serpent is gone
Ivan-tsarevich refuses to be the younger, so Burya goes home alone and the other two wander on
The king has Burya thrown into prison and starved for three days
Burya pounds the wall and threatens to break out, and the king comes to him
Burya tells the king what happened and that only he can catch the brothers, who have gone to the land of the dragons
At the king's pleading, Burya takes a battle club and a sword-kladenets and sets out
Burya overtakes his brothers at the guelder-rose bridge by the Black Sea, where a post says three dragons ride out
Burya orders a hut on hen's legs to turn round; they go in, find a meal laid, eat and rest
Lots are cast for the night watch; it falls to Ivan the maid's son, and Burya warns him to spit on and smash a dancing jug, not watch it
The maid's son falls asleep, so Burya keeps watch himself and smashes the dancing jug
The six-headed dragon comes out of the sea, calls his horse and rides onto the bridge, and the horse stumbles, sensing Burya
Burya answers the dragon's taunt and they fight; Burya cuts off all six heads, throws the body into the sea and hides the heads under the bridge
Burya ties the dragon's horse to the sleeping maid's son's feet, lays the sword by his head and goes back to sleep in the hut
The maid's son wakes, finds the horse and boasts that God gave it to him for watching the jug
On the second night Ivan-tsarevich keeps watch, is warned, watches the dancing jug and falls asleep
Burya keeps watch himself, smashes the jug, and fights and kills the nine-headed dragon, disposing of the body and heads
Burya ties the dragon's horse to the sleeping tsarevich's feet and goes back to sleep
Ivan-tsarevich wakes, finds the horse and boasts that God gave him a better horse
On the third night Burya goes on watch himself, leaving his brothers cards, a candle and a towel, and telling them to run to his help when blood fills the plate
Burya smashes the jug, and the twelve-headed dragon rides onto the bridge; they agree not to strike a fallen man
Burya cuts off three heads, the dragon knocks him down, and on Burya's reminder lets him rise
They fight for hours; Burya cuts off three more heads each round until his club breaks
Burya throws his boots at the hut to wake his brothers, knocking it to pieces, but they sleep on
Burya throws a piece of his club through the stable door, and the two stallions run out and knock the dragon from the saddle
Burya cuts off the last three heads, disposes of the body and heads, stables the three horses and hides under the bridge
In the morning the brothers find the hut fallen apart and the plate full of blood, search three days for Burya, decide he is dead and get ready to ride home
Burya comes out from under the bridge and reproaches them for sleeping while he saved them, and they kneel and beg his pardon
Burya restores the hut by a spell, they eat and ride off
Burya says he has forgotten his whip and turns back alone, sends his horse into the meadows, turns into a fly and sits on the stove in the hut
Baba Yaga comes, and her three daughters-in-law, the dragons' widows, each tell her how she will destroy the brothers: as a meadow with a well and a bed, as a garden, as an old hut
Baba Yaga approves and says that if they fail she will turn into a sow and swallow all three herself
Burya flies out, becomes a man again, calls his horse, ties a bit of bast to a stick and rejoins his brothers, saying he cannot live without this whip
On a scorching day they reach a meadow with a bed and a well; the brothers want to rest, but Burya hacks the well and blood spurts out, and the heat breaks
At a beautiful garden the brothers want apples, but Burya cuts down every tree, and they are angry with him
At nightfall the brothers want to sleep in a hut, but Burya hacks it to pieces and blood spurts
At a fork in the road the brothers refuse to follow Burya and take the right-hand road, while he takes the left
In a village Burya has twelve smiths cover their smithy in iron, forge twelve iron rods and heat tongs red, and tells them what to answer the sow
A huge sow comes and demands the guilty one, and the smiths tell her to put her tongue into the smithy to receive him
The sow puts out her tongue; Burya seizes it with red-hot tongs and the smiths beat her with iron rods until her ribs show, and Burya breaks her ribs
The sow begs for mercy and, held by the ears, spits out the two brothers with their horses
Burya dashes the sow against the ground and she falls to pieces
The brothers kneel and admit their fault, and they ride on together
They pitch their tents in the forbidden meadows of the king of India, and the king sends his first minister to ask who they are
Burya tells the minister they have come to woo the princess for Ivan-tsarevich, and the king must give her or send his army
The princess refuses, and the king sends out his army, which frightens the two Ivans
Burya, cooking porridge, kills the whole army with two sweeps of his ladle, leaving one one-eyed and one blind man
Burya sends them to the king with the same demand, and the princess agrees to marry and asks for a carriage to be sent
The king receives Ivan-tsarevich and his brothers with honour and feasts them
Burya tells Ivan-tsarevich to let the princess go when she asks leave to go out
The princess asks leave to change, turns into a dove and flies to the sea, and Burya follows as a falcon
At the sea the princess asks her grandfather, who has a golden head, for three of his hairs to set the tsarevich a riddle, and flies home with them
Burya takes the princess's form, calls the grandfather out again and tears off his head
Burya flies back as an eagle ahead of the princess and gives the head to Ivan-tsarevich, telling him how to answer
The princess shows the tsarevich the three hairs and asks him to guess what root they come from, promising to marry him if he does
Ivan-tsarevich slams the head on the table as the root
The princess asks leave again and flies to the sea as a dove, and Burya sends the head back, where it grows onto its body
The princess questions her grandfather, who says he must have lost his head while she was last there, and she flies home and sits by the tsarevich
Next day Ivan-tsarevich and the princess are married
Burya gives the tsarevich three rods and persuades him to let Burya take his place in the bridal bed
In bed the princess lays her legs on Burya and tries to smother him with a pillow
Burya leaps up and beats her until he has broken the iron, copper and tin rods on her, and she swears never to do such things again
In the morning Burya tells Ivan-tsarevich his wife is tamed and bids them live happily and remember him
A childless tsar and tsaritsa pray for a child and go to sleep
They dream that the tsaritsa will conceive if she eats a gold-finned ruff from a pond near the palace, and the nurses judge the dream may come true
The tsar orders fishermen to catch the ruff, and they catch it with their first cast
The tsaritsa rewards the fishermen and gives the ruff to her cook, ordering that no one else touch it
The cook cleans and cooks the ruff; a cow drinks the slops, the tsaritsa eats the fish and the cook licks the dish
The tsaritsa, the cook and the cow all conceive and give birth at the same time to three sons: Ivan-tsarevich, Ivan the cook's son and Ivan Bykovich
The boys grow by the hour, all alike
In their tenth year they ask the tsar for a fifty-pood iron staff, and he has it forged
To decide who is eldest, each strikes the others with the staff; Ivan Bykovich drives his brothers into the ground up to their necks
They throw the staff into the air; Ivan Bykovich's stays up longest, and he is named eldest brother
In the garden Ivan Bykovich kicks away a huge stone the others cannot move, uncovering a cellar with three heroic horses and armour
The brothers ask the tsar's blessing to travel to foreign lands; he gives it with money, and they ride off
They make Baba Yaga's hut turn round and go in; Baba Yaga greets them rudely, and Ivan Bykovich rebukes her
Baba Yaga bows to Ivan Bykovich, and he tells her they are going to the guelder-rose bridge on the river Smorodina to fight the monsters, which she approves
They spend the night with Baba Yaga and ride on to the river Smorodina, where human bones lie everywhere, and stop in an empty hut
Ivan Bykovich proposes they keep watch in turn, and lots give the nights to Ivan-tsarevich, the cook's son and himself
On the first night Ivan-tsarevich goes on watch and falls asleep in the bushes
Ivan Bykovich, not trusting him, goes and stands under the bridge himself
The six-headed monster rides up, his horse stumbles, and he boasts that Ivan Bykovich is not yet born
Ivan Bykovich leaps out and challenges him; they fight and he cuts off three heads, refuses the monster a rest, and cuts off the rest
Ivan Bykovich hacks up the body, throws it in the river, puts the heads under the bridge and returns to the hut
In the morning Ivan-tsarevich claims nothing passed him in the night
On the second night the cook's son goes on watch and falls asleep, and Ivan Bykovich stands under the bridge himself
The nine-headed monster rides up and boasts; Ivan Bykovich leaps out and cuts off six heads, and the monster drives him knee-deep into the ground
Ivan Bykovich throws earth in the monster's eyes and cuts off the rest of its heads, and disposes of the body and heads
In the morning the cook's son claims nothing passed him, and Ivan Bykovich shows the brothers the heads under the bridge and shames them as sluggards
On the third night Ivan Bykovich hangs up a towel over a bowl and tells his brothers to stay awake and, if the blood runs over, let loose his horse and come to his help
The twelve-headed monster rides up and boasts; Ivan Bykovich leaps out and says he has come to fight to the death
Ivan Bykovich cuts off three heads, but the monster puts them back with his fiery finger and drives Ivan knee-deep into the ground
Ivan Bykovich asks for a breather, and the monster grants it; Ivan throws his right glove at the hut, breaking the windows, but the brothers sleep on
He cuts off six heads, which grow back, and is driven waist-deep; on a second breather he throws his left glove, which breaks through the roof, but the brothers sleep on
He cuts off nine heads, which grow back, and is driven shoulder-deep; on a third breather he throws his hat, which knocks the hut to pieces
The brothers wake, see the blood overflowing, loose the horse and hurry after it
The horse beats the monster with its hooves, while Ivan Bykovich climbs out of the ground and cuts off its fiery finger
Ivan Bykovich cuts off all the heads and throws the hacked body into the river
The brothers come running, and Ivan Bykovich reproaches them that he nearly lost his head through their sleeping
Next morning Ivan Bykovich turns into a sparrow and flies to a white stone palace, where an old witch feeds him grain and complains that he has killed her sons-in-law
The monsters' three wives promise revenge: one will become an apple tree, one a well, one a golden bed, each to kill whoever uses it
Ivan Bykovich flies back, becomes a man again, and the three brothers set off home
Starving, they come to an apple tree with gold and silver apples, and Ivan Bykovich rides ahead and hacks it so that blood spurts
He does the same to the well and the golden bed, and the monsters' wives perish
The old witch disguises herself as a beggar woman and begs from them on the road
At the tsarevich's urging, Ivan Bykovich offers her a gold piece, and she seizes his hand and vanishes with him
The brothers, finding him gone, gallop home in fear
The witch drags Ivan Bykovich underground to her husband, an old man who cannot see for his brows and lashes
Twelve mighty warriors lift the old man's brows and lashes with iron pitchforks, and he looks at Ivan Bykovich, who says he is ready for anything
The old man orders Ivan to fetch him the golden-haired tsaritsa from an unseen kingdom to marry, and Ivan privately thinks to have her himself
The old witch, enraged, ties a stone round her neck and drowns herself
The old man gives Ivan a club and tells him to call one ship out of an oak and then to close the oak, warning him not to forget
Ivan strikes the oak countless times and calls everything out, then sails off with a countless fleet of ships and boats following and thanking him
Five old men in boats ask to join him, saying they can eat bread, drink, steam in a bathhouse, read the stars and swim as a ruff, and he takes them all aboard
They reach the unseen kingdom, where countless loads of bread and barrels of drink have been prepared for Ivan Bykovich
The Eater and the Drinker devour all the bread and drink and shout for more, and the servants report to the tsaritsa that there is not enough
The tsaritsa has Ivan invited into a bathhouse heated for three months; Ivan refuses, and the old bath-steamer goes in and chills it to snow
Ivan Bykovich demands the golden-haired tsaritsa, and she comes out, gives him her hand and sails off with him
On the way the tsaritsa grows sad, turns into a star and flies into the sky
The star-reader turns into a star, finds the extra star and knocks it down, and it falls onto the ship and becomes the tsaritsa again
The tsaritsa turns into a pike and swims off, and the old man who swims as a ruff pricks her sides until she leaps back on the ship and becomes the tsaritsa
The old men take their leave and go home, and Ivan brings the tsaritsa to the monsters' father
The old man has his lashes lifted, looks at the tsaritsa and promises to pardon Ivan and let him go free
Ivan Bykovich says that whoever walks the pole across a deep pit he has made shall have the tsaritsa, and the old man tells him to go first
The tsaritsa wishes Ivan across lighter than swan's down, and he crosses without the pole bending
The old man steps onto the pole and falls into the pit
Ivan Bykovich takes the tsaritsa home, they are married and feast, and he boasts to his brothers
The tsar dreams that a horse with silver hair and a bright moon on its brow is tied to the golden ring of the post in his yard
The tsar proclaims that whoever explains the dream and gets the horse shall have his daughter and half the kingdom, but none of the lords can
The tsar is told of Ivan, a poor old man's son, and has him summoned
Ivan explains that it was no dream: a twelve-headed dragon came on that horse to carry off the princess
Ivan says he can get the horse when he is fifteen, and the tsar keeps him at the palace until then
At fifteen Ivan asks for a horse, but every horse in the tsar's stables falls under his hand, and the tsar lets him go to look for one in the open field
Ivan searches three years without finding one and heads back weeping
An old man asks why he weeps; Ivan answers rudely and drives him off, and the old man warns him
Ivan thinks better of it, runs after the old man, begs his pardon and tells him his trouble
The old man tells him of a mangy colt in a certain peasant's stable that will match his strength
Ivan lays his hand on the colt, which does not flinch, takes it from the peasant and feeds it up
Ivan rides to the tsar and tells how he got the horse, declines an army and takes six men for errands
They reach a fiery river with a bridge, pitch a tent in the forest and feast
Ivan has his companions keep watch by turns, but each gets drunk and sees nothing
Ivan keeps watch himself; at midnight a three-headed dragon rides over the bridge boasting that his only rival, Ivan, is nowhere near
Ivan leaps out from under the bridge, cuts off all three heads and takes the dragon's horse
On the next nights Ivan kills a six-headed and a nine-headed dragon and throws them into the fiery river
On the fourth night the twelve-headed dragon angrily calls Ivan out for killing his sons
Ivan gets leave to go to his tent first and tells his companions to come to him when the basin fills with blood
Ivan fights the dragon, cutting off heads at each clash while sinking deeper into the ground, until he is in up to his neck
The companions at last see the blood overflowing, run up, cut off the last head and pull Ivan out
Ivan takes the dragon's horse to the tent
Next morning Ivan turns into a cat, crosses the bridge to the dragons' house and makes friends with the cats
He hears the dragons' mother and three daughters-in-law plot to kill him as an apple tree, a well and a bed, and the mother to swallow them all with her jaws gaping from earth to sky
Ivan turns back into a man, returns to his companions and they set off
Struck by hunger, they find an apple tree; Ivan forbids them the apples and hacks it, and blood flows
Struck by thirst, they find a well, and Ivan hacks it, and blood flows
Struck by sleepiness, they find a bed on the road, and Ivan hacks it to pieces
They come to the jaws gaping from earth to sky and try to leap across, and only Ivan gets over, carried by his wonderful horse
At a river, a tiny man with seven-verst whiskers demands Ivan's horse and threatens to take it by force
Ivan threatens to trample him, but the tiny man knocks him down and rides off on the horse
In a hut Ivan grieves, and a man with no arms or legs tells him the tiny man ate his limbs for eating bread at his table
The cripple tells Ivan to run a ferry for three years and take no money from anyone if he wants his horse back
Ivan runs the ferry for three full years without pay
Three old men he ferries offer him money, ask why he refuses, and on hearing his story offer to get his horse back
The old men, Studenets, Obzhora and a sorcerer, draw a boat on the sand, and it flies them all to the tiny man's house on a stony mountain
Ivan asks for his horse, and the tiny man says he must steal the tsar's daughter and bring her to him
The old men leave Ivan and go to the tsar
The tsar has a bathhouse heated red hot to suffocate them, but Studenets cools it and they bathe
The tsar serves a huge dinner, and Obzhora eats it all
At night the old men steal the princess, give her to the tiny man and get back the horse
Ivan bows to the old men, mounts his horse and rides towards the tsar
Ivan wakes in his tent to find the princess beside him; she says she turned into a pin and stuck herself in his collar
She turns back into a pin, Ivan puts it in his collar and rides on
The tsar receives Ivan with honour and tells him his daughter has been stolen, and Ivan says he has brought her back
The princess turns back into a maiden, and Ivan leads her in to the tsar
The tsar takes the horse and gives his daughter to Ivan in marriage
A childless tsar asks a beggar what to do to have children
The beggar tells him to have seven-year-old girls spin and boys weave a net in one night, catch a gold-finned bream with it and give it to the tsaritsa to eat
The bream is caught and given to the kitchen; the cook throws the guts to a bitch, gives the slops to three mares, gnaws the bones, and the tsaritsa eats the fish
At the same time the tsaritsa, the cook and the bitch each bear a son and the three mares bear three foals
The tsar names the boys Tsarenko Ivan, Povarenko Ivan and Suchenko Ivan
The boys grow by the minute, and Suchenko sends Ivan-tsarevich to ask the tsar's leave to saddle the three foals and ride about the town, which he gives
Outside the town they decide to go to foreign lands, make themselves nine-pood maces and ride off
Suchenko says they need an eldest brother, and they shoot arrows to decide; Suchenko's arrow flies to the thrice-tenth kingdom, so he is made eldest
They come to a tent on the steppe, and Suchenko sends the tsarevich to see who is inside
Belyi Polyanin, lying in the tent, fells Tsarenko with a flick of his little finger and throws him under the bed
Suchenko sends Povarenko, and Belyi Polyanin fells him the same way and throws him under the bed
Suchenko goes himself and strikes Belyi Polyanin senseless with one blow, then carries him out
Belyi Polyanin revives in the fresh air and begs to be spared and taken as youngest brother, and Suchenko spares him
The four ride on and come to an empty two-storey house with a golden roof, stocked with food and drink, and settle there

Three brothers go hunting and leave Tsarenko at home; an old man in a mortar comes begging, and when Tsarenko gives him bread he seizes him, strips the skin off his back and throws him under the floor
The brothers return and ask Tsarenko whether anyone came, and he says no
Next day the old man does the same to Povarenko, who also says nothing
On the third day he does the same to Belyi Polyanin, who also says nothing
