On the fourth day Suchenko stays home; the old man seizes him, but the mortar breaks
Suchenko drags the old man to a willow stump, splits it and wedges the old man's beard in the crack
The brothers come home complaining of their backs, and Suchenko tells them what he has done to the old man
They go to look, but the old man has torn out the stump by its roots and carried it off to the other world
The brothers follow his tracks to a hatch in a mountain, open it, sound the depth with a stone on a rope, and tie Suchenko to the rope
Suchenko tells them to pull him up when he shakes the rope after three days, and they lower him into the other world
Suchenko recalls the three princesses carried off to the other world by three dragons and sets out to find them
At a two-storey house a girl questions him; he tells her to give him water, food and drink first, which she does, and she takes him to the princess
He tells the princess he has come for her and will fight her six-headed husband, and she hides him behind the door
The dragon flies in and smells a Russian; the princess puts him off, then asks what he would do if one of her kin came, and he says he would drink with him
Suchenko comes out, and the dragon asks whether he has come to fight or to make peace; Suchenko chooses to fight
Each blows a threshing floor: the dragon's is cast iron with silver hoops, Suchenko's silver with gold hoops
Suchenko kills the dragon with one blow, burns him to ash and scatters it on the wind, and the princess gives him a ring
At a second house he is questioned by a girl, fed, and taken to the second princess, who warns him of her nine-headed husband and hides him
The nine-headed dragon flies in and is put off by the princess, and Suchenko comes out and chooses to fight
Suchenko blows the better threshing floor, kills the dragon with one blow and burns him, and the princess gives him a ring
At a third house he is questioned by a girl, fed, and taken to the third princess, who warns him of her twelve-headed husband
Suchenko finds the twelve-headed dragon asleep, takes the dragon's forty-pood mace and kills him with one blow, burns him and scatters the ash
The princess gives him a ring and asks him to live with her, but he asks her to come with him
She turns all her riches into a golden egg and gives it to him, and they go back to her sisters, who turn their riches into silver and copper eggs and give them to him
At the hole Suchenko ties on the youngest princess, tells her to call out to Tsarenko that she is his, and shakes the rope
He sends up the second princess, telling her to call out to Povarenko that she is his
He sends up the third princess, telling her to keep silent and be his
The third princess keeps silent, and Belyi Polyanin, angered, cuts the rope as they haul Suchenko up
Suchenko falls, gets up, goes to the old man and says he has come to fight
They fight until they tire and run for water; the old man mistakenly gives Suchenko strong water and drinks plain water himself
Suchenko gains the upper hand, and the old man begs for mercy, telling him to take flint, steel and three kinds of hair from the cellar
Suchenko strikes a fire and singes the grey hair and the black hair, and a grey horse and a black horse come, but both are too slow to carry him out
He singes the red hair, and the red horse comes and carries him at once to his own land
Suchenko hires himself to a goldsmith as his helper
The youngest princess orders a gold wedding ring from the goldsmith, and Suchenko offers to make it for a sack of nuts
Suchenko eats the nuts, smashes the gold, takes out the princess's own ring, cleans it and gives it to the goldsmith
The princess sees the ring, recalls she gave one like it to Suchenko, and invites the goldsmith to her wedding
Suchenko calls the grey horse, climbs through its ears and becomes a handsome youth, and tears the chimney off the wedding house, and the wedding breaks up
The second princess orders a ring; Suchenko makes it the same way for two sacks of nuts, and she invites the goldsmith to her wedding
Suchenko calls the black horse, becomes handsome, and tears the roof off the wedding house; people shoot at the horse and miss, and the wedding breaks up
The eldest princess, who must marry Belyi Polyanin, orders a ring; Suchenko makes it for three sacks of nuts, and she recognises her own ring and invites the goldsmith to her wedding
Suchenko calls the red horse and tears off the ceiling of the wedding house as he rides there
Riding back, he seizes Belyi Polyanin by the forelock, lifts him high and throws him down, and Belyi Polyanin is smashed to pieces
Suchenko comes down and embraces his bride, the tsarevich and Povarenko rejoice, and all three marry the princesses and live happily
The king shuts his three beautiful daughters away in underground chambers
The princesses read in a book of the wide world and tearfully beg their father to let them out into the garden
The king tries to dissuade them but at last gives in
The princesses rejoice in the garden, and a whirlwind snatches them up and carries them off
The nurses run to tell the king, who sends his servants everywhere with a promise of reward, but they come back with nothing
The king asks his council three times who will find his daughters, offering any princess in marriage, and the boyars are silent
The king weeps and has a call proclaimed through the realm for anyone of the common people to take the task on
A poor widow's three mighty sons, Vechorka, Polunochka and Zorka, born in one night, hear the call, take their mother's blessing and ride to the capital
They offer to find the princesses, asking only that the king care for their mother, and the king takes her into the palace
After three months' riding they come to an empty hut by a forest and stay there
Zorka leaves Vechorka at home to cook while the other two hunt, and Vechorka slaughters and roasts the best ram from the fold
A tiny old man with an elbow-long beard bursts in and angrily asks how he dares slaughter his ram, and Vechorka mocks him
The old man beats Vechorka half to death with a crust of bread, throws him under the bench, eats the ram and goes into the forest
The brothers return, and Vechorka tells them he got a headache from the heat of the stove
Next day Polunochka stays home, roasts a ram, and is beaten half to death by the old man, who eats the ram and leaves
Polunochka tells the brothers he was overcome by the fumes
On the third day Zorka stays home and roasts a ram, and the old man comes, counts his sheep, finds one missing and strikes Zorka on the head
Zorka leaps up and drags the old man about by his beard, and the old man begs for his life
Zorka wedges the old man's beard into an oak post with an iron wedge and waits for his brothers
Zorka leads his brothers out to see the "fumes" he has caught, but the old man has escaped, leaving half his beard and a trail of blood
Following the trail, the brothers reach a deep chasm; Zorka makes a bast rope and has his brothers let him down
In the other world Zorka unties himself and comes to a copper palace, where the youngest princess asks why he has come and he tells her
The princess feeds him and gives him a phial of strong water, and drinking it he feels great strength
A wind rises, and the princess hides Zorka in another room
The three-headed dragon flies in and smells a Russian, and the princess puts him off
The princess gives the dragon food and drink laced with a sleeping potion, and he falls asleep with his head in her lap
The princess calls Zorka, who cuts off all three heads, burns the dragon and scatters the ash
Zorka takes leave of the princess, promising to return for her when he has found her sisters
At a silver palace Zorka kills a six-headed dragon, where the middle princess lives
At a golden palace Zorka kills a twelve-headed dragon and frees the eldest princess
The eldest princess rolls her golden kingdom into an egg and goes with Zorka for her sisters, who roll up their kingdoms likewise
At the chasm Vechorka and Polunochka pull Zorka and the three princesses up into the world
Back in their own kingdom the princesses roll their eggs across a field, and the copper, silver and golden kingdoms appear
The king rejoices and marries Zorka, Vechorka and Polunochka to his daughters
At his death the king makes Zorka his heir
A childless old man sends his wife to buy a turnip for dinner, and she buys two
They eat one and put the other in the oven to steam, and a voice cries from the oven
The old woman opens the oven and finds a live girl, whom they joyfully name Repka
Repka grows up, and the village girls beg the old woman to let her go berrying with them, promising not to abandon her
The old woman lets her go, and the girls wander deep into the forest to a hut where a bear sits
The bear feeds them porridge, saying he will marry whichever does not eat, and Repka alone does not eat
The bear sends the others home, keeps Repka and makes her rock him in a sledge hung from the ceiling
Repka sings "bye-bye, old horseradish", and the bear makes her sing "bye-bye, dear friend"
Repka lives with the bear nearly a year and becomes pregnant
When the bear goes hunting and blocks the door with oak stumps, Repka struggles free and runs home
Repka gives birth to a son, half man and half bear, who is christened Ivashko-Medvedko
Ivashko grows by the hour, and at fifteen tears off the arms and heads of the boys he plays with
The villagers demand that the old man send Ivashko away
Ivashko asks the grieving old man why he is sad, hears the reason, and asks for a twenty-five-pood iron club
The old man makes the club, and Ivashko takes leave of his grandparents and sets off at random
At a wide river Ivashko meets Usynya, who dams it with his mouth and catches fish with his whiskers, and Usynya asks to come along
They meet Gorynya, who is carrying a mountain into a ravine; he praises Ivashko's strength, learns who he is and joins them
They meet Dubynya, who is levelling oak trees; he too praises Ivashko and joins them
In a dense forest Ivashko orders a hut on a hen's leg to turn round, and they find it empty with poultry in the yard
Ivashko proposes casting lots for who stays home while the others hunt, and the lot falls on Usynya
While Usynya combs his curls, Baba Yaga rises from under a stone in her iron mortar, demanding food and drink
Usynya invites her in and serves her; she gives the second helping to her dog and complains of his hospitality
Baba Yaga beats Usynya under the bench with her pestle, cuts a strap of skin from his back, eats everything and leaves
Usynya tells the returning brothers he cooked nothing because of the stove fumes
Next day Baba Yaga does the same to Gorynya, who also blames the fumes
On the third day she does the same to Dubynya, who also blames the fumes
On the fourth day Ivashko stays home; Baba Yaga comes, eats, complains and starts beating him
Ivashko wrests the pestle from her, beats her half to death, cuts three straps from her back and locks her in the storeroom
Ivashko serves the brothers a big dinner, and they marvel that Baba Yaga did not come to him
In the bathhouse the brothers hide their backs, and Ivashko makes them confess what Baba Yaga did
Ivashko takes their straps of skin back from Baba Yaga and puts them on their backs, which heal at once
Ivashko hangs Baba Yaga by the leg from the gate and has the four of them shoot at the rope; only Ivashko cuts it
Baba Yaga falls, jumps up, lifts a stone and escapes underground
None of the others can lift the stone, but Ivashko kicks it aside, uncovering a hole
No one else will go down, so Ivashko sets up a post with a bell on the rope and tells them to pull him up when he rings
The brothers lower him; the rope falls short, so he ties on Baba Yaga's three straps and reaches the other world
At a palace three beautiful maidens warn him that their mother, Baba Yaga, will eat him
They tell him to wake her gently with two golden apples on a silver dish, and while she eats to seize her sword and cut off her head with a single blow
Ivashko does so and cuts off Baba Yaga's head
Ivashko takes the maidens to the hole, sends up the eldest calling her Usynya's wife, and the second calling her Gorynya's wife, and they are hauled up
He sends up the youngest, calling her his own wife
Dubynya, angered, cuts the rope with his club as they haul Ivashko up
Ivashko falls and is badly hurt, and sits three days without food or drink
Ivashko eats and drinks his fill in Baba Yaga's storerooms, finds an underground passage and comes out into the world
In a field he finds his bride herding cattle; she tells him her sisters are marrying the heroes, and Dubynya has set her to herd cows because she will not marry him
In the evening Ivashko follows her home, where the three heroes sit feasting, and asks them for a glass of wine
Ivashko drinks three glasses, his heroic heart flares, and he kills all three heroes with his club and throws their bodies to the beasts
Ivashko takes his bride back to the old man and woman, and they hold a merry wedding
A priest rides to a village twelve versts off to give a man communion, is well entertained, and forgets to get a present for his daughter
On the road home the priest sees a human head burning away to ash and puts the ash in his pocket to take home and bury
At home his daughter helps him from his horse, and as his head aches she puts him to bed
Thinking he has brought her a present, the daughter feels in his pocket, where the ash has turned into a little casket
Not knowing how to open it, she licks the casket and conceives
The daughter's pregnancy advances by the hour, she gives birth to a son, and he is christened Nadzei the priest's grandson
Nadzei grows by the hour, and at six weeks plays ball in the street, knocking off the other children's legs, arms and heads
The children's fathers beg the priest not to let his grandson out to play
The priest keeps Nadzei in until summer, when the grown boy asks what work they will do, and the delighted priest proposes clearing a forest plot
In the marsh Nadzei asks his grandfather's blessing instead of letting him start, and by noon fells a desyatina and a half of forest
Nadzei says they need not burn the felled trees, and in three days the plot is ready; they sow it and a marvellous crop of oats grows
A bear takes to eating the oats, and the priest, finding much eaten, tells his grandson a wild horse is spoiling the crop
Nadzei, angry at the damage to his labour, makes a halter, eats, and goes to sit on a stump in the middle of the field to keep watch
The bear comes out of the forest and grazes the oats, and Nadzei marvels at this strange horse
The bear comes right up to Nadzei, taking him for a stump, and Nadzei seizes it by the ears and presses it to the ground
Nadzei bridles the bear with the halter and leads it home, the bear tearing up trees by the roots on the way, and ties it to a post in the yard
The grandfather is horrified, and they marvel; Nadzei asks what work to give the horse, and the grandfather tells him to haul firewood
Nadzei harnesses the bear to a cart and in three days hauls so much firewood that it blocks the whole village
The church clerks complain to the priest and ask him to send his grandson away
The priest tells Nadzei to go wherever he likes, and Nadzei says he would have gone long ago had he been told
Nadzei asks his mother to bake him a loaf, and she bakes it and packs it in his bag
Nadzei asks his mother's and grandfather's blessing and sets out, travelling seven days through forests and bogs to the thrice-tenth kingdom
Nadzei meets Gorynya the warrior digging mountains with his foot and praises his strength
Gorynya says his strength is nothing to that of Nadzei the priest's grandson, and Nadzei reveals that he is Nadzei
Gorynya asks Nadzei to take him as his younger brother, and Nadzei takes him
Together they travel far, defeat many warriors and capture many towns
Afterwards they marry and live richly
A decree comes from the tsar that whoever builds a ship that can fly shall marry the princess
The two clever elder brothers decide to try their luck, and their mother gives them white bread, meat and vodka and sends them off
The fool begs to go too; his mother tries to dissuade him, then gives him black bread and a flask of water and sends him off
The fool meets an old man and tells him he is going to win the princess, though he cannot build a flying ship
The old man bids him share his food, and when the fool unties his bag the black bread has become white rolls and the water vodka
They eat and drink, and the old man tells him how to get a ready ship from the first tree in the forest and to take aboard everyone he meets
The fool thanks him, goes to the forest, crosses himself three times, strikes the first tree with his axe and falls asleep face down
Someone wakes him, he sees a ready ship, gets in, and it flies off through the air
The fool takes aboard a man lying with his ear to the ground, listening to what goes on in the other world
He takes aboard a man hopping on one leg, who could cross the world in one stride with the other untied
He takes aboard a marksman who shoots at game a thousand versts away
He takes aboard the Eater, for whom a sack of bread is not one bite
He takes aboard the Drinker, for whom a lake is not one gulp
He takes aboard a man with a bundle of firewood that becomes an army when scattered
He takes aboard a man with a sack of straw that brings frost when scattered
The ship lands at the tsar's palace, and the tsar sends a servant to find out who has come
The servant reports that the ship holds only peasants, and the tsar decides to get rid of such a son-in-law by setting hard tasks
The tsar orders the fool to bring healing and living water before the tsar's dinner is over, and the listener overhears and tells the fool
The fool despairs, but the swift runner promises to do it, and the fool tells the servant he will bring it
The runner unties his leg and fetches the water in a moment, but sits down under a mill to rest and falls asleep
The listener hears him asleep under the mill, and the marksman shoots at the mill and wakes him
The runner brings the water before the tsar rises from table
The tsar orders the fool and his comrades to eat twelve roast oxen and twelve sacks of bread at one sitting, and the Eater eats it all and asks for more
The tsar orders forty barrels of wine drunk, and the Drinker drinks them all and asks for more
The tsar orders the fool to wash before the wedding in an iron bathhouse heated red-hot to suffocate him
The man with the straw goes in with the fool, they are locked in, and he scatters the straw so that it freezes
The fool spends the night on the stove, and in the morning is found alive and singing
The tsar orders the fool to raise a whole regiment by the morrow, and the fool despairs, but the man with the firewood reassures him
The fool tells the servant he will do it, and that if the tsar still refuses he will conquer his kingdom and take the princess by force
At night the man with the firewood scatters it over the field, and a countless army appears
In the morning the tsar, frightened, sends the fool rich clothes and invites him to the palace to marry the princess
The fool dresses in them and becomes a handsome youth
The fool marries the princess, receives a large dowry and becomes wise and quick
The tsar and tsaritsa come to love him, and the princess dotes on him
A peasant, worn out by his seven idle sons, all named Semyon, takes them to the tsar and puts them all into his service
The tsar thanks him and asks the eldest Semyon what he can do, and he says he can steal
The second Semyon says he can forge all kinds of precious things
The third Semyon says he can shoot a bird on the wing
The fourth Semyon says he can swim like a dog to fetch what the marksman shoots
The fifth Semyon says he can see from a high place into all kingdoms and tell what goes on there
The sixth Semyon says he can knock a ship together in a trice
The seventh Semyon says he can heal people
Long afterwards the tsar tests the seer Semyon, who climbs up high and tells what is happening everywhere, and it agrees with the newspapers
The tsar wishes to marry a certain princess, summons the seven Semyons, orders them to fetch her and gives them soldiers
The Semyons build a ship in a trice and sail off
Near the princess's kingdom the seer looks out from the mast and says the princess is alone and can be stolen
The smith forges precious things and goes with the thief to sell them
The thief steals the princess
They cut the anchors and sail away
The princess, seeing she is being carried off, turns into a white swan and flies from the ship
The marksman shoots her in the left wing
The swimmer leaps into the sea, seizes the swan and brings her aboard
The swan turns back into the princess with her left arm wounded, and the healer heals it at once
They reach home safely and fire a cannon
The tsar, who has forgotten the Semyons, sends to find out what ship it is, rejoices at the news and has them met with honour
The princess will not marry the tsar, who is old, and when he asks whom she wants, she names the one who stole her, the thief Semyon
The tsar without another word has them married
The tsar retires, sets Semyon in his place and makes all his brothers great boyars
A dragon appears near Kiev and exacts a tribute of a girl from every household, whom he eats
When the tsar's daughter's turn comes, the dragon carries her off to his lair but, as she is beautiful, takes her for his wife instead of eating her
The tsar and tsaritsa write to the princess, by way of her little dog, asking her to find out who is stronger than the dragon
The princess grows kinder to the dragon and keeps asking, and at last he lets slip that Kozhemyaka in Kiev is stronger than he
The princess writes to her father to find Nikita Kozhemyaka in Kiev and send him to free her
The tsar finds Nikita and goes himself to ask him to free the land from the dragon and rescue the princess
Nikita, frightened at the sight of the tsar, trembles and tears the twelve hides he is holding
However the tsar and tsaritsa plead, Nikita will not go against the dragon
They gather five thousand small children, who tearfully beg Nikita to go, and Nikita weeps too
Nikita wraps himself in three hundred poods of tarred hemp, so the dragon cannot eat him, and goes against the dragon
The dragon locks himself in, and Nikita threatens to tear the lair apart and starts breaking the doors
The dragon comes out into the open field, and after a long fight Nikita throws him down
The dragon begs Nikita not to kill him and proposes that they divide the whole world between them
Nikita agrees but says a boundary must be ploughed
Nikita makes a three-hundred-pood plough, harnesses the dragon to it and ploughs a furrow from Kiev to the Caspian Sea
The dragon says they have divided the land, and Nikita says they must divide the sea too
The dragon goes out into the middle of the sea, and Nikita kills him and drowns him there
Nikita takes nothing for his work and goes back to currying hides
A dragon flies to a village and devours all its people but one peasant
A Gypsy arrives in the empty village in the evening and finds the last peasant weeping
The peasant warns the Gypsy that the dragon will come in the morning and eat them both
The Gypsy says the dragon may choke, and stays the night to see it
The dragon arrives in a storm and gloats that he will breakfast on two men
The Gypsy calls the dragon a liar and boasts that he is the stronger
The dragon challenges him to a trial of strength
The dragon crushes a millstone to sand in one hand
The Gypsy squeezes a bundle of curds until whey runs, passing it off as squeezing water from a stone
The dragon concedes and proposes a whistling contest
The dragon whistles so that the leaves fall from every tree
The Gypsy tells the dragon to blindfold himself lest his eyes pop out at the Gypsy's whistle
The dragon believes him and binds his eyes
The Gypsy strikes the dragon on the head with a cudgel
The dragon begs him to stop and proposes that they become sworn brothers, the Gypsy the elder
The dragon sends the Gypsy to drag home the fattest ox from the herd
The Gypsy ties the oxen together by their tails, claiming he will drag fifty home at once
The dragon grows impatient, skins the fattest ox himself and carries the meat home
The dragon sends the Gypsy to fetch water in the oxhide
The Gypsy, unable to carry even the empty hide, digs around the well, claiming he will bring the whole well
The dragon fills the hide at the well himself and carries it home
The dragon sends the Gypsy to drag a dry oak from the forest
The Gypsy twists a long rope and winds it round the oaks, claiming he will pull twenty at once
The dragon uproots the thickest oak himself and drags it home
The Gypsy pretends to be offended and refuses to eat
The dragon eats a whole ox and drinks a hideful of water
The dragon asks what offends him and offers to make peace
The Gypsy demands, as the price of peace, that the dragon come visit him
The dragon harnesses a troika and they drive together to the Gypsy camp
The Gypsy's children run out shouting that their father has brought a dragon
The Gypsy tells the frightened dragon that his hungry children will set upon him
The dragon leaps from the cart and runs away
The Gypsy sells the troika and cart and lives in plenty
A peasant's eldest son hires himself to a harsh merchant, lasts a week and comes home
The middle son does the same and quits after a week
The youngest son asks his father's leave to go, is mocked as a fool, and goes anyway
The youngest son hires himself to the merchant for a year, asking as wages one flick for the merchant and one pinch for his wife
The merchant agrees, glad to have hired him so cheaply
In the evening the labourer tucks the rooster's head under its wing and sleeps until sunrise, the rooster not having crowed
He does the same on the next two nights
The puzzled merchant sets out to find another rooster, taking the labourer with him
They meet four peasants leading a huge bull to slaughter
The labourer kills the bull with a flick and strips off its hide with a pinch
The frightened merchant forgets the rooster, goes home and takes counsel with his wife
The wife proposes sending the labourer into the forest at night to be eaten by wild beasts
The wife tells the labourer that a cow is missing and sends him into the forest
The labourer finds a bear in its den, takes it for the cow and beats it with his cudgel
He drags the bear home by the neck and shuts it in the shed with the cows
The bear kills all the cows during the night
In the morning the labourer says he found the cow, and the merchant and his wife find the cows dead and scold him
The labourer kills the bear with a flick
The merchant sends the labourer to the devils' mill to collect a debt the devils owe him
The labourer drives to the mill, sits on the dam and twists a rope
A devil jumps out of the water and the labourer says he will drag the devils out to dry in the sun
The labourer demands that the devils pay his master's debt
The devil dives to ask his chief
The labourer digs a deep pit, covers it with brushwood and sets his hat with a hole cut in it over it
The devil returns and asks how he can drag devils from bottomless pools
The labourer ties the ends of his rope together and the devil measures it without finding an end
The labourer names the debt as a hatful of silver
The chief devil reluctantly pays, and the labourer brings a cartload of silver to the merchant
The merchant and his wife agree to run away from home, and she bakes pies and bread and fills two sacks
The labourer empties the sacks, puts millstones in one and climbs into the other
At night the merchant and his wife run off with the sacks on their backs
The labourer calls from the sack to wait for him, and they run faster still
At a lake the merchant throws down his sack and the labourer complains from inside it
They lie down on the shore, the merchant planning to throw the labourer into the lake when he sleeps
While they sleep the labourer dresses the wife in his own coat and cap, puts on hers, and wakes the merchant
The merchant and the labourer throw the sleeping wife into the lake
The labourer reproaches the merchant for drowning his wife
The merchant goes home with the labourer, who serves out the year
The labourer gives the merchant a flick on the forehead, killing him
The labourer takes the merchant's property and lives well
In a year of famine the labourer Shabarsha comforts his worried master
Shabarsha goes to the mill dam to fish, begs hemp from the miller and twists a line
A little devil jumps out of the water and asks what he is doing
Shabarsha says he means to clean out the pond and drag the devils out
The little devil dives to tell his grandfather
Shabarsha digs a pit and sets over it his hat with the crown cut out
The little devil returns to bargain, and Shabarsha asks for his hat filled with gold and silver
The little devil returns: the grandfather wants him first to wrestle Shabarsha
Shabarsha says he could not beat even his middle brother Mishka, and sends him to the bear in the ravine
The little devil strikes the bear with a cudgel and the bear crushes him
He tears himself free and reports to the grandfather
The grandfather sends him to race Shabarsha
Shabarsha says his little brother the hare will outrun him, and sends him to the hare
The little devil touches the hare's ear and the hare leaves him far behind
He reports his defeat to the grandfather
The grandfather sends him to try who whistles louder
The little devil whistles so that Shabarsha barely keeps his feet and the leaves fall
Shabarsha tells the little devil to lie face down and stop his ears
The little devil does so, and Shabarsha strikes him on the neck with a cudgel while whistling
He reports the blow to the grandfather
The grandfather sends him with his iron cudgel to try who throws it higher
The little devil throws the cudgel high into the sky
Shabarsha waits for a cloud, saying he will throw the cudgel up to his brother the smith
The little devil snatches the cudgel back and dives to his grandfather
The frightened grandfather orders money carried out to buy Shabarsha off
The little devil carries money but the hat over the pit stays empty
The little devil empties the grandfather's last chest and at last fills the hat
Shabarsha lives gloriously ever after
A rich peasant's wife goes into the forest for mushrooms, gets lost and wanders into a bear's den
The bear keeps her and she bears him a son, half man and half bear, whom she names Ivanko Medvedko
Ivanko grows up and he and his mother run away to the village while the bear is at the beehives
The peasant rejoices at his wife's return, and she tells him all about the bear and the son
The peasant tells Ivanko to kill the sheep that looks at him
Ivanko shouts at the sheep, they all look at him, and he kills and skins them all
The peasant scolds him and Ivanko answers that every sheep looked at him
The peasant orders Ivanko to store the meat and skins and guard the barn door at night
In a storm Ivanko breaks the barn door off, takes it to the bathhouse and sleeps there
Thieves and dogs carry off everything in the open barn
The peasant finds the barn empty and Ivanko in the bathhouse, and scolds him
Ivanko answers that he guarded the door, which nobody stole
The peasant, wanting to be rid of him, sends Ivanko to twist ropes of sand at a lake full of devils
Ivanko sits on the shore twisting ropes of sand, and a little devil jumps out of the water
Ivanko says he will wrinkle the lake and torment the devils for not paying rent
The little devil dives to tell his grandfather
He returns: the grandfather will pay if Ivanko outruns him, and otherwise Ivanko is to be dragged into the pool
Ivanko says his grandson born yesterday will outrun him, and starts up a hare
The hare runs off and the little devil falls far behind
Ivanko offers to race him himself on pain of death, and the little devil dives away
The little devil brings his grandfather's iron staff: whoever throws it higher wins
The little devil throws the staff so high it is barely seen and it sinks half into the earth
Ivanko cannot stir the staff, but says he will wait for a cloud and throw it onto it
The little devil snatches the staff and dives into the water
The little devil returns: whoever carries a horse round the lake more times wins
The little devil carries the horse round the lake ten times and tires
Ivanko rides the horse round the lake until it drops dead
The little devil admits defeat and asks how much rent to pay
Ivanko asks for his hat filled with gold and a year's service as his labourer
Ivanko cuts out the bottom of the hat and sets it over a deep pit
The little devil carries gold all day until the hat is full
Ivanko loads a cart with the gold and drives it home with the little devil in harness
Ivanko gives his father the gold and the devil as a labourer
A soldier, discharged after his service, sets out for home and lodges with a poor old woman in a capital
The old woman tells him that a rejected foreign prince set an unclean power on the tsar's daughter, which has tormented her for three years
The soldier goes to the palace to try his luck and is brought to the tsar
The soldier offers to cure the princess, and the tsar promises to shower him with gold
The soldier asks for iron bullets, walnuts, candles, cards, an iron rod, an iron scraper and an iron man with springs
The soldier locks and crosses every window and door but one and stands guard at it
At midnight a devil flies round the palace, finds the open door and, in human shape, asks to be let in
The devil asks for nuts and the soldier gives him an iron bullet, which he cannot crack, while the soldier eats twenty nuts
The devil proposes cards, and they agree to play for flicks
The devil wins three flicks, but the soldier makes him play on to ten
The soldier wins ten flicks from the devil
The devil begs to be flicked gently and offers money instead
The soldier offers to have his younger brother deliver the flicks, and the devil accepts
The soldier leads the devil to the iron man and flicks him with it three times, hurling him across the room
The devil smashes through the window and flees
The princess tells the tsar she spent a quiet night
Over thirteen nights thirteen devils come in turn, and the soldier treats each the same
Their grandfather Satan goes to the palace himself
The soldier beats Satan at cards and leads him to his younger brother
The iron man clasps Satan tight and the soldier flogs him with the iron rod and scrapes him with the scraper
Satan tears himself free and flees to his swamp, groaning to his grandsons
The devils resolve to buy the soldier out of the palace with gold
The devils come to the soldier, who pretends to call his brother, and they offer him gold to leave
The soldier refuses the gold but promises to leave if they all climb into his knapsack
The devils all climb into the knapsack, Satan on top, and the soldier buckles and crosses it
The soldier has the tsar make thirty iron hammers, and the smiths beat the knapsack on the anvil
The soldier reports to the tsar that the princess will be troubled no more
The tsar thanks him and lets him carouse a month at the treasury's expense
The soldier declines the tsar's offer to stay and is sent home with a carriage, horses and boundless money
On the way he meets a comrade from his regiment and goes to buy wine, leaving his knapsack with him
The comrade takes the knapsack into his hut and tells the women not to touch it
The women unbuckle the knapsack and the devils burst out and run
The devils meet the soldier coming back, take fright, and hide forever in the pool under a mill
The soldier scolds the women and carouses with his comrade
The soldier comes home and lives rich and happy
A soldier on leave walks home, finds a stream and soaks three rusks in it
He sits by the stream playing his fiddle, and the devil comes to him in the shape of an old man with a book
The devil offers to trade his book for the fiddle, saying anyone can read it
The illiterate soldier finds he can read the book and trades away his fiddle
The devil cannot play the fiddle and begs the soldier to stay three days and teach him, promising to take him home in a day by troika
The devil feasts the soldier on fine food and drink
The soldier agrees to stay and teaches him for three days
The devil drives him home by troika in a flash
At home the soldier learns he has been away three years and is counted a deserter
Frightened, he blames the devil, who appears and offers to make him happy
The devil makes him a merchant with a great shop in the capital
The devil leaves, saying he will go and torment Princess Marya in a far kingdom
The soldier prospers and the other merchants grow envious and come to question him
He puts them off until the next day
He takes his money and slips out of the city by night for the far kingdom
At the frontier he tells the sentry he is a doctor come to cure the king's sick daughter
The king promises him his daughter if he cures her
The soldier asks for cards, wine, spirit, nuts, lead bullets and candles
He buys a fiddle and carouses and plays in the princess's rooms
At midnight the devil comes to the music and the soldier gives him strong spirit instead of kvass
The soldier gives him lead bullets for nuts and the devil breaks his teeth on them
They play cards until the cocks crow and the devil vanishes
The princess tells the king she slept peacefully
The second night passes the same way
The soldier has the king forge fifty-pood pincers and rods of copper, iron and tin
The devil comes again and asks about the pincers
The soldier says he straightens crooked fingers of fiddlers in them, and the devil asks to have his own straightened
The devil puts both hands in the pincers and the soldier clamps them and flogs him with the rods
The devil begs for mercy, promising not to come within thirty versts of the palace
The devil tears free and threatens to seize the soldier if he ever goes thirty versts from the city, then vanishes
The soldier marries the princess
The king dies and the soldier becomes king
His queen praises a garden thirty versts from the city
The new king drives there with the queen
The devil meets him and says he will not escape now
The king asks leave to say goodbye to his young wife, and the devil tells him to be quick
A peasant is taken as a soldier and leaves his pregnant wife fifty roubles to keep for the child
His wife bears twin boys and names them both Ivan, soldier's sons
At ten the twins are sent to school and outdo the children of boyars and merchants
The envious children beat and pinch the twins every day
The twins agree to stand by each other and beat all their tormentors
The watchmen bind them and put them in jail
The tsar questions them and orders them released as not to blame
Grown up, the twins ask their mother for their father's money to buy horses
The mother gives them fifty roubles and bids them bow to everyone they meet
At the horse fair they find no horse worth buying until they see two stallions chained to posts
The owner mocks them, and the brothers knock the stallions over with their knees, breaking the chains
The stallions run loose into the field, and the brothers take pity on the owner, call them back and chain them again
On the way home they pass an old man without greeting him, then run after him and bow
The old man leads them to a mountain and gives them heroic horses from behind an iron door
The brothers ride home, and their mother weeps that they will not be her providers
The brothers go to a smith for swords of three hundred poods, and he cannot make them
The old man meets them again and gives them two heroic swords from the mountain
Their mother sees the swords and weeps again
The brothers take their mother's blessing and ride out
At a crossroads two posts say that whoever goes right will be tsar and whoever goes left will be killed
The stronger brother chooses the left road and sends the other right
They exchange handkerchiefs, agreeing that blood on one means the other's death
The brother who goes right reaches a kingdom, and the tsar gives him his daughter Nastasya and the rule of the kingdom as Ivan-tsarevich
Ivan-tsarevich finds two flasks of healing and living water sewn into his saddle and leaves them there
The other Ivan reaches a mourning capital and lodges with a poor old woman
She tells him a twelve-headed dragon eats a person a day and the eldest princess has just been taken to the sea
Ivan rides to the sea, finds the princess chained to a rock, and she warns him to leave
He breaks her chain and lies down with his head on her lap, asking her to wake him when the dragon comes
The princess wakes him as the dragon rises from the sea
The dragon threatens to swallow Ivan
Ivan cuts off all twelve heads, puts them under the stone and throws the body into the sea
Ivan goes back to the old woman and sleeps three days
The tsar sends a water-carrier to gather the princess's bones
The water-carrier finds her alive, takes her into the forest and threatens to kill her unless she says he saved her
She agrees, and the tsar makes the water-carrier a colonel
Ivan sends the old woman to market for news
She reports that a second dragon has demanded the middle princess by an arrow-borne letter
Ivan rides to the sea and the middle princess bids him go
Ivan cuts off the second dragon's twelve heads
Ivan goes home and sleeps three days and nights
The water-carrier again takes the princess into the forest and makes her swear to his story
The tsar makes the water-carrier a general
Ivan wakes and the old woman brings news that a third dragon demands the youngest princess
Ivan rides to the sea, breaks the youngest princess's chain and lies on her lap
The princess cannot wake him until her tear falls on his cheek
The dragon threatens to eat Ivan and they fight
Ivan's sword grows red-hot and he begs the princess for her handkerchief
The princess wets her handkerchief in the sea and gives it to him
Ivan wraps the sword and cuts off all twelve heads
Ivan rides home and sleeps three days
The water-carrier threatens the youngest princess in the forest and she swears to his story
The tsar resolves to marry his favourite youngest daughter to the water-carrier
Ivan hears of the wedding and goes to the palace feast
The princess sees her handkerchief on his sword and tells her father he is her rescuer
The tsar has the water-carrier hanged
The tsar marries the princess to Ivan
Meanwhile Ivan-tsarevich chases a swift deer while hunting until it vanishes
He shoots two ducks on a stream
He enters an empty white-stone palace, roasts the ducks and eats
A beautiful maiden appears and says she fears his magic horse
Ivan-tsarevich says he came on an ordinary horse
She swells into a lioness and swallows him whole; she is the sister of the three dragons
Ivan the soldier's son finds blood on his brother's handkerchief
He takes leave of his wife and father-in-law and rides to find his brother
He learns his brother vanished while hunting and follows the same road
He chases the deer, shoots the ducks, and roasts them in the empty palace
He eats on the porch, and the maiden appears and says she fears his magic horse
He tells her he came on a common nag, and she believes him
She swells into a lioness, but his magic horse runs up and pins her
Ivan threatens to cut her to pieces unless she spits out his brother
The lioness spews up Ivan-tsarevich, dead and rotting
Ivan revives his brother with the healing and living water from the saddle
Ivan-tsarevich says he has slept long, and Ivan says he would have slept forever but for him
Ivan goes to cut off the lioness's head, she turns back into a maiden and begs mercy
Ivan takes pity on her beauty and lets her go
The brothers feast three days and part, each to his own kingdom
Ivan the soldier's son gives a gold piece to a begging child, who swells into a lion and tears him to pieces
Ivan-tsarevich gives a gold piece to a begging old man, who turns into a lion and tears him to pieces
Koshchei the Deathless carries off the tsar's wife
The eldest son sets out with his father's blessing to seek his mother and vanishes
The middle son sets out too and vanishes
Ivan-tsarevich asks his father's blessing, is refused, insists, and is blessed
Every horse Ivan lays his hand on falls down
An old woman asks why he is downcast, and he rebuffs her
She meets him again and he tells her he cannot find a horse
She leads him to a mountain and tells him to dig there
Ivan uncovers an iron door, breaks the twelve locks, and finds a heroic horse that breaks its twelve chains
Ivan puts on heroic armour, saddles the horse, pays the old woman and rides off
At a steep mountain he meets his brothers and they ride on together
His brothers cannot lift a great iron stone, and Ivan throws it up the mountain, and a stair appears
Ivan leaves his horse and gives his brothers a glass of his blood, which will blacken if he dies
Ivan climbs the mountain and reaches the house of a princess carried off by Koshchei
The princess tells him how to open the door in the fence, and he enters
She feeds him and he tells her he seeks his mother
She bids him first lift Koshchei's five-hundred-pood sword, and he tosses it in the air
At the next house Ivan finds his mother, and they embrace and weep
Ivan tests his strength by throwing a huge ball
His mother hides him and Koshchei arrives smelling a Russian
The mother denies anyone is there and coaxes Koshchei into telling where his death lies
Koshchei tells her his death is in an egg in a duck in a hare in a box under an oak, and flies away
Ivan sets out for Koshchei's death with his mother's blessing
Starving, he is about to kill a wolf cub, and the she-wolf begs it off, promising help
He spares a crow which promises help
He spares a young pike at the sea when its mother promises help
The pike lies across the sea and Ivan crosses on it
At the oak Ivan opens the box and the hare escapes
The wolf catches the hare and brings it to him
Ivan cuts open the hare and the duck flies away, and he misses it
The crow and her young catch the duck and bring it to him
Ivan takes the egg and drops it in the sea while washing it
The pike brings him the egg and carries him back across the sea
Ivan returns to his mother, who hides him again
Koshchei arrives smelling Russians and feels ill as Ivan squeezes the egg
Ivan comes out and shows Koshchei the egg
Koshchei kneels and begs to be spared, offering to rule the world together
Ivan crushes the egg and Koshchei dies
Ivan and his mother set off for home, taking the princess along
At the mountain the princess asks Ivan to go back for her wedding dress, ring and unsewn shoes
Ivan lets down his mother and the princess to his brothers
The brothers cut the rope so that Ivan cannot come down
The brothers threaten the mother and the princess into keeping silent about Ivan
They come home and the father rejoices, grieving only for Ivan
Ivan goes back to the princess's house and takes the ring, dress and shoes
On the mountain he tosses the ring from hand to hand, and twelve youths appear and carry him down
Ivan goes to his father's city and lodges with an old woman
She tells him the eldest brother wants to marry the princess, who demands a ring like hers first
Ivan sends the old woman to tell the tsar she will make the ring
The tsar accepts her offer on pain of death
The frightened old woman scolds Ivan, who sleeps and has the ring ready by morning
Ivan sends her with the ring, telling her to take only one gold piece and not to name him
The bride is pleased, and the old woman takes one gold piece only
The old woman likewise brings the wedding dress and the unsewn shoes made by Ivan
On the wedding day the old woman tells Ivan the bride is being brought to church
Ivan dresses in royal clothes and the old woman begs his pardon for scolding him
In church Ivan stands beside the bride and they are married
The eldest brother meets them on the way to the palace and turns back in shame
The father rejoices, learns of the brothers' treachery, exiles them and makes Ivan his heir
Dying, the parents of Ivan-tsarevich bid him give his three sisters to the first suitors who ask
Ivan buries his parents and walks in the garden with his sisters
A storm drives them home, and a falcon bursts through the ceiling, becomes a youth and asks for Marya
Ivan consents, Marya agrees, and the falcon marries her and carries her off
A year later an eagle comes the same way, woos Olga and carries her off with Ivan's consent
A year later a raven comes the same way, woos Anna and carries her off with Ivan's consent
Lonely after a year, Ivan sets out to find his sisters
He finds a slain army and a survivor tells him Marya Morevna destroyed it
Marya Morevna meets him at her white tents and invites him to stay
Ivan stays two nights, wins her love and marries her
Marya Morevna takes him to her kingdom
Leaving for war, she gives him charge of everything but forbids him to look into one closet
Ivan opens the closet and finds Koshchei the Deathless chained there
Koshchei begs for water and Ivan gives him three buckets
Koshchei regains his strength, breaks his chains and tells Ivan he will never see Marya Morevna again
Koshchei flies out in a whirlwind, overtakes Marya Morevna on the road and carries her off
Ivan weeps and sets out to find her
At a palace the falcon and his sister Marya greet him, and he stays three days
Ivan leaves his silver spoon with the falcon as a keepsake
At the eagle's palace he visits Olga three days and leaves a silver fork
At the raven's palace he visits Anna three days and leaves a silver snuffbox
Ivan reaches Marya Morevna, who reproaches him for releasing Koshchei
Ivan begs forgiveness and they flee while Koshchei is hunting
Koshchei's horse stumbles and tells him Ivan has taken Marya Morevna but can still be overtaken
Koshchei overtakes Ivan, spares him once for the water, warns him, and takes Marya Morevna back
Ivan returns and again carries Marya Morevna off while Koshchei is away
The horse tells Koshchei, who overtakes them and takes her back again
Ivan carries her off a third time, saying he cannot live without her
Koshchei overtakes him, cuts him to pieces, puts him in a tarred barrel and throws it in the sea
Koshchei takes Marya Morevna home
The silver keepsakes blacken and the brothers-in-law know Ivan is in trouble
The eagle pulls the barrel ashore while the falcon fetches living water and the raven dead water
They piece Ivan together and revive him with the dead and living water
Ivan says he has slept long, declines their invitation, and goes to Marya Morevna
Ivan asks Marya Morevna to learn from Koshchei where he got his horse
Koshchei tells her he herded Baba Yaga's mares beyond the fiery river for a foal, and crosses the river with a magic kerchief
Marya Morevna tells Ivan and steals the kerchief for him
Ivan crosses the fiery river and walks on toward Baba Yaga
Starving, he spares the chick of an overseas bird that promises help
He spares the honey of a queen bee that promises help
He spares the cub of a lioness that promises help
Ivan reaches Baba Yaga's house with eleven heads on twelve stakes
Baba Yaga agrees to give him a heroic horse if he herds her mares three days, or else his head goes on the last stake
The mares scatter over the meadows, and Ivan weeps and falls asleep on a stone
The bird wakes him at sunset with the mares driven home
Baba Yaga scolds the mares, who say birds pecked at them, and she tells them to hide in the forest next day
Baba Yaga warns Ivan again and the mares scatter into the forest
The lioness gathers the mares and wakes Ivan
The mares say beasts nearly tore them apart, and Baba Yaga tells them to run into the sea
The mares hide in the sea up to their necks, and Ivan weeps and sleeps
The bee gathers the mares and tells Ivan to hide in the stable and steal the mangy foal at midnight
Ivan hides behind the manger while the mares tell Baba Yaga that bees stung them
At midnight Ivan steals the mangy foal and rides to the fiery river
He waves the kerchief three times for a high bridge, crosses, and waves twice to leave only a thin one
Baba Yaga finds the foal gone and gives chase in her mortar
On the bridge she falls into the fiery river and dies
Ivan pastures the foal until it grows into a wonderful horse
Ivan comes to Marya Morevna and they ride away on the heroic horse
Koshchei's horse tells him Ivan's horse is better, but Koshchei chases them anyway
Koshchei overtakes Ivan and is about to cut him down when Ivan's horse crushes his skull with a hoof
Ivan finishes Koshchei with a club, burns him and scatters the ashes
Ivan and Marya Morevna visit the raven, the eagle and the falcon, who welcome them with joy
They return to their own kingdom and live happily
The old tsar dies and his son Ivan-tsarevich takes the crown
The neighbouring kings march against Ivan with countless troops
Ivan asks his sisters what to do, and they mock him with the tireless White Polyanin who has fought Baba Yaga Golden-Leg thirty years
Ivan rides out, destroys the enemy army, and sleeps three days
The kings bring a larger army and Ivan's sisters mock him again
Ivan destroys the second army and sleeps six days
The kings bring a third army and his sisters mock him a third time
Ivan destroys the third army and sleeps nine days
Ivan leaves the kingdom to his ministers and rides off to see White Polyanin
An old man in a forest hut summons his birds, who know nothing of White Polyanin
The old man gives Ivan a ball of thread to lead him to his elder brother
The second old man summons his beasts, finds the one-eyed she-wolf missing and has her brought
The she-wolf says White Polyanin sleeps twelve days in a tent on a barrow after fighting Baba Yaga
The she-wolf leads Ivan to the tent
Ivan finds White Polyanin asleep and lies down beside him
A little bird urges White Polyanin to kill Ivan, and Ivan tears off its leg and throws it out
A second bird says the same, and Ivan tears off its wing
A third bird says the same, and Ivan tears off its beak and falls asleep
White Polyanin wakes and nearly kills the stranger, then refrains and wakes him
White Polyanin threatens him for his boldness and Ivan answers with a challenge
They charge, shattering their spears, and Ivan throws White Polyanin from the saddle
White Polyanin begs for his life and offers to be Ivan's younger brother
Ivan raises him and accepts him as his younger brother
White Polyanin explains he fights Baba Yaga to win her daughter, and Ivan offers to fight with him
Together they cut down Baba Yaga's army
Baba Yaga flees, and escapes under an iron plate into an abyss
They slaughter many bulls and plait a rope of hides long enough to reach the other world
White Polyanin lowers Ivan into the abyss, to haul him up when he tugs
Ivan finds tailors sewing soldiers for Baba Yaga, lines them up and cuts off their heads
Ivan finds shoemakers making soldiers for her and kills them the same way
In a great city a beautiful maiden calls Ivan in and learns he seeks Baba Yaga
She says she is Baba Yaga's daughter, that her mother sleeps for twelve days, and shows him the road
Ivan cuts off the sleeping Baba Yaga's head
The head bids him strike again, and he refuses
Ivan feasts with the maiden and asks if anyone is stronger than he and fairer than she
She tells him of a far fairer princess held by the Dragon-Tsar
Ivan leads her to the rope and White Polyanin hauls them both up
Ivan gives the maiden to White Polyanin as his bride
Ivan rides to the dragon kingdom
Ivan kills the Dragon-Tsar and frees the princess
Ivan marries the princess and returns home to live with her
The tsar's three sons ask his blessing to go hunting and ride off in different directions
The youngest, Ivan-tsarevich, gets lost and comes to a dead horse surrounded by beasts, birds and reptiles
A falcon lands on his shoulder and asks him to divide the carcass, which they have quarrelled over for thirty-three years
Ivan divides it: bones to the beasts, meat to the birds, hide to the reptiles and head to the ants
The falcon grants him the power to turn into a falcon and an ant at will
Ivan turns into a falcon and flies to a kingdom half drawn into a crystal mountain
Ivan takes service with that kingdom's tsar
The princess asks leave to ride with Ivan on the crystal mountain, and the tsar allows it
At the mountain a golden goat appears and Ivan chases it in vain
When he returns the princess is gone
Ivan disguises himself as an old man and hires himself to the tsar as herdsman
The tsar tells him to give the dragons three, six or twelve cows according to their heads
A three-headed dragon demands three cows and Ivan refuses
The angry dragon seizes six cows, and Ivan as a falcon cuts off its three heads
Ivan tells the tsar he gave the dragon nothing
A six-headed dragon demands six cows and Ivan refuses
The dragon seizes twelve cows, and Ivan as a falcon cuts off its six heads
Ivan tells the tsar the dragon took nothing
Ivan turns into an ant, creeps into the crystal mountain and finds the princess
She tells him a twelve-headed dragon carried her off, and that the seed in the egg in the duck in the hare in the chest inside the dragon will melt the mountain
The twelve-headed dragon demands twelve cows and Ivan refuses
Ivan fights and defeats the twelve-headed dragon
Ivan cuts the dragon open and takes out the seed from chest, hare, duck and egg
He lights the seed and holds it to the mountain, which melts
Ivan brings the princess out and takes her to her father
The tsar makes Ivan his son-in-law and they are married
Bukhtan Bukhtanovich lies on a stove built on posts in the middle of a field
A fox offers to marry him to the tsar's daughter and takes his only five-kopeck piece
The fox changes the coin into small change
The fox borrows a quarter-measure from the tsar to measure Bukhtan's money, sticks coins under its hoop and returns it
She does the same with a half-measure
She does the same with a full measure
The fox tells the tsar the money is all measured and asks his daughter for Bukhtan
The tsar asks to see the bridegroom
The fox has Bukhtan dress in what clothes he has and leads him to the tsar
On a dirty footbridge the fox pushes him into the mud and smears him with it
The fox tells the tsar Bukhtan has fallen in the mud and gets everyday clothes from him
Bukhtan changes and they come to the tsar
Bukhtan stares at his clothes, the tsar asks why, and the fox says he is ashamed of such poor clothes and gets him the tsar's Easter clothes
The fox whispers to Bukhtan not to look at himself
Bukhtan stares at the gilded chair, and the fox tells the tsar they have many such in their bathhouses
The tsar throws the chair out of the door
The fox whispers to Bukhtan to look about him
They settle the match and the wedding is held
Bukhtan and his wife sail home on three loaded ships while the fox runs along the shore
Bukhtan sees his stove and cries out, and the fox hushes him
The fox runs ahead and finds a great stone house in which lie Snake Snakeson, Raven Ravenson and Cock Cockson
The fox tells them the tsar and tsaritsa are coming to burn them
The fox shuts the cock in a barrel, the raven in a mortar, and wraps the snake in straw
When the ships arrive she has the Cossacks throw them all into the water
Bukhtan moves into the house and lives and rules there until his death
While Kuzenka is out hunting a fox kills, roasts and eats one of his hens, and he blames a kite
Next day the fox asks where he is going and again eats a hen while he hunts, and he suspects her
Kuzenka nails up his windows and doors, pretends to go hunting and follows the fox back
The fox comes down the chimney and Kuzenka catches her
The fox begs for her life, promising to make him Kozma Quick-Rich if he roasts her a hen in butter
Kuzenka agrees, and the well-fed fox rolls about in the tsar's preserved meadows
A wolf asks where she ate so well and she says at the tsar's feast
The wolf begs to be taken, and she bids him gather forty forties of wolves
The fox leads the wolves to the tsar and presents them as a gift from Kozma Quick-Rich
The delighted tsar has the wolves shut in a pen
The fox has Kuzenka roast another hen and rolls in the meadows again
A bear asks where she ate, she tells of the feast, and he begs to be taken
She has him gather forty forties of black bears and presents them to the tsar from Kozma Quick-Rich
The tsar has the bears shut in
The fox has Kuzenka roast the last hen and the cock
A sable and a marten ask where she ate, and she tells them of the feast
They beg to be taken, gather forty forties of sables and martens, and the fox presents them to the tsar
The tsar marvels at Kozma's wealth and has the animals killed and skinned
The fox borrows a pood-measure from the tsar to measure Kozma's silver
She has Kuzenka scour it with sand, sticks small coins in its seams and returns it
The fox asks the tsar for the princess for Kozma, and the tsar agrees and bids him come
The fox has workmen saw through a bridge, and it collapses with Kuzenka into the water
The fox cries that Kozma Quick-Rich is perishing
The tsar's men pull Kuzenka out, dress him finely and bring him to the tsar
Kuzenka marries the princess and stays at the tsar's court
The tsar proposes visiting his son-in-law's home, and they set out
The fox runs ahead and makes Tsar Zmiulan's shepherds say the sheep belong to Kozma, threatening them with Tsar Fire and Tsaritsa Lightning
She does the same with the swineherds, cowherds, horseherds and camel-herds
The fox tells Tsar Zmiulan that Tsar Fire and Tsaritsa Lightning are burning everything
On her advice Zmiulan hides in a hollow oak in his garden
On the road the herdsmen tell the princess and the tsar that every herd is Kozma's
The fox welcomes them into Zmiulan's palace and they feast for a week
The fox tells Kuzenka to go with his father-in-law and shoot the oak to pieces
Kuzenka and the tsar shoot the oak and kill Tsar Zmiulan
Kozma becomes tsar of that kingdom and lives with the princess
They feast the fox on hens every day until she has spoiled all the hens
The two clever brothers go to buy goods, bidding the fool honour their wives and promising him red boots, caftan and shirt
The fool promises, then lies on the stove
The sisters-in-law scold him and send him for water
The fool catches a pike in his bucket and means to cook it for himself alone
The pike begs to be let go, promising that whatever he says will happen at the pike's command
At his word the buckets walk home and set themselves in place, and the sisters-in-law marvel
The sisters-in-law send him for firewood
The fool sends his sledge to the forest without a horse, crushing many people as he passes the town
In the forest he has the axes cut and stack the wood and cut him a cudgel
Driving back, he is seized by the townspeople, and sets the cudgel on them, beating many
The fool gets home and sits on the stove
The townspeople complain to the king and advise luring the fool with red clothes
The king's messengers summon the fool with the promise of red clothes
The fool rides to the king on his stove
The king means to execute him, but his daughter falls for the fool and begs to marry him
The angry king marries them and has them sealed in a tarred barrel and cast into the sea
At his wife's request the fool has the barrel thrown ashore and burst
At her request he has a marble palace built opposite the king's
The king sees the palace, learns his daughter lives there and summons them
The king forgives them and they all live together
A poor peasant who toils without gain fasts and prays all day
On Easter morning, going for water, he catches a large pike in his bucket
The pike begs to be freed, promising that whatever he asks at its command will appear
He throws the pike back into the well
At his word a table appears laden with food, and he breaks his fast after church
The tsar's daughter gives alms to the poor in the street but forgets him
He wishes that the princess conceive and bear a son, and she does
The tsar questions the princess, who swears she has sinned with no one
The boy grows fast and is shown all the boyars, but names none his father
The nurses carry him through every street, and at the poor man's hut he cries Daddy
The poor man is brought to the tsar and says the child is God's
The angry tsar marries him to the princess and has them and the child sealed in a tarred barrel and cast into the sea
The barrel is washed ashore, and at the poor man's word it falls apart
They wander hungry, and he reproaches the princess for denying him alms
At his word a rich palace with gardens and ponds appears and servants feast them
The princess regrets there are no birds on the ponds
At his word twelve ducks and a drake with gold and silver feathers appear
The grown son asks leave to seek a bride and sets out
An old woman tells him of a peerless princess over the sea
He sails there and asks the king for his daughter
The king says a mighty champion also woos her, and bids them fight for her
Kings and princes gather from all lands, the princess's father among them, to watch
The son beats his rival and cuts off his head
The son marries the princess
He invites all the kings and princes to his parents' home, where they feast and marvel at the ducks
As the guests leave the host calls them back and accuses them of stealing a duck
The guests agree to be searched, on pain of his head if no duck is found
At his word a duck appears under the tsar's caftan, and the host finds it there
The others mock the tsar as a thief, and he swears he did not steal it
The princess reveals that she is the daughter he sealed in the barrel
She tells him everything and they all live together
An Old Man sets off to catch fish, telling the Old Woman to bake pies
The Old Man catches a whole cartload of fish and drives home
The Old Man finds a Fox lying curled up on the road as if dead
The Old Man puts the Fox on the cart as a present for his wife and walks ahead
The Fox quietly throws all the fish off the cart, one by one
The Fox slips away
The Old Man tells his wife he has brought her a fur collar
The Old Woman finds neither collar nor fish and scolds her husband for lying
The Old Man realises the Fox was not dead and grieves
The Fox gathers up the scattered fish and eats them
A Wolf meets the Fox and asks her for fish
The Fox refuses and tells him to catch his own
The Fox tells the Wolf to put his tail in an ice-hole and sit long, and fish will cling to it
The Wolf goes to the river, puts his tail in the ice-hole and sits all night
The Wolf's tail freezes fast in the ice
Women coming for water see the Wolf and beat him with yokes and pails
The Wolf tears off his own tail and runs away
The Wolf vows to pay the Fox back
The Fox sneaks into a hut where women are baking pancakes, to steal more
The Fox falls head first into the tub of batter and runs off smeared with it
The Wolf meets the Fox and reproaches her for getting him beaten
The Fox lies that she was beaten worse than he, so that her brains are showing
The Wolf offers to carry the Fox and carries her on his back
Riding, the Fox mutters "the beaten one carries the unbeaten"
The Wolf asks what she said, and the Fox lies that she said "the beaten carries the beaten"
The Fox proposes that they build themselves huts, and the Wolf agrees
They build the huts, bark for the Fox and ice for the Wolf, and live in them
Spring comes and the Wolf's ice hut melts
The Wolf says the Fox has tricked him again and he must eat her
The Fox leads the Wolf to a deep pit and proposes a jump: whoever fails is eaten
The Wolf jumps and falls into the pit
The Fox tells him to stay there and goes off
The Fox, carrying a rolling pin, begs a peasant for a night's lodging
The peasant says there is no room, and the Fox promises to take hardly any
They let her in, and she lies down with the rolling pin under the stove
Early in the morning the Fox burns her rolling pin
The Fox demands her rolling pin, saying she would not take even a goose for it
The peasant gives her a goose for it
The Fox begs a second peasant for lodging and is let in with the goose
In the morning the Fox plucks and eats the goose
The Fox demands her goose, and the peasant gives her a turkey for it
The Fox begs a third peasant for lodging and is let in with the turkey
In the morning the Fox plucks and eats the turkey
The Fox demands her turkey, and the peasant gives her his son's young wife for it
The Fox puts the young wife in a sack and goes on singing
The Fox begs a fourth peasant for lodging and is let in with the sack
The peasant quietly lets the young wife out of the sack and puts a dog in it
In the morning the Fox takes the sack and tells the young wife to sing, and the dog growls
The Fox, frightened, flings down the sack and runs
The Fox urges a Cockerel on a gate to come down and be confessed for his seventy wives
The Cockerel comes down, and the Fox seizes and eats him
A peasant drives through the forest with a load of smelts
The Fox steals smelts from him and puts them in a jug
The Fox sits down under a haystack to eat
A hungry Wolf comes running and asks the Fox for some
The Fox refuses and tells him to catch his own
The Fox tells the Wolf to tie the jug to his tail and let it into the ice-hole
The Wolf obeys
The Fox chants to herself, "Shine, stars; freeze, wolf's tail!"
The Fox runs to the village, gets her head stuck in a dough trough and raises an alarm
The Fox runs from the village straight toward the Wolf, with people chasing her
The Wolf strains in fear against his frozen tail and tears off half of it
The Wolf catches up with the Fox in the forest, and she pretends to be sick
The Fox complains that her head has been beaten and she cannot walk
The Wolf tells her to get on his back, and she rides him
The Fox sings "the beaten one carries the unbeaten"
The Wolf asks what she said, and the Fox lies that she is raving
The Fox finishes her song: "the beaten one's rump is sore"
The Fox gets hold of some fish somewhere
The Fox climbs a haystack in a village backyard and eats the fish
A Wolf passing at night greets the Fox and asks what she is eating
The Fox lies that she caught the fish in the pond and offers to teach him
The Fox leads the Wolf to an ice-hole
The Fox tells the Wolf to sit and put his tail in the water so fish will crawl onto it
The Wolf sits down and lowers his tail into the ice-hole
The Fox mutters, "Shine, sky; freeze, wolf's tail!"
The Wolf asks what she is saying, and the Fox lies that she is calling the fish for him
The ice-hole freezes over
The Fox says she will run to the village for honey
The Fox runs off and is gone
Peasants see the tricked Wolf on the pond with his tail frozen in and kill him
The Old Man's cockerel finds an ear of wheat, and the Old Woman's hen finds a poppy head
The Old Man threshes the grain and grinds flour
The Old Woman makes a poppy-seed and honey pie and sets it on the window to bake in the sun
The Fox, passing with the Wolf, proposes that they steal the pie and share it
The Wolf agrees
The Fox steals the pie
The Fox claims the pie is not done and coaxes the Wolf to sleep while it bakes
The Wolf falls asleep
The Fox eats the sweet filling, fills the pie with dung, and seals it up
They wake and start sharing the pie, and the Fox accuses the Wolf of eating the filling
The Wolf swears he did not, but the Fox does not believe him
The Fox proposes a test: whoever sweats wax lying in the sun ate the honey, and they agree
The Wolf falls asleep without a care
The Fox steals honeycomb from an apiary, eats it, and plasters the Wolf with the wax
The Wolf wakes, is "convicted", confesses, and accepts the Fox's sentence: no share of the next catch
They part to go hunting
The Fox lies on the road as if dead and breaks wind with all her might
Carters smell her, take her for dead, and put her on their cart of fish
The Fox gnaws through the cart's bark side and throws out fish
The Fox slips off the cart, gathers the fish into a pile and eats
The Wolf returns empty-handed and begs the Fox for a fish
The Fox refuses him even a bone
The Fox tells the Wolf to sit with his tail in an ice-hole saying "Bite, fish, small and big"
The Fox leads the Wolf to the ice-hole
The Wolf puts his tail in and chants for fish
The Fox runs around him chanting "Freeze, freeze, wolf's tail!"
The Wolf asks what she says, and the Fox lies that she is helping him
The Fox stops the Wolf from pulling out his tail, saying it is too early
In the hard frost the Fox tells the Wolf "Pull!"
The Wolf pulls, but his tail is frozen fast and he is stuck
The Fox runs to the village shouting for people to come and beat the Wolf
All the villagers rush out and beat the Wolf
The Wolf tears off his tail and runs
The Wolf jumps into a sledge a peasant has left and drives out of the village
In the turmoil the Fox gets into an empty hut and rolls in a trough of dough
The Fox runs to the road and lies down
The Wolf finds the Fox on the road and she complains she was beaten till her brains came out
The Wolf promises to protect her
The Fox asks to ride in the sledge, and the Wolf refuses
The Fox walks behind and begs to rest one paw on the sledge, and the Wolf at last agrees
Paw by paw and then her tail, the Fox talks her way wholly into the sledge
The sledge creaks, the Wolf scolds, and the Fox lies that she is cracking nuts
The sledge creaks again, and the Fox tells the same lie
The sledge falls to pieces
The Wolf goes to cut wood for a new sledge, and the Fox stays to graze the horse
The Fox eats out the horse's insides, stuffs it with live sparrows and plugs it with straw
The Wolf finishes the sledge and harnesses the horse, but it will not move
The Wolf pulls out the straw, the sparrows fly off and the horse's skin collapses
The Fox, still pretending to be hurt, talks the Wolf into pulling her in the sledge
The Wolf pulls her, chanting "the beaten one carries the beaten"
The Fox whispers "the beaten one carries the unbeaten"
The Wolf asks what she said, and the Fox lies that she said "the beaten carries the beaten"
A very hungry Fox, seeing fishermen coming, lies down on the ground and keeps still
One of the fishermen throws the Fox into his cart
The Fox gnaws a hole in the cart, throws all the fish out through it, and jumps out
The Fox gathers the fish and eats
A Wolf comes and asks the Fox for fish
The Fox refuses and tells him to go and catch his own
The Fox gives the Wolf one fish to whet his appetite and leads him off
At a frozen lake the Fox breaks a hole and tells the Wolf to put his tail in it
The Wolf obeys, puts his tail in and sits
The Fox runs about the lake shouting "Freeze, freeze, gossip's tail!"
The Wolf asks what she says, and the Fox lies that she wishes him fish small and big
The Wolf's tail freezes in
The Fox runs to the village to tell people to come and beat the Wolf
The people run out with sticks and clubs to beat the Wolf
The Fox runs into a hut where bread is being kneaded and rolls in the dough
The Fox runs out and sits on a haystack
The Wolf tears off his tail and barely escapes
The Wolf finds the Fox eating on the haystack, reproaches her for tricking him, and asks for food
The Fox lets him lick once
The Wolf begs for another lick
The Fox refuses, lying that she is eating her own brains, and tells him to smash his head on a pine
The Wolf obeys, runs head first into a pine and kills himself
The Fox eats the Wolf's brains
The Fox hides in her burrow
The Fox goes to an old woman's hut and asks her for fire
The old woman takes a sweet poppy-seed pie out of the oven to cool
When the old woman bends to the oven, the Fox grabs the pie and runs off
Running, the Fox eats the poppy filling and stuffs the pie with rubbish
The Fox asks some boys herding bullocks to trade her a bullock for the pie
The boys agree
The Fox tells them not to break the pie till she has led the bullock behind the mound
The boys do as she says
Behind the mound the Fox turns off into the forest
The Fox makes herself a sledge and drives off
The Wolf meets her, asks where she got the bullock and sledge, and she says she made them
The Wolf asks for a ride, and the Fox refuses
The Wolf asks to put just one leg on, and the Fox allows it
The Wolf puts one leg on
The Wolf begs to put a second leg on, and the Fox says she fears he will break the sledge
The Wolf puts the second leg on
Something cracks, the Fox scolds, and the Wolf lies that he cracked a nut
The Wolf begs to put a third leg on, and the Fox lets him
Something cracks louder, the Fox cries out, and the Wolf again lies about a nut
The Fox asks for a nut too, and the Wolf says he has none left
The Wolf begs to put his last leg on, and the Fox agrees
The Wolf puts his last leg on and the sledge breaks to pieces
The Fox flies into a rage at him
The Fox sends the Wolf to cut wood, telling him to say "Cut, wood, crooked and straight"
The Wolf goes and keeps saying "Cut, wood, all straight"
The Wolf brings the wood
The Fox sees it is the wrong wood, gets angry and says he did not say it right
The Wolf insists he said just what she told him
The Fox leaves the Wolf to wait and goes to the forest to cut wood herself
Left alone, the Wolf eats out the bullock's insides, fills it with sparrows and plugs it with straw
The Wolf stands the bullock up and runs away
