The Goat and the Ram give up their mischief and become meek and obedient
A peasant drives into the forest for wood
A Bear meets him and asks who dappled his horse
The peasant boasts that he did it and offers to make the Bear even more dappled
The Bear promises him a beehive in payment
The peasant says he must tie the Bear up, and the Bear agrees
The peasant ties the Bear up tight with reins and ropes
The Bear begs to be untied, and the peasant refuses
The peasant cuts wood, makes a hot fire and puts his axe in it
The peasant brands the Bear with the red-hot axe
The Bear bursts the ropes and runs off through the forest
The Bear roams until he is exhausted, unable to lie down for his burns
The Bear vows revenge on the peasant
Next day the peasant's wife goes to reap, taking bread and a jug of milk
She sets the jug aside and reaps
The peasant drives out to see his wife
A Fox sticks her head into the jug and cannot pull it out
The Fox pleads with the jug to let her go
The peasant hits the Fox across the legs with a log
The Fox dashes her head against a stone and breaks the jug
The Fox, chased by the peasant, escapes on three legs into the forest
The peasant goes back to loading sheaves
A Gadfly bites the peasant on the neck
The peasant catches the Gadfly
The peasant sticks a straw into the Gadfly's rear and lets it go
The Gadfly flies off, dragging the straw
The Gadfly reaches the forest and struggles onto a tree, panting so hard the tree shakes
The Bear under the tree takes fright and asks the Gadfly to come down
The Gadfly comes down
The Bear and the Gadfly learn that the peasant has hurt them both
The Fox comes hopping on three legs and tells the Bear the peasant broke her leg
The Bear proposes that the three of them go and kill the peasant
The three of them go to the field
The peasant sees them and is frightened
The peasant throws his wife down and lifts her legs high in the air
The Bear refuses to go on, saying the peasant is dappling someone again
The Fox says he is breaking someone's legs
The Gadfly says he is sticking a straw into someone
The Bear and the Fox run off into the forest
The peasant is left safe and sound
A Wolf comes to the old couple and sings a song about their livestock
The old woman praises the song and tells the old man to give the Wolf a sheep
The old man gives him a sheep
The Wolf eats it
The Wolf keeps coming back with the same song until he has eaten the sheep, the stallion, the heifer and the old woman
The Wolf comes with his song to the old man, now alone
The old man beats the Wolf with a poker
The Wolf runs away and never comes back
The old man is left to grieve alone
A Wolf learns that the old man has many animals and goes to beg from him
The Wolf demands the old woman
The old man gives him the cat instead
The Wolf eats the cat
The Wolf comes back demanding the old woman
The old man gives him the dog instead
The Wolf eats the dog
The Wolf comes back for the old woman again
The old man gives him the sheep instead
The old man then gives him the cow
The old man keeps the old woman, and they live on together
A Lion asks a woodcutter for his daughter's hand in marriage
The Woodman, afraid to refuse, agrees on condition that the Lion lets him pull out his teeth and cut off his claws
The Lion cheerfully agrees
The Lion, now toothless and clawless, returns to repeat his request
The Woodman, no longer afraid, attacks him with his club and drives him into the forest
A Swallow back from abroad builds her nest in the wall of a Court of Justice
She hatches seven young
A Serpent from a hole in the wall eats the nestlings
The Swallow finds her nest empty
She laments that she alone suffers wrong in the place where everyone else's rights are protected
The Hares go to war with the Eagles
The Hares ask the Foxes for help
The Foxes refuse, saying they know who the Hares are and whom they are fighting
A Wolf with a bone stuck in his throat hires a Crane for a large sum to draw it out
The Crane puts her head into the Wolf's mouth and pulls out the bone
The Crane asks for the promised payment
The Wolf refuses, grinning, and says her reward is having taken her head out of his jaws safely
A Bat falls to the ground and a Weasel catches him
The Bat begs for his life
The Weasel refuses, saying he is the enemy of all birds
The Bat says he is not a bird but a mouse
The Weasel lets him go
The Bat falls again and another Weasel catches him
The Bat begs this Weasel not to eat him
The Weasel says he especially hates mice
The Bat says he is not a mouse but a bat
The Bat escapes a second time
A Cock scratching for food for himself and his hens finds a precious stone
The Cock tells the stone it is useless to him and says he would rather have one barleycorn than every jewel in the world
A Hare mocks the Tortoise's short feet and slow pace
The Tortoise laughs and boasts that she will beat the Hare in a race
The Hare, thinking this impossible, accepts
They agree that the Fox will choose the course and set the goal
On the appointed day the two start together
The Tortoise walks slowly and steadily without stopping, all the way to the end of the course
The Hare lies down by the wayside and falls fast asleep
The Hare wakes up and runs as fast as he can
The Hare sees that the Tortoise has already reached the goal and is dozing there
A Charcoal-Burner meets his friend, a Fuller
The Charcoal-Burner begs the Fuller to come and live with him, since they would be good neighbors and save on expenses
The Fuller refuses, saying the charcoal would blacken whatever he whitened
A Fisherman takes his flute and his nets to the seashore
He sets his net below a rock and plays tunes on it, hoping the fish will dance into the net
After waiting in vain for a long time, he puts his flute aside
He casts his net into the sea and makes an excellent catch
Seeing the fish leap in the net, he scolds them for dancing now that he has stopped piping
The Ass and the Fox form a partnership for mutual protection
They go into the forest to hunt
They meet a Lion
The Fox promises the Lion to help him catch the Ass if the Lion pledges not to harm the Fox
The Fox assures the Ass that he will not be hurt
The Fox leads the Ass to a deep pit and makes him fall in
The Lion, seeing the Ass trapped, seizes the Fox
The Lion attacks the Ass at his leisure
Flies are drawn to a jar of honey that has spilled in a housekeeper's room
They put their feet in the honey and eat greedily
Their feet get so smeared that they cannot use their wings or free themselves
They suffocate
As they die, they cry out that they have destroyed themselves for a little pleasure
A Bear boasts of his love for man, saying he respects man so much he will not touch a dead body
A Fox hears him and says with a smile that he wishes the Bear would eat the dead and not the living
A Tortoise basking in the sun complains to the sea-birds that no one will teach her to fly
An Eagle hears her and asks what reward she would give him for taking her up into the air
The Tortoise promises him all the riches of the Red Sea
The Eagle agrees to teach her to fly
The Eagle carries her in his talons almost up to the clouds
The Eagle suddenly lets her go
She falls on a high mountain and her shell breaks to pieces
As she dies, the Tortoise says she deserves her fate, since a creature that can barely walk had no business with wings and clouds
A Dog lies in a manger and growls and snaps to keep the oxen from eating the hay
One Ox tells the others the Dog is selfish: he cannot eat the hay himself, yet he will not let those who can eat it
A Lion, too old and weak to hunt by force, decides to get his food by a trick
He lies down in his den, pretends to be sick, and makes sure everyone hears of it
The beasts come one at a time to his den to express their sorrow
The Lion eats them
The Fox figures out the trick
The Fox stands outside the cave at a safe distance and asks the Lion how he is
The Lion invites the Fox to come inside
The Fox refuses, pointing out many tracks going into the cave and none coming out
A Fox caught in a trap escapes but loses his tail
Ashamed and mocked, he plans to convince the other Foxes that having no tail is more attractive
He gathers a large number of Foxes
He publicly advises them to cut off their tails, saying they would look better and be rid of the weight
One of the Foxes interrupts, saying he would not give this advice if he had not lost his own tail
A Cat catches a Cock
The Cat considers how to find a reasonable excuse for eating him
The Cat accuses the Cock of bothering men by crowing at night and keeping them awake
The Cock defends himself, saying he crows so that men will get up in time for work
The Cat replies that, however good the Cock's excuses sound, he will not go without supper
The Cat eats the Cock
A Miser sells everything he owns and buys a lump of gold
He buries it in a hole beside an old wall
One of his workmen notices his frequent visits to the spot and decides to watch him
The workman discovers the hidden treasure
The workman digs down to the gold and steals it
On his next visit the Miser finds the hole empty
He tears his hair and wails loudly
A neighbor learns the cause and advises him to put a stone in the hole and pretend it is the gold, since he never used the gold anyway
The Horse tells the Groom that if he wants him in good condition he should groom him less and feed him more
A Muleteer sets out on a journey, driving an Ass and a Mule that are both heavily loaded
On the steep mountain path, the Ass finds his load more than he can bear
The Ass begs the Mule to take a small part of his load
The Mule ignores the request
The Ass falls dead under his burden
The Muleteer skins the Ass
The Muleteer puts the Ass's load on the Mule on top of his own, with the Ass's hide on top of that
Groaning under the weight, the Mule says to himself that he deserves this for not helping the Ass
Three or four times, a Shepherd-boy brings the villagers running by falsely crying "Wolf!"
When his neighbors come to help, he laughs at them
At last the Wolf really comes
The terrified boy begs for help, crying that the Wolf is killing the sheep
No one pays attention or comes to help
The Wolf mauls or kills the whole flock at his leisure
Jupiter decides to give the birds a king
Jupiter announces that all the birds must appear before him on a set day, when he will choose the most beautiful as king
The Jackdaw, aware of his ugliness, gathers feathers that have fallen from the other birds
He sticks the feathers all over his body
On the appointed day the birds gather before Jupiter
The Jackdaw appears in his borrowed feathers
Jupiter proposes to make the Jackdaw king because of his beautiful plumage
The birds protest angrily
Each bird plucks back its own feathers, leaving the Jackdaw a plain Jackdaw
An Old Woman who has lost her sight calls in a Physician to cure her
Before witnesses, she agrees to pay him if he cures her and nothing if he does not
On every visit the Physician puts salve on her eyes and steals some of her belongings
Once he has taken everything, he cures her
He demands the promised payment
The Old Woman, seeing that her belongings are gone, refuses to pay
The Physician insists and, when she still refuses, takes her before the Judge
In court she argues that she is still blind, since she can no longer see any of the goods in her house
A Heifer sees an Ox pulling a plow and taunts him about his hard life
At the harvest festival the owner takes the Ox out of his yoke
The owner ties up the Heifer and leads him to the altar to be sacrificed
The Ox, seeing this, tells the Heifer with a smile that he was left idle only because he was going to be sacrificed
An aging Charger is sent to work in a mill instead of going to war
Forced to grind, he complains to the Miller about his change of fortune and recalls his former splendor
The Miller tells him to stop dwelling on the past
Jupiter announces a royal reward for the beast whose offspring is judged the handsomest
The Monkey comes with the others and enters her ugly, hairless baby for the prize
Everyone laughs at her
She declares firmly that, whatever Jupiter decides, her son is the handsomest of all in his mother's eyes
A river carries two Pots downstream, one of earthenware and one of brass
The Earthen Pot asks the Brass Pot to keep away, because the lightest touch would break it
A man visits his daughter who married a gardener and asks how she is
She says she is doing well and wishes only for heavy rain to water the plants
He visits his daughter who married a tile-maker and asks how she is
She says she needs nothing and wishes only for dry, sunny weather to dry the bricks
He asks her which of his two daughters' wishes he should add his own to
A Mouse becomes close friends with a Frog
The Frog, meaning mischief, ties the Mouse's foot tightly to his own
The Frog leads the Mouse to the meadow where they usually find food
Little by little he leads the Mouse to the edge of his pool
The Frog suddenly jumps in, dragging the Mouse with him
The Frog swims about croaking happily
The Mouse drowns, and his body floats on the water, still tied to the Frog's foot
A Hawk sees the body, swoops down on it, and carries it into the air
The Frog, still tied to the Mouse, is carried off with it
The Hawk eats the Frog
A Fisherman makes a very good cast and catches a large haul of fish
By handling his net skillfully, he keeps all the large fish and pulls them to shore
He cannot stop the smaller fish from slipping back through the net into the sea
A Huntsman coming home with his dogs meets a Fisherman carrying a basket of fish
Each wants what the other has, and they agree to exchange their catch
Pleased with the trade, they make the same exchange every day for some time
A neighbor warns them that doing it so often will ruin the pleasure and each will want his own catch again
At shearing time, a poor widow shears her only Sheep herself to save money
She uses the shears so clumsily that she cuts his flesh along with the fleece
The Sheep, writhing in pain, reproaches her and tells her to go to the butcher for his flesh or the shearer for his wool
An Ass climbs onto the roof of a building
Frisking about up there, he breaks the tiles
The owner goes up, drives him down, and beats him hard with a thick wooden stick
The Ass protests that everyone laughed when the Monkey did the same thing yesterday
A Stag, hotly chased by hounds, takes shelter in a farmyard and hides in a shed among the oxen
An Ox warns him that he is putting himself in danger in his enemy's house
The Stag asks to be allowed to stay, promising to find a good chance to escape
In the evening the herdsman comes to feed the cattle and does not see the Stag
The farm-bailiff and several laborers pass through the shed and do not notice him
The Stag congratulates himself on being safe and thanks the Oxen
One Ox warns him that the danger is not over, because the master, who has a hundred eyes, has yet to come through
The master comes in, complains that the oxen have not been properly fed, and inspects everything
He spots the tips of the Stag's antlers sticking out of the straw
He calls his laborers and orders them to seize and kill the Stag
A starving Lion approaches a straw-yard where an Ass and a Cock are
Just as the Lion is about to spring on the Ass, the Cock crows loudly
The Lion runs away as fast as he can
The Ass, seeing the Lion's fear, takes courage and gallops after him to attack him
The Lion turns, seizes the Ass, and tears him to pieces
The Rivers join together to complain to the Sea that it turns their sweet water salty and undrinkable
The Sea, seeing that they mean to blame him, tells them to stop flowing into him if they do not want to be salty
A queen Bee goes up to Olympus and offers Jupiter fresh honey
Jupiter, delighted, promises to give her whatever she asks for
The Bee asks for a sting so that she can kill any mortal who tries to take her honey
Jupiter is displeased but, bound by his promise, grants the sting, warning that it will stay in the wound and she will die if she uses it
Two men are traveling together
One of them picks up an axe from the path and says, "I have found an axe"
The other tells him to say "We have found an axe" instead
They see the owner of the axe chasing them
The man who picked up the axe says, "We are undone"
The other refuses, telling him to keep his first way of speaking and say "I am undone"
A Lion enters a farmyard
The Farmer, hoping to catch him, shuts the gate
Finding that he cannot escape, the Lion kills the sheep
The Lion then attacks the oxen
The Farmer, now afraid for his own life, opens the gate and lets the Lion go
After the Lion leaves, the Farmer mourns the loss of his sheep and oxen
His wife tells him it serves him right for shutting in a Lion when he trembles just hearing one roar from far away
A Birdcatcher is about to sit down to a meal of herbs when a friend arrives unexpectedly
His trap is empty, so he decides to kill the tame Partridge he uses as a decoy
The Partridge begs for his life, pointing out how useful he is
The Birdcatcher spares the Partridge
He decides to kill a fine young Cock instead
The Cock pleads pitifully, pointing out that he tells him when dawn is coming
The Birdcatcher agrees that the Cock is useful but says he and his friend must have their dinner
A starving Fox sees bread and meat that shepherds left in a hollow oak, creeps in, and eats a big meal
He is now so full that he cannot get back out
He begins to groan and bemoan his fate
Another Fox passing by hears him and asks what is wrong
On hearing the story, the other Fox tells him he must stay there until he is as thin as when he went in
The pool where two Frogs live dries up in the summer heat
The Frogs leave it together to look for a new home
They come across a deep well full of water
One Frog suggests they go down and live in the well
The other holds back, asking how they would get out if the water ran dry
A Lamp, overfilled with oil and burning brightly, boasts that it gives more light than the sun
A sudden gust of wind blows the Lamp out
Its owner lights it again
The owner tells the Lamp to stop boasting and shine quietly from now on
A Cat learns that a house is overrun with Mice and gets into it
She catches and eats the Mice one at a time
Afraid for their lives, the Mice stay hidden in their holes
Unable to reach them, the Cat decides to lure them out with a trick
She hangs from a peg and pretends to be dead
A Mouse peeks out, sees her, and says they will not go near her even if she turns into a meal-bag
A rich man holds a great feast
His Dog invites a friend, a stranger Dog, to come and share the leftovers with him that night
The invited Dog arrives at the agreed time
Seeing the preparations, the guest rejoices and resolves to eat enough to last him today and tomorrow
The Cook sees him among the dishes, grabs him by the paws, and throws him out the window
He lands hard and limps away, howling
Other street dogs hear him, come up, and ask how he enjoyed his supper
He tells them he drank so much wine that he remembers nothing, not even how he got out of the house
A Prince has some Monkeys trained to dance
Dressed in fine robes and masks, the Monkeys perform the dance many times to great applause
A mischievous courtier throws a handful of nuts onto the stage
At the sight of the nuts the Monkeys forget their dancing and act like monkeys again
They pull off their masks, tear their robes, and fight each other for the nuts
The show ends with the audience laughing at them and mocking them
A Seagull swallows a fish that is too large and bursts its gullet
The Seagull lies down on the shore to die
A Kite sees him and says he deserves his fate, since a bird of the air has no business looking for food in the sea
A Lion comes across a Hare who is fast asleep
Just as he is about to seize her, a young Hart trots past
The Lion leaves the Hare and goes after the Hart
The noise frightens the Hare awake and she runs away
After a long chase the Lion fails to catch the Hart
The Lion comes back to eat the Hare
Finding the Hare gone, the Lion says it serves him right for letting go of the food he had in hand in the hope of getting more
A Bald Knight who wears a wig goes out hunting
A sudden gust of wind blows off his hat and wig
His companions burst out laughing
He stops his horse and joins in the joke, saying it is no wonder borrowed hair flies off him when it had already left the man it grew on
The young Monkey its Mother loves is smothered by her excessive affection
The young Monkey she neglects survives and grows up in spite of her neglect
A Shepherd penning his sheep for the night is about to shut a wolf in with them
His Dog sees the wolf and asks him how the sheep can be safe if he lets a wolf into the fold
The Woodcutter cuts down a Mountain Oak
He splits the trunk with wedges made from the Oak's own branches
The Oak sighs that it does not mind the axe blows but grieves at being torn apart by wedges made from its own branches
A Wasp settles on a Snake's head and stings him over and over, wounding him fatally
The Snake, in agony, sees a wagon heavily loaded with wood
He deliberately puts his head under its wheels, saying that he and his enemy will at least die together
A Cottager and his wife come to believe that their Hen, which lays a golden egg each day, has a lump of gold inside it
They kill the Hen to get the gold
They find the Hen no different inside from their other hens
Hoping to get rich all at once, they lose the gain they were sure of each day
Seeing travelers approach, the Crow flies up into a tree and perches on a branch
The Crow caws as loudly as she can
The travelers turn toward the sound and wonder what it foretells
One traveler tells his companion to go on, since a crow's cry is no omen
A skillful Bowman goes to the mountains to hunt
All the beasts of the forest flee as he approaches
The Lion alone challenges him to combat
The Bowman shoots an arrow and wounds the Lion
The Bowman tells the Lion that the arrow is his messenger, a sample of what he himself will be when he attacks
The wounded Lion rushes away in great fear
A Fox who saw it all urges the Lion to take courage and not retreat at the first attack
The Lion refuses, saying that if the messenger is so fearful he cannot face the man himself
When Man first sees the Camel, he is frightened by its size and runs away
Seeing how meek the Camel is, Man gathers courage and approaches him
Finding the Camel spiritless, Man puts a bridle in his mouth
Man lets a child drive the Camel
A Shepherd watching his Ass graze is suddenly alarmed by the cries of the enemy
The Shepherd begs the Ass to flee with him so that they are not both captured
The Ass refuses: the conqueror will not load him with two sets of panniers, so it does not matter whom he serves
A Woman decides to give her Hen a double ration of barley so that it lays two eggs a day
The Hen grows fat and sleek
The Hen never lays another egg
An Eagle builds her nest at the top of a tall oak
A Cat moves into a hole in the middle of the trunk
A Wild Sow and her young take shelter in a hollow at its foot
The Cat resolves to destroy the colony
The Cat climbs to the Eagle's nest and lies that the Sow means to uproot the oak and feed their young to her litter
The Eagle is frightened out of her senses
The Cat creeps down to the Sow's cave and lies that the Eagle will pounce on her piglets when she goes out
The Sow is filled with fear
The Cat pretends to hide herself in the hollow of the tree
At night the Cat goes out silently and gets food for herself and her kittens
By day the Cat pretends to be afraid and keeps watch
The Eagle, fearing the Sow, sits still on the branches
The Sow, terrified of the Eagle, does not dare leave her cave
The Eagle and the Sow and their families die of hunger
Their bodies give the Cat and her kittens plenty of food
A Serpent and an Eagle fight to the death
The Serpent gains the upper hand and is about to strangle the Eagle
A countryman sees them, runs up, loosens the Serpent's coil and frees the Eagle
The angry Serpent injects poison into the countryman's drinking horn
Unaware of the danger, the countryman is about to drink
The Eagle strikes his hand with its wing
The Eagle seizes the drinking horn in its talons and carries it off into the air
A Crow dying of thirst sees a pitcher and flies to it, hoping for water
He finds there is too little water in it for him to reach
He tries everything to reach the water, without success
He drops stones one by one into the pitcher
The water rises within his reach, and he saves his life
A Thief takes a room at an inn, hoping to steal enough to pay his bill
After waiting days in vain, he sees the Innkeeper sitting before his door in a handsome new coat
The Thief sits down beside him and talks with him
As the talk dies down, the Thief yawns and howls like a wolf
Asked why he howls, the Thief asks the Innkeeper to hold his clothes and lies that at his third yawn he turns into a wolf and attacks men
The Thief yawns a second time and howls again
Believing him, the Innkeeper is alarmed, gets up and tries to run away
The Thief catches hold of his coat and begs him to stay and hold his clothes
The Thief yawns a third time and howls terribly
The frightened Innkeeper leaves his new coat in the Thief's hand and runs into the inn
The Thief makes off with the coat and never returns
A Kid coming home from the pasture without protection is chased by a Wolf
Unable to escape, the Kid turns and asks the Wolf to play a tune for him to dance to before he dies
The Wolf agrees and plays the pipe while the Kid dances
Hounds hear the music, run up and chase the Wolf
The Wolf tells the Kid he deserves this for turning piper when he is only a butcher
A Man sends his Wife home to her father's house on a pretext, to see whether she is disliked there too
After a short time she comes back
Asked how she was treated, she says the herdsmen and shepherds looked at her with dislike
He tells her that if those who saw her only at dawn and dusk disliked her, those who spent the whole day with her must have felt much worse
A Horse, an Ox and a Dog, driven by the cold, seek shelter from Man
Man takes them in kindly, lights a fire and warms them
He gives the Horse oats, the Ox plenty of hay and the Dog meat from his own table
The grateful animals resolve to repay him
They divide his lifespan among themselves, each giving one part his own qualities
The Horse takes Man's earliest years and gives them his traits
The Ox takes the middle years
The last years are left to the Dog
Two travelers, one truthful and one a liar, come by chance to the land of the Apes
The Ape king orders them seized and brought before him
He has the Apes lined up on both sides and a throne set up for himself
He has the men brought in and asks what sort of king he seems to them
The Lying Traveler flatters him as a mighty king and his courtiers as fit to be ambassadors and generals
The Ape and his court order a handsome present for the flatterer
The truthful Traveler expects a bigger reward for telling the truth
Asked the same question, the truthful Traveler says the king is an excellent Ape and his companions are excellent Apes
The enraged king hands him over to the teeth and claws of his companions
A Fox meets a Lion for the first time and nearly dies of fright
Meeting him a second time, the Fox is alarmed, but less so
At the third meeting, the Fox boldly goes up to the Lion and starts a friendly conversation
The Peacock complains to Juno that the nightingale's song pleases everyone while his own voice makes him a laughingstock
Juno consoles him that he far surpasses others in beauty and size
The Peacock objects that silent beauty is useless while he is surpassed in song
A man carves a wooden image of Mercury and offers it for sale
When nobody buys it, he calls out that the statue is of a god who gives wealth
A bystander asks why he sells it when he could enjoy those gifts himself
The man replies that he needs help now and the god is slow with his gifts
A Lark builds her nest in the young green wheat in early spring
Her young grow almost to full strength and get their wings and feathers
The owner of the field sees the ripe crop and says he must ask his neighbors to help with the harvest
A young Lark hears him, tells his mother, and asks where they should move
The mother says there is no need to move yet, since a man who relies on friends is not in earnest
A few days later the owner returns and sees the overripe wheat shedding its grain
He says he will come himself tomorrow with laborers and hired reapers
The Lark tells her brood it is time to leave, since the man is now in earnest
The Goat, envying the Ass his larger ration, tells him he is shamefully treated with milling and heavy loads
The Goat advises the Ass to pretend to have a fit and fall into a ditch to get some rest
The Ass follows the advice, falls into a ditch and is badly bruised
The master sends for a doctor and asks his advice
The doctor tells him to put a Goat's lungs on the wounds
They kill the Goat at once
They heal the Ass
A Fox gets into an actor's house and rummages through his things
He comes upon a Mask shaped like a human head
Putting his paws on it, he says it is a beautiful head but worthless, since it has no brains
The Owl, kept awake by the Grasshopper's noise, begs her to stop chirping
The Grasshopper refuses and chirps louder the more the Owl pleads
The Owl turns to a trick, praises the Grasshopper's song, and invites her to share some nectar from Pallas
The thirsty, flattered Grasshopper eagerly flies up
The Owl comes out of her hollow, seizes her and kills her
A Fowler goes out with bird-lime and twigs to catch birds
Seeing a thrush in a tree, he fits his twigs and watches it intently, eyes on the sky
Looking up, he treads without knowing it on a sleeping Viper
The Viper turns and bites him
He falls into a faint
He laments that while hunting another he has himself fallen into the snares of death
A Lion lies in wait for three Bulls but is afraid to attack them while they stay together
Through cunning speeches he separates them
He attacks them as they graze alone
He eats them one by one at his leisure
A Wolf sees a Goat grazing on top of a steep cliff, out of his reach
He begs her to come down so she won't fall, adding that the tenderest grass is where he stands
The Goat refuses, saying he invites her not for the grass but because he wants food
The thirsty Wasps and Partridges come to a Farmer and beg him for water
They promise to repay him handsomely
The Partridges promise to dig around his vines for better grapes
The Wasps promise to stand guard and drive off thieves with their stings
The Farmer cuts them short and refuses: his two oxen do all this without promising, so he would rather give the water to them
Playing one day, a handsome Brother and an ugly Sister look into a mirror together
The Brother praises his own good looks
The Sister grows angry, taking his words as aimed at her
She runs to their father to get revenge
She spitefully accuses her Brother of using something that belongs only to girls
The father embraces and kisses both of them equally
He tells them both to look in the mirror every day: the son so as not to spoil his beauty by bad conduct, the daughter to make up for her plainness by virtue
A Fox sees a Lion locked in a cage, stands near him and insults him bitterly
The Lion replies that it is not the Fox who insults him but his own misfortune
A Frog comes out of the marsh and announces to all the beasts that he is a learned doctor who can cure every disease
A Fox asks how he can treat others when he cannot cure his own limp and wrinkled skin
A Crow is caught in a snare
He prays to Apollo for release and vows frankincense at his shrine
He is rescued
He forgets his promise
He is caught in a snare again
Passing over Apollo, he makes the same promise of frankincense to Mercury
Mercury appears and turns him down: how can he trust one who has cheated his former patron?
A young spendthrift runs through his inheritance until only one good cloak is left
He sees a Swallow, out before its season, skimming over a pool and twittering
Thinking summer has come, he sells his cloak
Winter returns with fresh frost and cold
He finds the Swallow dead on the ground
He blames the bird for coming too early, killing itself and ruining him
A Trumpeter leading the soldiers into battle is captured by the enemy
He begs his captors to spare him, pleading that he has killed no one and carries only a trumpet
They refuse, saying that is exactly why he must die, since his trumpet stirs the others to fight
The Ills, by their numbers, drive the Goods out of their share in human affairs and take over the earth
The Goods rise to heaven and ask for vengeance on their persecutors
They beg Jupiter to separate them from the Ills and make a lasting law to protect them
Jupiter grants the request and decrees that the Ills will visit earth together and the Goods one by one
An Ass puts on a Lion's skin
He roams the forest, frightening the foolish animals he meets
Coming upon a Fox, he tries to frighten him too
When he hears the voice, the Fox exclaims that he might have been frightened had he not heard the bray
A caged Dove boasts of how many young she has hatched
A Crow tells her to stop boasting, since the bigger her family, the more she has to grieve at seeing them imprisoned
Jupiter makes the first man, Neptune the first bull, and Minerva the first house
They argue over whose work is most perfect
They agree to make Momus judge and accept his decision
Envious Momus faults Neptune for not putting the bull's horns below its eyes
He faults Jupiter for not putting man's heart on the outside
He faults Minerva for not putting iron wheels under her house
Jupiter, angered by the endless faultfinding, removes Momus as judge
Jupiter expels Momus from Olympus
An Eagle swoops down from a high rock, seizes a lamb and carries it off
A Jackdaw who saw this is envious and decides to copy the Eagle
The Jackdaw flies around with whirring wings and lands on a large ram, meaning to carry it off
His claws get tangled in the fleece, and for all his fluttering he cannot free himself
The shepherd sees this, runs up and catches him
The shepherd clips the Jackdaw's wings
He takes him home at night and gives him to his children
When the children ask what bird it is, he says it is a Daw that would like them to think it an Eagle
The Lark is created before the earth
Her father dies
With no earth yet, she can find nowhere to bury him
She leaves him unburied for five days
On the sixth day she buries him in her own head
She gets her crest from this
A Gnat settles on a Bull's horn and stays there a long time
About to fly off, the Gnat buzzes and asks the Bull whether he would like him to go
The Bull replies that he never noticed the Gnat come and will not miss him when he goes
A Robber attacks two Soldiers traveling together
One Soldier runs away
The other stands his ground and fights back
The Robber is killed
The timid Soldier runs up, draws his sword, throws back his cloak and boasts that he will show the Robber whom he attacked
The brave Soldier rebukes him and tells him to sheathe his sword and hold his tongue, since he has seen how fast he runs away
An Eagle stops flying and asks a Lion to form an alliance with him
The Lion agrees only if the Eagle offers a guarantee, since he could fly away from any bargain
An Ass being driven along a highway suddenly bolts to the edge of a deep cliff
As he is about to throw himself over, his owner grabs his tail to pull him back
The Ass keeps struggling
The owner lets him go
The owner tells him to have his way, but to his own cost
A starving Wolf prowls in the morning looking for food
Passing a cottage, he hears a Mother threaten to throw her child out to the Wolf
The Wolf waits all day at the door
In the evening he hears the woman, cuddling her child, say that they will kill the Wolf if he comes
The Wolf goes home, gasping with cold and hunger
Asked by his mate why he is back so tired and without supper, he says it is because he believed a woman's words
A Hen finds a viper's eggs and keeps them warm
She hatches them
A Swallow rebukes her for hatching vipers that will harm everyone, starting with her
A Rich Man who cannot stand the smell of his neighbor's tannery presses the Tanner to move away
The Tanner keeps putting off his move, promising to leave soon
The Tanner stays on
The Rich Man gets used to the smell
No longer bothered, the Rich Man stops complaining
A Lion roaming through a forest steps on a thorn
He comes to a Shepherd and fawns on him as if asking for help
The Shepherd examines him, finds the thorn and pulls it out
Freed of his pain, the Lion goes back into the forest
Later the Shepherd is imprisoned on a false charge
He is sentenced to be thrown to the Lions
The Lion is let out of his cage
The Lion recognizes the Shepherd as the man who healed him
Instead of attacking, the Lion goes up to him and puts his paw in his lap
Hearing the story, the King orders the Lion freed into the forest
The King orders the Shepherd pardoned and returned to his friends
The Camel sees the Bull's horns, envies him and wants horns of his own
He goes to Jupiter and begs him for horns
Jupiter, annoyed at his greed, refuses
Jupiter takes away part of the Camel's ears
A man captures an Eagle
He clips the Eagle's wings at once
He puts him in the poultry-yard with the other birds
The Eagle is overcome with grief
A neighbor buys the Eagle
The neighbor lets his feathers grow back
The Eagle flies off
He catches a hare and brings it as a gift to his benefactor
A Fox who sees this advises him to win over his former owner instead, so that the man does not catch him and clip his wings again
A King dreams that his son will be killed by a lion
Afraid, he builds his son a palace decorated with life-size pictures of animals, including a lion
When the Prince sees the painted lion, his grief at being shut in bursts out again
Standing by the lion, he curses it and threatens it
He reaches toward a thorn-tree to cut a stick to beat the lion
A thorn pierces his finger, causing great pain and swelling
He faints
A violent fever sets in
The Prince dies a few days later
A starving Crow sees a Serpent asleep in a sunny corner
The Crow flies down and seizes him
The Serpent turns and gives the Crow a fatal bite
Dying, the Crow laments that what he took for a lucky find has been his ruin
The Father fails to end his quarrelling sons' disputes by exhortation
The Father tells his sons to bring him a bundle of sticks
The sons bring him the bundle
The Father puts the bundle into each son's hands in turn and orders him to break it
The sons try with all their strength and cannot break it
The Father unties the bundle and hands them the sticks one by one
The sons break the separate sticks easily
The Swallow and the Crow argue about their plumage
The Crow ends the argument, saying the Swallow's feathers do well in spring but his own protect him in winter
A Boy hunts locusts and catches many
The Boy takes a Scorpion for a locust and reaches out to grab him
The Scorpion shows his sting and warns the Boy that touching him would have cost him all his locusts too
The beasts argue over which animal bears the most young at a birth
The beasts rush to the Lioness, demand that she settle the dispute, and ask how many young she bears
The Lioness laughs and answers that she bears only one, but that one is a Lion
One winter a Farmer finds a Snake frozen stiff
The Farmer pities the Snake and puts it in his bosom
The Snake revives in the warmth
The Snake bites the Farmer and wounds him mortally
The Farmer dies, crying that he is rightly served for pitying a scoundrel
A Man and a Lion travel together through the forest
The Man and the Lion boast to each other of their strength
They pass a statue of a Man strangling a Lion, and the Man points to it as proof that men are stronger
The Lion replies that a man made the statue, and that lions would carve the Man under the Lion's paw
A Raven sees a Swan and wants plumage like his
Thinking the Swan's whiteness comes from washing, the Raven leaves the altars where he found food and moves to the lakes and pools
The Raven washes his feathers again and again but cannot change their colour
The Raven dies for lack of food
A team of Oxen drags a heavy wagon along a country lane
The Axle-trees groan and creak loudly
The Oxen turn and rebuke the wheels, saying the Oxen do the work and should be the ones to cry out
Cranes feed on the Farmer's newly sown wheat fields
For a long time the Farmer scares them off by swinging an empty sling
The Cranes find that the sling is only swung in the air and stop moving
The Farmer loads his sling with stones and kills many Cranes
The remaining Cranes leave his fields, telling each other that the man now means business
A Wolf resolves to disguise himself to get food more easily
Wearing a sheep's skin, the Wolf grazes with the flock and deceives the shepherd
In the evening the shepherd shuts the Wolf in the fold and secures the gate
At night the shepherd comes for meat, takes the Wolf by mistake for a sheep, and kills him
A Goatherd tries to call a stray Goat back to the flock by whistling and sounding his horn
The Goat ignores the summons
The Goatherd throws a stone and breaks the Goat's horn
The Goatherd begs the Goat not to tell his master
The Goat replies that the horn will speak even if he stays silent
A Man back from foreign travels boasts of the wonderful feats he performed
The Man claims that at Rhodes he made a leap no one could match, and that many people there could vouch for it
A bystander interrupts and tells him to suppose this is Rhodes and leap for them
A Boy puts his hand into a pitcher of filberts and grabs as many as he can hold
The Boy tries to pull out his hand, but the neck of the pitcher stops it
Unwilling to let go of the filberts, the Boy bursts into tears and laments
A bystander tells the Boy to settle for half and he will get his hand out easily
The Frogs, unhappy to have no ruler, send ambassadors to Jupiter asking for a King
Jupiter throws a huge log into the lake
Terrified by the splash, the Frogs hide at the bottom of the pool
Seeing that the log does not move, the Frogs swim up, climb onto it, and squat on it in contempt
The Frogs send a second deputation asking Jupiter for another ruler
Jupiter gives them an Eel to rule them
Finding the Eel too good-natured, the Frogs send a third time asking for another King
Jupiter, displeased, sends them a Heron
The Heron eats the Frogs day after day until none are left
A Lion, tired by the heat, falls asleep in his den
A Mouse runs over the Lion's mane and ears and wakes him
The Lion gets up in a rage and searches the den for the Mouse
A Fox mocks the Lion for being afraid of a Mouse
The Lion replies that he does not fear the Mouse but resents its impudence
A greying middle-aged Man courts two women at once, one young and one old
Each time he visits, the older woman pulls out some of his black hairs
The younger woman pulls out every grey hair she can find
The Man soon finds that he has no hair left
One evening an Astronomer, walking with his eyes on the sky, falls into a deep well
The Astronomer laments his bruises and cries for help
A neighbour runs to the well and learns what happened
The neighbour asks why, while prying into the heavens, he cannot see what is on earth
The Wolves blame the Dogs and tell the Sheep there could be peace if the Sheep sent the Dogs away
The Sheep are taken in and send the Dogs away
The Wolves destroy the unguarded flock
A Kid standing safe on a roof sees a Wolf passing and taunts him
The Wolf replies that it is the roof, not the Kid, that mocks him
An Ox drinking at a pool treads on young frogs and crushes one to death
The Mother Frog arrives, misses a son, and asks his brothers what happened to him
The young frogs tell her that a huge four-footed beast crushed him
The Mother Frog puffs herself up and asks whether the beast was as big as that
Her son tells her to stop, since she would burst before matching the monster's size
A dying Father, wanting his sons to care for the farm, calls them to his bedside
The Father tells his sons that a great treasure is hidden in one of his vineyards
The Father dies
The sons dig over every part of the land with spades and mattocks
The sons find no treasure, but the vines give an extraordinary crop
Two Game Cocks fight for mastery of the farmyard
One Cock puts the other to flight
The beaten Cock slinks off and hides in a quiet corner
The winning Cock flies up onto a high wall and crows in triumph
An Eagle swoops on the winning Cock and carries him off
The beaten Cock comes out of his corner and rules the farmyard unchallenged
A Monkey dances before the Beasts and pleases them
The Beasts elect the Monkey their King
A Fox, envious of the Monkey, finds a piece of meat in a trap
The Fox leads the Monkey to the trap, says she saved the meat for him as treasure, and urges him to take it
The Monkey approaches carelessly and is caught in the trap
The Monkey accuses the Fox of leading him into the snare on purpose
The Fox asks whether, with a mind like his, he means to be King of the Beasts
A passing Goat nibbles the Vine's young tendrils and leaves
The Vine rebukes the Goat and warns that it will supply the wine poured over him when he is sacrificed
The Dolphins and the Whales fight a fierce war
At the height of the battle a Sprat offers to settle their quarrel if they accept him as umpire
A Dolphin replies that they would rather be destroyed than let the Sprat interfere
A Shepherd finds a Wolf's cub and raises it
The Shepherd teaches the Wolf to steal lambs from neighbouring flocks
The Wolf warns the Shepherd to keep watch or he will lose some of his own flock
A mother Crab tells her son to walk straight instead of sideways
The young Crab promises to walk straight if she will show him how
The mother Crab tries and fails
The mother Crab accepts her child's reproof without protest
A Wolf is badly wounded by dogs and lies sick in his lair
Needing food, the Wolf asks a passing Sheep to bring him water, saying he will find meat himself
The Sheep refuses, saying the Wolf would then make him provide the meat too
A Wild Ass and a Lion form a hunting alliance, the Lion giving strength and the Ass speed
The Wild Ass and the Lion catch as many beasts as they need
The Lion divides the prey into three shares
The Lion claims the first share as King and the second as partner, and threatens the Ass with harm unless he gives up the third and runs off
Boatmen sailing past see the one-eyed Doe and wound her mortally
The dying Doe laments that the seashore she chose for safety proved more dangerous than the land
A farmer's daughter carries her pail of milk from the field to the farmhouse
She daydreams of selling the milk, buying eggs, raising chickens, buying a gown, and refusing every suitor
She tosses her head, the pail falls, and the milk and all her plans are lost
A Wolf meets a well-fed Mastiff with a wooden collar on his neck
The Wolf asks who feeds him so well yet makes him drag the log, and the Mastiff answers that it is his master
The Wolf says he would wish no friend of his such a plight, since the chain's weight would spoil any appetite
A Boar charges the dying old Lion and takes revenge for an old injury with his tusks
A Bull gores the Lion with his horns
Seeing that the Lion can be attacked safely, the Ass kicks him in the forehead
The dying Lion says that suffering this from the Ass is like dying twice
Travellers on the seashore climb a cliff and see what they take for a large ship
The travellers wait, hoping to see it come into harbour
As the wind drives it nearer, they find it is at most a small boat
When it reaches the beach, they find it is only a bundle of sticks
One traveller tells the others they have waited for nothing but a load of wood
Mercury decides to find out how highly mortals value him
Mercury disguises himself as a man and visits a Sculptor's studio
Mercury asks the price of statues of Jupiter and Juno, and the Sculptor names it
Mercury points to a statue of himself and says it must cost much more
The Sculptor replies that he will throw that one in free if Mercury buys the other two
A Fox running from the hounds begs a Woodcutter to show him a safe hiding place
The Woodcutter tells the Fox to shelter in his hut
The Fox creeps into the hut and hides in a corner
The huntsman arrives and asks the Woodcutter whether he has seen the Fox
The Woodcutter says he has not, but all the while points to the hut
The huntsman ignores the pointing, believes his words, and hurries on
The Fox leaves without thanking the Woodcutter
The Woodcutter calls the Fox ungrateful for owing him his life and not thanking him
The Fox replies that he would have thanked him if his hands had not betrayed his words
A Wolf steals a lamb from a fold and carries it toward his lair
A Lion meets the Wolf and takes the lamb from him
From a safe distance the Wolf protests that the Lion has wrongly taken what was his
The Lion jeers, asking whether the lamb was rightfully his, the gift of a friend
An Ant goes to the river to drink, is swept away by the current, and nearly drowns
A Dove on an overhanging tree drops a leaf into the stream near the Ant
The Ant climbs onto the leaf and floats safely to the bank
A birdcatcher comes, stands under the tree, and sets his lime-twigs for the Dove
The Ant sees what he is doing and stings him on the foot
In pain, the birdcatcher throws down his twigs
The noise makes the Dove fly away
The Hares, weary of their own timidity, resolve to end their lives by leaping from a cliff into a lake
The Hares run off in great numbers to do it
The Frogs on the bank hear them coming and rush into the deep water
Seeing the Frogs vanish, one Hare tells the others to stop, since there are creatures more timid than they are
A rich man buys a Goose and a Swan at the market
The rich man fattens the Goose for his table and keeps the Swan for its song
When the time comes to kill the Goose, the cook goes to fetch him at night, in the dark
The cook catches the Swan by mistake
Threatened with death, the Swan bursts into song and so makes himself known
The Swan's song saves his life
A Fisherman catches a single small Fish after a day's work
The Fish begs for his life, asking to be put back to grow large and be caught again later
The Fisherman refuses, saying he will not give up a certain gain for an uncertain larger one
A timid Hunter looking for a Lion's tracks asks a woodman whether he has seen its footprints or knows its lair
The woodman offers to show him the Lion himself at once
The Hunter, pale and teeth chattering, declines, saying he wants only the tracks, not the Lion
An Arab camel-driver finishes loading his Camel and asks whether he would rather go uphill or downhill
The Camel asks in return whether the level road through the desert is closed
A Miller and his son drive their Ass to a fair to sell him
Women at a well mock them for walking when they could ride
The Miller puts his son on the Ass
Old men rebuke the son for riding while his old father walks
The Miller makes his son get down and rides the Ass himself
Women and children scold the Miller for riding while the boy struggles to keep up
The Miller takes his son up behind him
A citizen near the town tells them they would be better able to carry the Ass than it them
The Miller and his son tie the Ass's legs and try to carry him on a pole over a bridge
Crowds gather to laugh at the sight
The Ass, upset by the noise and the handling, breaks the cords, slips off the pole, and falls into the river
The Miller, vexed and ashamed, goes home, having lost his Ass
Thieves break into a house, find only a Cock, steal him, and flee
At home the thieves get ready to kill the Cock
The Cock begs for his life, saying he is useful because he wakes men to their work
The thieves refuse, saying that is exactly why they must kill him
From the shore a Philosopher watches a ship sink and everyone on board drown
The Philosopher denounces Providence for letting many innocent people die for the sake of one criminal
Ants surround the Philosopher near their nest, and one climbs up and stings him
The Philosopher tramples all the Ants to death
Mercury appears, strikes him with his wand, and asks whether he, who treated the Ants the same way, should judge Providence
A Peasant finds an Eagle caught in a trap and, admiring it, sets it free
Seeing the Peasant sitting under an unsafe wall, the Eagle flies at him and snatches a bundle from his head
The Peasant gets up to chase the Eagle, and the Eagle drops the bundle
The Peasant picks up the bundle, goes back, and finds that the wall has collapsed
The Peasant marvels at the service the Eagle has done him
The Lion, the Fox and the Ass agree to hunt together
The three take a large haul of game
The Lion asks the Ass to divide the haul
The Ass divides it into three equal shares and invites the other two to choose first
The Lion flies into a rage and devours the Ass
The Lion asks the Fox to divide the haul
The Fox heaps nearly everything into one pile and keeps only a scrap for himself
The Lion asks the Fox who taught him the art of division
The Fox answers that he learned it from what happened to the Ass
A Bull running from a Lion hides in a cave the shepherds had recently used
A He-Goat left in the cave attacks the Bull with his horns
The Bull tells the Goat to butt away, since he fears only the Lion, and warns that he will show the Goat his strength once the Lion is gone
The Oaks complain to Jupiter that, of all trees, they are most in danger of the axe
Jupiter answers that they have only themselves to thank, because they are so useful to carpenters and farmers
A Hound starts a Hare from his lair
After a long run the Hound gives up the chase
A goat-herd mocks the Hound, saying the little one is the better runner
The Hound replies that he ran only for a dinner, but the Hare ran for his life
A Bull finds a lion's cub asleep and gores him to death
The Lioness comes up and bitterly laments her whelp
A wild-boar Hunter, from a distance, tells her to think of all the men whose children she has killed
A Fox swimming a rapid river is swept into a deep ravine and lies there bruised and unable to move
A swarm of hungry blood-sucking flies settles on him
A passing Hedgehog offers to drive the flies away
The Fox refuses and begs him not to disturb them
The Fox explains that the sated flies would only be replaced by hungrier ones that would drain his remaining blood
A Stag asks a Sheep to lend him a measure of wheat, naming the Wolf as his surety
The Sheep, suspecting fraud, excuses herself, saying she could never find either of them on the day of payment
A Wizard sits in the marketplace telling the fortunes of passers-by
Someone runs up and tells him his house has been broken into and his goods are being stolen
The Wizard sighs heavily and runs off home
A neighbour sees him running and mocks him for not foreseeing his own fortune
A Gnat tells a Lion he does not fear him, boasts that he is the stronger, and challenges him to fight
The Gnat sounds his horn, fastens on the Lion and stings him on the nostrils and hairless parts of the face
Trying to crush the Gnat, the Lion tears himself with his own claws
The Gnat, victorious, flies away buzzing a song of triumph
The Gnat gets caught in a cobweb
A spider eats the Gnat
The Gnat laments that he, who beat the hugest beasts, should die by the smallest of insects
A starving Fox sees clusters of ripe grapes hanging from a vine
She tries every trick to reach them, but tires herself out in vain
She turns away, hiding her disappointment, and says the grapes are sour
Passers-by break the Walnut-Tree's branches with stones and sticks to get its nuts
The Walnut-Tree cries out that those it cheers with its fruit repay it with such pain
A Stag intrudes on the Horse's plain and shares his pasture
The Horse, wanting revenge, asks a man to help him punish the Stag
The man says he will make weapons against the Stag if the Horse takes a bit and carries him
The Horse agrees and lets the man mount him
The Horse finds that, instead of getting revenge, he has made himself man's slave
A Thief comes at night to break into a house, bringing slices of meat to quiet the Housedog
The Thief throws the pieces of meat to the Dog
The Dog refuses to be silenced, saying the sudden kindness only makes him more watchful
A Weasel, too old and weak to catch mice, rolls himself in flour
The Weasel lies down in a dark corner
A Mouse, taking him for food, leaps on him
The Weasel catches the Mouse and squeezes it to death
A second, a third and more mice die the same way
A very old Mouse sees through the trick from a safe distance
The old Mouse tells the Weasel he may prosper only as much as he really is what he pretends to be
The Hares make speeches to the assembly, arguing that all should be equal
The Lions reply that the Hares' words are good but lack claws and teeth like theirs
A hungry Hawk sees a Nightingale singing on an oak, swoops down and seizes him
The Nightingale begs to be let go, saying he is too small and the Hawk should hunt bigger birds
The Hawk refuses, saying he would be mad to let go of food in hand for birds not yet in sight
A Dog and a Cock, great friends, agree to travel together
At nightfall they take shelter in a thick wood
The Cock perches on the branches of a tree and the Dog beds down in the hollow trunk
At dawn the Cock crows loudly several times
A Fox hears him, comes under the tree and flatters the Cock, hoping to eat him
The suspicious Cock asks the Fox to go round and wake his porter in the trunk below to let him in
The Fox approaches the tree
The Dog springs out, catches the Fox and tears him to pieces
The Geese and the Cranes feed in the same meadow
A birdcatcher comes to snare them in his nets
The Cranes, light of wing, fly away as he approaches
The Geese, slower and heavier, are caught
A Lion, wanting to catch a Bull but afraid of his size, decides to use a trick
The Lion falsely tells the Bull he has killed a fine sheep and invites him home to share it
Approaching the den, the Bull sees huge spits and caldrons and no sign of a sheep
The Bull quietly leaves without a word
The Lion asks why he is leaving so abruptly without greeting his host
The Bull replies that he sees no sign of a slaughtered sheep, only every preparation for dining on a bull
A Horse, proud of his fine trappings, meets an Ass on the highway
The heavily laden Ass moves slowly out of the way
The Horse threatens to kick him
The Ass keeps silent and appeals silently to the justice of the gods
The Horse becomes broken-winded and his owner sends him to the farm
The Ass sees the Horse pulling a dungcart and taunts him about his lost trappings
A Fly on a chariot's axle scolds the Draught-Mule for slowness and threatens to sting his neck
The Mule replies that he ignores the Fly's threats and heeds only the driver above
Some Fishermen haul in their nets
Finding the nets very heavy, they dance for joy, expecting a large catch
They drag the nets ashore and find only a few fish, the nets full of sand and stones
The Fishermen are bitterly downcast at the disappointment
An old man among them urges them to stop lamenting
A Wolf accuses a Fox of theft
The Fox flatly denies the charge
An Ape undertakes to judge between them
Each of them states his case in full
The Ape rules that the Wolf never lost what he claims, and that the Fox did steal what he denies
A Wolf's whelp is brought to a Blind Man, who is asked to feel it and say what it is
The Blind Man feels it
Unsure, he says he cannot tell fox cub from wolf whelp, but it would not be safe to let it into the sheepfold
A Wolf coming out of an oat field meets a Horse and urges him to go in, claiming he left the oats untouched for his friend
The Horse replies that if wolves ate oats, the Wolf would never have spared them
In winter a Dog, curled up small from the cold, decides to build himself a house
In summer he sleeps stretched out full length and seems to himself very large
He decides that building a house big enough for him would be neither easy nor necessary
At sundown a Wolf sees his own shadow stretched and magnified
The Wolf tells himself that someone his size need not fear the Lion and should be king of the beasts
A Lion falls on the Wolf and kills him
The Wolf cries, too late, that thinking too highly of himself has destroyed him
The Birds wage war on the Beasts, each side winning by turns
A Bat, fearing the outcome, keeps fighting on whichever side seems stronger
Peace is proclaimed
The Bat's deceit becomes plain to both sides
Both sides condemn the Bat for treachery
The Bat is driven out of the daylight
From then on the Bat hides in dark places and flies only alone and at night
An Owl advises the Birds to pull up the acorn as it sprouts, warning that it will give mistletoe and bird-lime to catch them
The Owl advises them to pluck up the flax seed men have sown
Seeing an archer approach, the Owl warns that he will make feathered darts that fly faster than birds
The Birds disbelieve her and call her mad
Later, finding her words true, the Birds marvel at her knowledge and think her the wisest of birds
The Owl gives them no more advice and laments their past folly alone
An eagle pounces on a Hare
The Hare sobs and cries like a child
A Sparrow scolds the Hare, asking where her famous speed has gone
A hawk suddenly seizes the Sparrow and kills him
The dying Hare, comforted, says the Sparrow who mocked her now has the same misfortune
A Flea asks an Ox why, so huge and strong, he slaves for men, while the tiny Flea feeds on them freely
The Ox replies that men love and care for him and often pat him, and he does not want to be ungrateful
The Flea exclaims that the patting the Ox likes means certain death for him
A Man who wants to buy an Ass agrees with its owner to try it out first
The Man takes the Ass home and puts him in the straw-yard with his other asses
The Ass leaves the others and joins the laziest and greediest of them
The Man puts a halter on the Ass and leads him back to his owner
Asked how he tested the Ass so quickly, the Man says he knows it will be just like the companion it chose
A Man and a Satyr drink together to seal an alliance
On a cold day the Man blows on his fingers
The Satyr asks why, and the Man says it is to warm his hands
Later they sit down to eat, and the food is scalding hot
The Man blows on his dish
The Satyr asks again, and the Man says it is to cool the meat
The Satyr breaks off the friendship with a man who blows hot and cold with the same breath
At the Beasts' grand entertainment, the Monkey stands up and dances
The Monkey delights the assembly and sits down to universal applause
The Camel, envious, offers to dance for the guests in his turn
The Camel dances ridiculously
The indignant Beasts beat the Camel with clubs and drive him out
Some starving Dogs see cowhides soaking in a river
Unable to reach the hides, they agree to drink up the river
The Dogs burst from drinking long before they reach the hides
A Workman felling wood by a river accidentally drops his axe into a deep pool
He sits on the bank and laments his loss
Mercury appears and asks why he is weeping
The Workman tells Mercury what has happened
Mercury dives, brings up a golden axe and asks if it is his
The Workman says it is not
Mercury dives again, brings up a silver axe and asks again
The Workman says it is not his
Mercury dives a third time and brings up the lost axe
