Medea promises to make Talos immortal
Medea draws out the nail at the end of his vein
All the ichor gushes out and Talos dies
Poeas shoots Talos dead in the ankle
Medea invokes the gods by whom Jason had sworn
Medea often upbraids Jason with his ingratitude
Medea sends the bride a robe steeped in poison
Glauce puts on the robe and is consumed by fierce fire
Her father Creon, going to her rescue, is consumed with her
Medea kills Mermerus and Pheres, her children by Jason
Medea gets from the Sun a car drawn by winged dragons
Medea flees on it to Athens
Medea comes to Athens
Medea plots against Theseus
Medea is driven from Athens with her son Medus
Medus conquers many barbarians
Marching against the Indians, Medus meets his death
Medea comes unknown to Colchis
Perses has deposed his brother Aeetes
Medea kills Perses
Medea restores the kingdom to her father
Medea, fleeing, leaves her infant children as suppliants on the altar of Hera of the Height
The Corinthians remove the children and wound them to death
Apis turns his power into a tyranny
Thelxion and Telchis conspire against Apis and kill him
Argus kills the bull that was ravaging Arcadia
Argus clothes himself in the bull's hide
A satyr wrongs the Arcadians and robs them of their cattle
Argus stands up to the satyr and kills him
Argus avenges the murder of Apis by putting the guilty to death
Zeus seduces Io while she is priestess of Hera
Hera catches Zeus with Io
Zeus turns Io into a white cow with a touch
Zeus swears that he has not known her
Hera asks Zeus for the cow for herself
Hera sets Argus the All-seeing to guard the cow
Argus ties the cow to the olive tree in the grove of the Mycenaeans
Zeus orders Hermes to steal the cow
Hermes cannot steal the cow secretly, because Hierax has told on him
Hermes kills Argus with a thrown stone
Hera sends a gadfly to torment the cow
The cow comes first to the gulf later named Ionian after her
Io journeys through Illyria and over Mount Haemus
Io crosses the Thracian Straits, later called the Bosphorus after her
Io goes to Scythia and the Cimmerian land and wanders over wide lands and seas of Europe and Asia
Io comes at last to Egypt
Io gets back her own form
Io gives birth to a son, Epaphus, beside the Nile
Hera asks the Curetes to do away with the child
The Curetes do away with Epaphus
Zeus learns of it and kills the Curetes
Io sets out to search for the child
Io roams all over Syria
Io learns that the wife of the king of Byblus is nursing her son
Io finds Epaphus
Io comes back to Egypt
Agenor goes away to Phoenicia and reigns there
Belus settles his son Danaus in Libya and his son Egyptus in Arabia
Egyptus conquers the country of the Melampods
Danaus and Egyptus quarrel over the kingdom
Fearing the sons of Egyptus, Danaus builds a ship on Athena's advice, the first ship ever built
Danaus puts his daughters on board and flees
Touching at Rhodes on the way, Danaus comes to Argos
The reigning king Gelanor hands over the kingdom to Danaus
Poseidon, angry with Inachus for testifying that the land belonged to Hera, has dried up even the springs, so the country is without water
Danaus sends his daughters to draw water
Searching for water, Amymone throws a dart at a deer and hits a sleeping satyr
The satyr starts up and tries to force her
Poseidon appears
The satyr runs away
Amymone lies with Poseidon
Poseidon shows her the springs at Lerna
The sons of Egyptus come to Argos, urge Danaus to give up his enmity, and ask to marry his daughters
Distrusting them and resenting his exile, Danaus still agrees to the marriage
Danaus shares out the girls among the sons of Egyptus, partly by lot
Danaus holds a feast and gives his daughters daggers
The daughters kill their bridegrooms in their sleep, all except Hypermnestra, who spares Lynceus because he respected her virginity
Danaus shuts Hypermnestra up under guard
The other daughters bury the bridegrooms' heads in Lerna and give funeral honors to their bodies before the city
Athena and Hermes purify the daughters at Zeus's command
Danaus later joins Hypermnestra to Lynceus
Danaus gives his other daughters to the winners of an athletic contest
Nauplius, who lured sailors to their death with beacon lights, dies the same death himself
The twins Acrisius and Proetus quarrel while still in the womb
Grown up, they make war on each other for the kingdom
Acrisius wins and drives Proetus out of Argos
Proetus goes to Lycia, to the court of Iobates
His father-in-law restores Proetus to his own land with a Lycian army
Proetus occupies Tiryns, which the Cyclopes fortify for him
The brothers divide the Argive land, Acrisius reigning over Argos and Proetus over Tiryns
The daughters of Proetus refuse to accept the rites of Dionysus
The daughters go mad
In their madness they roam over the whole Argive land
They run wildly through Arcadia, the Peloponnese and the desert
Melampus the seer promises to cure the girls if he is given a third of the kingdom
Proetus refuses to pay so high a fee
The daughters rave worse than ever, and the other women rave with them
The women leave their houses, kill their own children and flock to the desert
Proetus agrees to pay the fee
Melampus raises his price: as much land again for his brother Bias
Fearing a still higher price, Proetus agrees to these terms
Melampus and the strongest young men chase the women from the mountains to Sicyon with shouts and a frenzied dance
Iphinoe, the eldest daughter, dies in the chase
The other daughters are purified and recover their wits
Proetus gives the daughters in marriage to Melampus and Bias
The daughters of Proetus scorn the wooden image of Hera
The daughters go mad
Bellerophon accidentally kills his brother Deliades
Bellerophon comes to Proetus
Proetus purifies him
Stheneboea, Proetus's wife, falls in love with Bellerophon
Stheneboea sends him proposals for a meeting
Bellerophon rejects them
Stheneboea tells Proetus that Bellerophon made her an indecent proposal
Proetus believes her and gives Bellerophon a letter for Iobates, written to ask Iobates to kill him
Iobates reads the letter and orders Bellerophon to kill the Chimera, expecting the beast to kill him
Mounted on the winged horse Pegasus, Bellerophon flies up and shoots the Chimera down
Iobates orders him to fight the Solymi
Bellerophon finishes that task too
Iobates orders him to fight the Amazons
Bellerophon kills them
Iobates sets the bravest Lycians in ambush to kill him
Bellerophon kills them all
Admiring his prowess, Iobates shows him the letter and asks him to stay
Iobates gives him his daughter Philonoe
Dying, Iobates leaves him the kingdom
Acrisius asks the oracle how he can have male children
The god says his daughter will bear a son who will kill him
Afraid, Acrisius builds a bronze chamber underground and keeps Danae shut in it
Proetus seduces Danae (the first version given)
Zeus, in the shape of a stream of gold pouring through the roof into Danae's lap, lies with her
Acrisius learns that Danae has had a child, Perseus
Refusing to believe that Zeus seduced her, Acrisius shuts Danae and the child in a chest and throws it into the sea
The chest washes ashore on Seriphus
Dictys takes up the boy and brings him up
Polydectes, king of Seriphus, falls in love with Danae but cannot get at her, because Perseus is grown up
Polydectes calls his friends together, Perseus among them, on the pretext of collecting a wedding gift for Hippodamia
Perseus declares that he would not stop even at the Gorgon's head
Polydectes demands horses from the others
Not getting horses from Perseus, Polydectes orders him to bring the Gorgon's head
Guided by Hermes and Athena, Perseus makes his way to the daughters of Phorcus
Perseus takes their one eye and one tooth
When they ask for them back, Perseus says he will return them if they show him the way to the nymphs
The daughters of Phorcus show him the way
Perseus gives back the tooth and the eye
Perseus comes to the nymphs and gets what he wanted
Perseus slings the wallet about him, fits the winged sandals to his ankles and puts on the cap of Hades
Perseus receives an adamantine sickle from Hermes
Perseus flies to the ocean and finds the Gorgons asleep
With Athena guiding his hand, looking at the Gorgon's reflection in a bronze shield, Perseus cuts off Medusa's head
The winged horse Pegasus and Chrysaor spring from the Gorgon
Perseus puts the head in the wallet and goes back
The other Gorgons wake and chase Perseus
They cannot see him, because the cap hides him
Coming to Ethiopia, Perseus finds the king's daughter Andromeda set out as prey for a sea monster
Cassiepea, wife of Cepheus, competes with the Nereids in beauty and boasts that she is better than them all
The Nereids are angered
Poseidon, sharing their anger, sends a flood and a monster against the land
Ammon foretells deliverance if Andromeda is exposed as prey to the monster
Forced by the Ethiopians, Cepheus binds his daughter to a rock
Seeing Andromeda, Perseus falls in love with her
Perseus promises Cepheus to kill the monster if he may have the rescued girl as his wife
The terms are sworn to
Perseus stands up to the monster and kills it
Perseus frees Andromeda
Phineus, Cepheus's brother, to whom Andromeda was first promised, plots against Perseus
Perseus discovers the plot
By showing the Gorgon's head, Perseus turns Phineus and his fellow plotters to stone
Coming to Seriphus, Perseus finds that his mother and Dictys have fled to the altars from the violence of Polydectes
Perseus enters the palace, where Polydectes has gathered his friends
With his face turned away, Perseus shows the Gorgon's head, and all who see it are turned to stone where they stand
Perseus makes Dictys king of Seriphus
Perseus gives the sandals, the wallet and the cap back to Hermes
Perseus gives the Gorgon's head to Athena
Hermes returns the sandals, the wallet and the cap to the nymphs
Athena sets the Gorgon's head in the middle of her shield
Medusa wants to match Athena even in beauty
Medusa is beheaded for Athena's sake
Perseus hurries with Danae and Andromeda to Argos to see Acrisius
Learning of this and dreading the oracle, Acrisius leaves Argos for the Pelasgian land
Teutamides, king of Larissa, holds athletic games in honor of his dead father
Perseus comes to compete
In the pentathlon Perseus's quoit strikes Acrisius on the foot and kills him at once
Seeing that the oracle is fulfilled, Perseus buries Acrisius outside the city
Ashamed to claim the inheritance of the man he killed, Perseus goes to Megapenthes at Tiryns and exchanges kingdoms with him
Perseus reigns over Tiryns and fortifies Midea and Mycenae as well
Poseidon carries off Hippothoe to the Echinadian Islands
Poseidon lies with Hippothoe there
Poseidon makes her grandson Pterelaus immortal by planting a golden hair in his head
Zeus declares among the gods that the descendant of Perseus about to be born will reign over Mycenae
Out of jealousy Hera persuades the Ilithyias to hold back Alcmena's delivery
Hera arranges for Eurystheus, son of Sthenelus, to be born a seven-month child
The sons of Pterelaus come with some Taphians and claim from Electryon the kingdom of their grandfather Mestor
Electryon ignores the claim
The Taphians drive off Electryon's cattle
The sons of Electryon defend themselves, and the two sets of sons challenge and kill each other, leaving only Licymnius and Everes alive
The surviving Taphians sail away with the cattle and leave them with Polyxenus, king of the Eleans
Amphitryon ransoms the cattle from Polyxenus and brings them to Mycenae
Wishing to avenge his sons, Electryon plans a war on the Teleboans
Electryon hands over the kingdom and his daughter Alcmena to Amphitryon, binding him by oath to keep her a virgin until his return
As Electryon is receiving the cows back, one charges, and Amphitryon throws his club at her
The club bounces off the cow's horns, strikes Electryon on the head and kills him
Sthenelus uses this as a pretext to banish Amphitryon from all Argos
Sthenelus seizes the throne of Mycenae and Tiryns
Sthenelus sends for Atreus and Thyestes and hands Midea over to them
Amphitryon goes to Thebes with Alcmena and Licymnius
Creon purifies Amphitryon
Alcmena says she will marry Amphitryon when he has avenged her brothers' death
Amphitryon promises to do it, undertakes an expedition against the Teleboans and asks Creon to help
Creon says he will join if Amphitryon first rids the Cadmea of the vixen
Amphitryon takes on the task, although it is fated that nobody shall catch her
Amphitryon goes to Cephalus at Athens and persuades him, for a share of the spoils, to bring to the hunt the dog that catches whatever it chases
When the dog chases the vixen, Zeus turns them both to stone
With his allies, Amphitryon ravages the Taphian islands
Comaetho, daughter of Pterelaus, in love with Amphitryon, pulls the golden hair out of her father's head
Pterelaus dies
Amphitryon conquers all the islands
Amphitryon kills Comaetho
Amphitryon sails with the spoils for Thebes
Amphitryon gives the islands to Heleus and Cephalus
Before Amphitryon reaches Thebes, Zeus comes by night and makes the one night three times as long
Zeus takes the likeness of Amphitryon
Zeus sleeps with Alcmena
Zeus tells Alcmena what happened with the Teleboans
Amphitryon arrives, finds his wife does not welcome him, and asks why
Alcmena tells him that he came the night before and slept with her
Amphitryon learns from Tiresias how Zeus has enjoyed her
Alcmena bears two sons, Hercules by Zeus and Iphicles by Amphitryon
When the child is eight months old, Hera, wanting him destroyed, sends two huge serpents to the bed
Alcmena calls Amphitryon to help
Hercules gets up and strangles the serpents with his two hands
Hercules is taught chariot-driving by Amphitryon, wrestling by Autolycus, archery by Eurytus, fencing by Castor and the lyre by Linus
Linus, brother of Orpheus, has come to Thebes and become a Theban
Linus strikes Hercules
In a rage Hercules kills Linus with a blow of the lyre
Hercules is tried for murder
Hercules cites the law of Rhadamanthys on self-defence and is acquitted
Fearing he will do the like again, Amphitryon sends him to the cattle farm
There Hercules grows up and surpasses everyone in size and strength
In his eighteenth year, while with the herds, Hercules kills the lion of Cithaeron
Wishing to catch the lion, Hercules goes to Thespius, king of Thespiae
Thespius entertains Hercules for fifty days
Each night Thespius puts one of his fifty daughters to bed with Hercules, wanting all of them to have children by him
Thinking his bedfellow is always the same, Hercules lies with them all
Having overcome the lion, Hercules dresses in its skin and wears its scalp as a helmet
Returning from the hunt, Hercules meets heralds sent by Erginus to collect the Thebans' tribute
Amphitryon puts the serpents in the bed, wanting to learn which of the two children is his
Iphicles runs away
Hercules stands his ground
Amphitryon knows from this that Iphicles is his son
Perieres, charioteer of Menoeceus, wounds Clymenus, king of the Minyans, with a stone at Onchestus
Carried dying to Orchomenus, Clymenus charges his son Erginus to avenge his death
Erginus marches against Thebes and kills many Thebans
Erginus makes a sworn treaty that the Thebans pay him a hundred cattle a year for twenty years
Hercules mutilates the heralds, cutting off their ears, noses and hands
Hercules hangs these from their necks by ropes and tells them to take that tribute to Erginus and the Minyans
Angered, Erginus marches against Thebes
Given arms by Athena, Hercules takes command
Hercules kills Erginus
Hercules puts the Minyans to flight
Hercules makes the Minyans pay the Thebans double the tribute
Amphitryon falls fighting bravely
Creon gives Hercules his eldest daughter Megara as a prize for valor
Hercules receives a sword from Hermes, a bow and arrows from Apollo, a golden breastplate from Hephaestus and a robe from Athena
Hercules has cut himself a club at Nemea
Through Hera's jealousy Hercules is driven mad
Hercules throws his own children by Megara and two children of Iphicles into the fire
Hercules sentences himself to exile
Thespius purifies Hercules
Hercules goes to Delphi and asks the god where he should live
The priestess tells him to live at Tiryns, serve Eurystheus twelve years and perform the ten labours he sets, and so become immortal
Hercules goes to Tiryns and does what Eurystheus bids
Eurystheus orders him to bring the skin of the Nemean lion
On the way Hercules lodges at Cleonae with a day-laborer, Molorchus

At Nemea Hercules tracks the lion and shoots an arrow at it
Seeing that the beast cannot be wounded, Hercules raises his club and chases it
The lion takes refuge in a cave with two mouths
Hercules blocks up one entrance and comes in on the lion through the other
Hercules puts his arm round its neck and chokes it
Hercules carries the lion on his shoulders to Cleonae
Finding Molorchus on the last of the thirty days about to sacrifice to him as dead, Hercules sacrifices to Saviour Zeus
Hercules brings the lion to Mycenae
Amazed at his strength, Eurystheus forbids him to enter the city again and orders him to show his trophies outside the gates
Copreus, son of Pelops the Elean, kills Iphitus
Copreus flees to Mycenae
Eurystheus purifies Copreus
Copreus settles in Mycenae
Eurystheus orders Hercules, as a second labour, to kill the Lernaean hydra
With Iolaus driving his chariot, Hercules comes to Lerna
Hercules finds the hydra on a hill by the springs of Amymone
By shooting fiery arrows at it, Hercules forces it out
Hercules seizes it and holds it fast
The hydra winds itself round one of his feet and clings to him
Hercules smashes its heads with his club to no effect, since two grow for every one smashed
A huge crab comes to help the hydra and bites his foot
Hercules kills the crab
Hercules calls on Iolaus for help
Iolaus sets fire to part of the nearby wood and burns the roots of the heads with the brands, so they cannot grow again
Hercules cuts off the immortal head, buries it and puts a heavy rock on it
Hercules slits open the hydra's body and dips his arrows in the gall
Eurystheus says the labour will not count, because Iolaus helped
Eurystheus orders him, as a third labour, to bring the Cerynitian hind alive to Mycenae
Wishing neither to kill nor wound it, Hercules hunts it for a whole year
Worn out, the hind takes refuge on Mount Artemisius and goes on to the river Ladon
Hercules shoots it just as it is about to cross the river
Hercules catches it, puts it on his shoulders and hurries through Arcadia
Artemis and Apollo meet him, try to take the hind from him, and rebuke him for trying to kill her sacred animal
Pleading necessity and blaming Eurystheus, Hercules calms the goddess's anger
Hercules carries the hind alive to Mycenae
Eurystheus orders him, as a fourth labour, to bring the Erymanthian boar alive
Passing through Pholoe, Hercules is entertained by the centaur Pholus
Pholus serves Hercules roast meat while eating his own raw
Hercules asks for wine, and Pholus says he is afraid to open the jar that belongs to all the centaurs
Hercules tells him to take heart and opens the jar
Smelling the wine, the centaurs come to Pholus's cave armed with rocks and fir trees
Hercules drives back the first to enter, Anchius and Agrius, with firebrands
Hercules shoots the rest and chases them as far as Malea
The centaurs take refuge with Chiron
Hercules shoots at them, and the arrow passes through the arm of Elatus and sticks in Chiron's knee
Distressed, Hercules runs to Chiron, pulls out the arrow and applies a medicine Chiron gives him
Chiron's wound proves incurable
Chiron goes into his cave and wishes to die but cannot, being immortal
Prometheus offers himself to Zeus to be made immortal in Chiron's place
Chiron dies
The other centaurs scatter, some to Mount Malea, Eurytion to Pholoe and Nessus to the river Evenus
Poseidon takes in the rest at Eleusis and hides them in a mountain
Pholus draws an arrow from a corpse and wonders that so small a thing could kill such big creatures
The arrow slips from his hand, falls on his foot and kills him at once
Returning to Pholoe, Hercules finds Pholus dead and buries him
Hercules goes on to the boar hunt and drives the boar out of a thicket with shouts
Hercules drives the exhausted boar into deep snow and snares it
Hercules brings the boar to Mycenae
Eurystheus sets him a fifth labour: to carry out the dung of Augeas's cattle in a single day
Without mentioning Eurystheus's command, Hercules offers to clear the dung in one day if Augeas will give him a tenth of the cattle
Augeas, not believing it possible, promises
With Augeas's son Phyleus as witness, Hercules breaks through the foundations of the cattle yard
Having made an outlet, Hercules turns the rivers Alpheus and Peneus through the yard
Learning it was done at Eurystheus's command, Augeas refuses to pay, denies his promise and offers to go to arbitration
Called by Hercules, Phyleus testifies against his father before the arbitrators
In a rage, before the vote, Augeas orders Phyleus and Hercules out of Elis
Phyleus goes to Dulichium and settles there
Hercules goes to Dexamenus at Olenus
Hercules finds Dexamenus about to betroth his daughter Mnesimache, against his will, to the centaur Eurytion
Asked for help, Hercules kills Eurytion when he comes for his bride
Eurystheus will not count this labour either, saying it was done for pay
Eurystheus sets him a sixth labour: to drive away the Stymphalian birds
Countless birds have flocked to the lake in the wood for refuge, fearing the wolves
Not knowing how to drive them out, Hercules receives bronze castanets from Athena
Clashing them on a mountain above the lake, Hercules frightens the birds
Unable to bear the noise, the birds fly up in fright
Hercules shoots them
Eurystheus sets him a seventh labour: to bring the Cretan bull
This bull had carried Europa across the sea for Zeus (the first version given, Acusilaus's)
Hercules comes to Crete to attack the bull
Hercules asks Minos for help, and Minos tells him to fight and catch it himself
Hercules catches the bull and brings it to Eurystheus
After showing it to Eurystheus, Hercules lets it go free
Minos promises Poseidon to sacrifice whatever appears out of the sea
Poseidon sends up a bull from the sea
Struck by its beauty, Minos sends it to his herds and sacrifices another to Poseidon
Angered, Poseidon makes the bull savage
The bull roams to Sparta and all over Arcadia
The bull crosses the Isthmus and reaches Marathon in Attica
The bull harries the people there
Eurystheus sets him an eighth labour: to bring the mares of Diomedes the Thracian to Mycenae
Hercules sails with a band of volunteers
Hercules overpowers the grooms in charge of the mangers
Hercules drives the mares to the sea
The Bistones come in arms to the rescue
Hercules leaves the mares in the keeping of Abderus, his favorite
The mares kill Abderus by dragging him along
Hercules fights the Bistones, kills Diomedes and puts the rest to flight
Hercules brings the mares and gives them to Eurystheus
Eurystheus lets the mares go
The mares come to Mount Olympus
There the mares are killed by wild beasts
Eurystheus sets him a ninth labour: to bring the belt of Hippolyte, queen of the Amazons
Hercules sets sail with volunteers in a single ship and puts in at Paros
Two of the crew land and are killed by the sons of Minos
Angered, Hercules kills the sons of Minos on the spot
Hercules besieges the rest closely
The besieged send envoys asking him to take any two men he likes in place of the dead
Hercules raises the siege and takes on board Alcaeus and Sthenelus, sons of Androgeus
Hercules comes to Mysia, to Lycus, and is entertained by him
In a battle between Lycus and the king of the Bebryces, Hercules sides with Lycus and kills many, King Mygdon among them
Hercules takes much land from the Bebryces and gives it to Lycus
At the harbor of Themiscyra Hippolyte visits Hercules, asks why he has come, and promises him the belt
Hera, in the likeness of an Amazon, goes through the crowd saying the strangers are carrying off the queen
The Amazons in arms charge on horseback down to the ship
Seeing them armed, Hercules suspects treachery, kills Hippolyte and strips off her belt
After fighting the rest, Hercules sails away and puts in at Troy
Apollo and Poseidon, wanting to test Laomedon's insolence, take the likeness of men and undertake to fortify Pergamum for wages
Apollo and Poseidon fortify Pergamum
Laomedon will not pay them their wages
Apollo sends a pestilence
Poseidon sends a sea monster
Carried up by a flood, the monster snatches away the people of the plain
Oracles foretell deliverance if Laomedon exposes his daughter Hesione to the monster
Laomedon exposes Hesione, fastening her to the rocks by the sea
Seeing Hesione exposed, Hercules promises to save her if Laomedon will give him the mares Zeus gave for Ganymede
Laomedon says he will give them
Hercules kills the monster and saves Hesione
Laomedon will not give the promised reward
Hercules puts to sea, threatening to make war on Troy
Hercules puts in at Aenus and is entertained by Poltys
Sailing away, Hercules shoots dead Sarpedon, Poltys's lewd brother, on the beach at Aenus
At Thasos Hercules subdues the Thracians and gives the island to the sons of Androgeus
At Torone, challenged to wrestle by Polygonus and Telegonus, sons of Proteus, Hercules kills them in the match
Hercules brings the belt to Mycenae and gives it to Eurystheus
Hercules is ordered, as a tenth labour, to fetch the cattle of Geryon from Erythia
Journeying through Europe, Hercules kills many wild beasts
Hercules sets foot in Libya and goes on to Tartessus
Scorched by the Sun on the way, Hercules bends his bow at the god
Admiring his boldness, the Sun gives him a golden goblet
Hercules crosses the ocean in the goblet
Reaching Erythia, Hercules camps on Mount Abas
The dog Orthus rushes at him, and Hercules strikes it with his club
The herdsman Eurytion comes to help the dog, and Hercules kills him too
Menoetes, who pastures the cattle of Hades there, tells Geryon what has happened
Geryon catches Hercules by the river Anthemus driving off the cattle, fights him and is shot dead
Hercules loads the cattle into the goblet, sails to Tartessus and gives the goblet back to the Sun
Passing through Abderia, Hercules comes to Liguria
Ialebion and Dercynus, sons of Poseidon, try to rob him of the cattle, and Hercules kills them
Hercules goes on through Tyrrhenia
At Rhegium a bull breaks away, plunges into the sea and swims to Sicily
The bull passes through the country since called Italy and comes to the plain of Eryx, king of the Elymi
Eryx mixes the bull in with his own herds
Hercules leaves the cattle with Hephaestus and hurries off to look for the bull
Hercules finds it in Eryx's herds
Eryx refuses to give it up unless Hercules beats him at wrestling
Hercules beats Eryx three times and kills him in the wrestling
Hercules takes the bull and drives it with the herd to the Ionian Sea
At the creeks of the sea Hera sends a gadfly on the cows, and they scatter into the foothills of Thrace
Hercules pursues them, catches some and drives them to the Hellespont; the rest stay wild
Having gathered the cows with difficulty, Hercules blames the river Strymon and makes it unnavigable by filling it with rocks
Hercules brings the cattle to Eurystheus
Eurystheus sacrifices them to Hera
After eight years and a month, Eurystheus orders him, as an eleventh labour, to fetch golden apples from the Hesperides, refusing to count the labours of Augeas's cattle and the hydra
On his way Hercules comes to the river Echedorus
Cycnus, son of Ares and Pyrene, challenges him to single combat
Ares takes Cycnus's side and marshals the combat
A thunderbolt falls between the two and parts them
Going through Illyria to the river Eridanus, Hercules comes to the nymphs, daughters of Zeus and Themis
The nymphs show him where Nereus is
Hercules seizes Nereus asleep and, though the god turns into every kind of shape, binds him and holds him until he learns where the apples and the Hesperides are
Told the way, Hercules crosses Libya
Antaeus, son of Poseidon, forces Hercules to wrestle
Hercules hugs Antaeus, lifts him up, breaks him and kills him
After Libya, Hercules crosses Egypt
During a nine years' dearth in Egypt, the seer Phrasius declares it will end if a stranger is slaughtered to Zeus every year
Busiris slaughters the seer first, and then the strangers who land
Hercules too is seized and dragged to the altars
Hercules bursts his bonds and kills Busiris and his son Amphidamas
Crossing Asia, Hercules puts in at Thermydrae, harbor of the Lindians
Hercules unyokes a bullock from a cowherd's cart, sacrifices it and feasts
Unable to protect himself, the cowherd stands on a mountain and curses
Passing Arabia, Hercules kills Emathion, son of Tithonus
Traveling through Libya to the outer sea, Hercules receives the goblet from the Sun
Crossing to the mainland opposite, Hercules shoots on the Caucasus the eagle that was eating Prometheus's liver
Hercules frees Prometheus, taking the olive wreath as a bond for himself
Hercules presents Chiron to Zeus, as willing to die in Prometheus's place
(Told back) Prometheus had told Hercules not to go for the apples himself but to send Atlas, first taking the sky from him
Coming to Atlas in the land of the Hyperboreans, Hercules takes the advice and relieves Atlas of the sky
Atlas gets three apples from the Hesperides
Atlas, not wanting to hold the sky again, says he will carry the apples to Eurystheus himself and tells Hercules to hold the sky in his place
Hercules agrees, but on Prometheus's advice asks Atlas to hold the sky while he puts a pad on his head
Atlas lays the apples on the ground and takes the sky back
Hercules picks up the apples and leaves
Hercules brings the apples to Eurystheus
Eurystheus gives the apples to Hercules
Athena gets the apples from Hercules and takes them back, since they may not be set down anywhere
Hercules is set a twelfth labour: to bring Cerberus from Hades
Before setting out, Hercules goes to Eumolpus at Eleusis wishing to be initiated, offering to be adopted by Pylius since foreigners may not be initiated
Barred from the mysteries because he is not cleansed of killing the centaurs, Hercules is cleansed by Eumolpus and initiated
At Taenarum in Laconia Hercules goes down to Hades
Seeing him, the souls flee, all but Meleager and the Gorgon Medusa
Hercules draws his sword on the Gorgon as if she were alive
Hercules learns from Hermes that she is an empty phantom
Near the gates of Hades Hercules finds Theseus and Pirithous bound fast
Theseus and Pirithous stretch out their hands to him, hoping to be raised by his strength
Hercules takes Theseus by the hand and raises him up
When Hercules tries to raise Pirithous, the earth quakes and he lets go
Hercules rolls away the stone of Ascalaphus
Wishing to give the souls blood, Hercules kills one of the cattle of Hades
Menoetes, son of Ceuthonymus, challenges Hercules to wrestle and has his ribs broken
At Persephone's request Menoetes is let go
Hercules asks Pluto for Cerberus
Pluto tells him to take the beast if he can master it without his weapons
Hercules finds Cerberus at the gates of Acheron and, protected by his breastplate and the lion's skin, throws his arms round its head
Though the dragon in its tail bites him, Hercules keeps his grip until the beast gives in
Hercules carries Cerberus off and comes up through Troezen
Demeter turns Ascalaphus into a short-eared owl
Hercules shows Cerberus to Eurystheus
Hercules takes Cerberus back to Hades
After his labours Hercules goes to Thebes and gives Megara to Iolaus
Wishing to marry, Hercules learns that Eurytus of Oechalia has offered his daughter Iole to whoever beats him and his sons at archery
Hercules comes to Oechalia and beats them at archery
Iphitus, Eurytus's elder son, says Iole should be given to Hercules
Eurytus and the others refuse, fearing he would kill his children again
Autolycus steals cattle from Euboea
Eurytus suspects Hercules of the theft
Iphitus does not believe it and goes to Hercules
(Told back) Hercules has saved the dead Alcestis for Admetus and is coming from Pherae
Iphitus meets Hercules and asks him to search for the cattle with him
Hercules promises and entertains him
Mad again, Hercules throws Iphitus from the walls of Tiryns
Wishing to be purified of the murder, Hercules goes to Neleus, prince of the Pylians
Neleus refuses because of his friendship with Eurytus
Hercules goes to Amyclae and is purified by Deiphobus
Stricken with a terrible disease for the murder of Iphitus, Hercules goes to Delphi and asks how to be rid of it
When the priestess gives him no oracle, Hercules tries to plunder the temple and carries off the tripod to set up an oracle of his own
Apollo fights him
Zeus throws a thunderbolt between them and parts them
Hercules receives an oracle: to be cured he must be sold, serve three years and pay compensation to Eurytus
Hermes sells Hercules
Omphale, queen of Lydia, buys him
Eurytus refuses the compensation when it is offered
Hercules serves Omphale as a slave
Hercules seizes the Cercopes at Ephesus and ties them up
Hercules burns the vines of Syleus, who made passing strangers dig, root and all
Hercules kills Syleus and his daughter Xenodoce
Putting in at the island of Doliche, Hercules sees the body of Icarus washed ashore and buries it
In return Daedalus makes a portrait statue of Hercules at Pisa
Taking the statue at night for a living man, Hercules throws a stone at it and hits it
His servitude over and his disease gone, Hercules gathers noble volunteers and sails for Ilium with eighteen ships
At Ilium Hercules leaves Oicles to guard the ships and sets out with the rest against the city
Laomedon attacks the ships with his host and kills Oicles
Driven back by Hercules's troops, Laomedon is besieged
Telamon breaks through the wall and enters the city first, and Hercules after him
Seeing that Telamon entered first, Hercules draws his sword and rushes at him
Telamon gathers stones and says he is building an altar to Hercules the Glorious Victor
Hercules thanks him
Hercules takes the city and shoots Laomedon and his sons, all but Podarces
Hercules gives Laomedon's daughter Hesione to Telamon as a prize and lets her take any captive she wants
Hesione chooses her brother Podarces
Hercules says Podarces must first be a slave and then be ransomed by her
When Podarces is being sold, Hesione gives the veil from her head as his ransom
As Hercules sails from Troy, Hera sends terrible storms
Angered at this, Zeus hangs Hera from Olympus
Hercules sails to Cos, and the Coans, taking him for a pirate, try to keep him off with stones
Hercules forces his way in, takes the city by night and kills King Eurypylus
Hercules is wounded in the battle by Chalcedon
Zeus snatches Hercules away so that he comes to no harm
Having laid Cos waste, Hercules comes to Phlegra through Athena's doing
Hercules fights on the side of the gods in their victorious war on the giants
Hercules gathers an Arcadian army, joined by volunteers from the first men of Greece, and marches against Augeas
Hearing of it, Augeas makes Eurytus and Cteatus, the Molionides, generals of the Eleans
On the expedition Hercules falls sick and makes a truce with the Molionides
Learning he is ill, the Molionides attack his army and kill many
Hercules retreats
At the third Isthmian festival, when the Eleans send the Molionides to the sacrifices, Hercules ambushes and kills them at Cleonae
Hercules marches on Elis and takes the city
Hercules kills Augeas and his sons
Hercules brings back Phyleus and gives him the kingdom
Hercules marches against Pylus and takes the city
Hercules kills Periclymenus, the bravest of Neleus's sons, who changed his shape in battle
Hercules kills Neleus and his sons, all but Nestor
In the fight Hercules wounds Hades, who is fighting on the Pylians' side
Hercules marches against Lacedaemon to punish the sons of Hippocoon, who fought for Neleus and killed the son of Licymnius
Hercules kills the snake guarding the apples
Hercules picks the apples himself
As the son of Licymnius looks at Hippocoon's palace, a Molossian hound runs out and rushes at him
The son of Licymnius throws a stone and hits the dog
The sons of Hippocoon rush out and beat him to death with clubs
Coming to Arcadia, Hercules asks Cepheus to join him with his twenty sons
Fearing the Argives would attack Tegea if he left it, Cepheus refuses

Hercules gives Cepheus's daughter Sterope a lock of the Gorgon's hair in a bronze jar, which he had from Athena, telling her that if an army comes she should hold it up three times from the walls without looking, and the enemy will flee
Cepheus and his sons take the field
In the battle Cepheus and his sons are killed, and Iphicles, Hercules's brother, too
Hercules kills Hippocoon and his sons and conquers the city
Hercules brings back Tyndareus and hands the kingdom over to him
Passing Tegea, Hercules seduces Auge, not knowing she is the daughter of Aleus
Auge gives birth in secret and leaves the baby in the precinct of Athena
When a pestilence wastes the country, Aleus enters the precinct, searches, and discovers his daughter's motherhood
Aleus exposes the baby on Mount Parthenius
By the gods' providence a doe that has just given birth suckles the baby
Shepherds take up the baby and name him Telephus
Aleus gives Auge to Nauplius, son of Poseidon, to sell in a far country
Nauplius gives Auge to Teuthras, prince of Teuthrania, who makes her his wife
Coming to Calydon, Hercules woos Deianira, daughter of Oeneus
Hercules wrestles for her with Achelous, who takes the likeness of a bull
Hercules breaks off one of Achelous's horns
Hercules marries Deianira
Achelous gets his horn back by giving the horn of Amalthea in exchange
With the Calydonians, Hercules marches against the Thesprotians and takes the city of Ephyra
Hercules lies with Astyoche, daughter of King Phylas, and fathers Tlepolemus
Hercules sends word to Thespius to keep seven of his sons, send three to Thebes and send the other forty to Sardinia to found a colony
Feasting with Oeneus, Hercules kills with a blow of his knuckles the son of Architeles, a kinsman of Oeneus, as the boy pours water on his hands
Seeing that it was an accident, the boy's father pardons Hercules
Hercules chooses to suffer exile as the law requires and decides to go to Ceyx at Trachis
Taking Deianira with him, Hercules comes to the river Evenus, where the centaur Nessus ferries travelers across for pay
Hercules crosses the river by himself
Asked for the fare, Hercules entrusts Deianira to Nessus to carry across
While carrying her across, Nessus tries to rape Deianira
Deianira cries out, and Hercules hears her
Hercules shoots Nessus to the heart as he comes out of the river
Dying, Nessus tells Deianira that for a love charm to use on Hercules she should mix his spilt seed with the blood from the arrow wound
Deianira does so and keeps the mixture
Short of food in the country of the Dryopes, Hercules unyokes one of the bullocks Thiodamas is driving, slaughters it and feasts
Hercules comes to Ceyx at Trachis and is received by him
Hercules conquers the Dryopes
The Lapiths under Coronus make war on Aegimius, king of the Dorians, over boundaries and besiege him
Aegimius calls on Hercules for help, offering him a share of the country
Hercules comes to his help, kills Coronus and others, and hands the whole country over to Aegimius free
Hercules kills Laogoras, king of the Dryopes, and his children as they feast in a precinct of Apollo
Passing Itonus, Hercules is challenged to single combat by Cycnus, son of Ares and Pelopia, and kills him
At Ormenium King Amyntor takes up arms and forbids him to pass, and when Amyntor tries to stop him, Hercules kills him
Back at Trachis, Hercules musters an army against Oechalia to punish Eurytus
With Arcadian, Melian and Locrian allies, Hercules kills Eurytus and his sons and takes the city
Hercules buries his own dead: Hippasus, son of Ceyx, and Argius and Melas, sons of Licymnius
Hercules sacks the city and leads Iole away captive
Putting in at Cenaeum in Euboea, Hercules builds an altar of Cenaean Zeus
Meaning to sacrifice, Hercules sends the herald Lichas to Trachis for fine clothing
Deianira learns about Iole from Lichas
Afraid Hercules will love Iole more, and taking Nessus's blood for a love charm, Deianira smears the tunic with it
Hercules puts on the tunic and begins the sacrifice
As the tunic warms, the hydra's poison begins to eat into his skin
Hercules lifts Lichas by the feet and hurls him down from the headland
Hercules tears off the tunic, which clings to his body, and his flesh comes away with it
Hercules is carried by ship to Trachis
Learning what has happened, Deianira hangs herself
Hercules charges Hyllus, his elder son by Deianira, to marry Iole when he comes of age
Hercules goes to Mount Oeta, builds a pyre, climbs onto it and orders it lit
When no one will, Poeas, passing by in search of his flocks, sets it alight
Hercules gives Poeas his bow
Hercules obtains immortality
Hercules is reconciled with Hera
Hercules marries Hera's daughter Hebe
After Hercules is taken up to the gods, his sons flee from Eurystheus and come to Ceyx
Eurystheus demands their surrender and threatens war
Afraid, the sons of Hercules leave Trachis and flee through Greece
Pursued, they come to Athens, sit down at the altar of Mercy and claim protection
The Athenians refuse to give them up and bear the war against Eurystheus
The Athenians kill Eurystheus's sons Alexander, Iphimedon, Eurybius, Mentor and Perimedes
Eurystheus flees in a chariot, is pursued, and is killed by Hyllus at the Scironian cliffs
Hyllus cuts off Eurystheus's head and gives it to Alcmena
Alcmena gouges out its eyes with weaving pins
The Heraclids attack the Peloponnese and take all its cities
A year after their return a plague falls on the whole Peloponnese
An oracle declares that the plague is because the Heraclids came back before the proper time
The Heraclids leave the Peloponnese, withdraw to Marathon and live there
(Told back) Before they leave the Peloponnese, Tlepolemus accidentally kills Licymnius, who runs between him and a servant he is beating
Tlepolemus flees with many followers to Rhodes and settles there
Hyllus marries Iole, as his father commanded
Hyllus tries to bring about the Heraclids' return and goes to Delphi to ask how they should return
The god says they should wait for the third crop
Taking the third crop to mean three years, Hyllus waits that long and returns with his army to the Peloponnese, where Tisamenus, son of Orestes, is king
In another battle the Peloponnesians win and Aristomachus is killed
When the sons of Cleodaeus are grown, they ask the oracle about their return
The god gives the same answer as before
Temenus blames the god, saying they had obeyed and fared badly
The god answers that they misunderstood: the third crop meant the third generation, and the narrows meant the broad sea to the right of the Isthmus
Temenus gets the army ready and builds ships in Locris
While the army is there, Aristodemus is killed by a thunderbolt
A soothsayer comes to the army reciting oracles in a frenzy, and they take him for a sorcerer sent by the Peloponnesians to ruin them
Hippotes, a great-grandson of Hercules, throws a javelin at the soothsayer and kills him
The fleet is destroyed and the naval force perishes
The land force suffers from famine
The army breaks up
Temenus asks the oracle about the disaster, and the god says the soothsayer caused it and orders him to banish the slayer for ten years and take the Three-Eyed One as guide
The Heraclids banish Hippotes
The Heraclids look for the Three-Eyed One
The Heraclids come upon Oxylus, son of Andraemon, riding a one-eyed horse on his way back to Aetolia
Guessing the meaning of the oracle, the Heraclids make Oxylus their guide
The Heraclids meet the enemy, beat them by land and sea, and kill Tisamenus
Their allies Pamphylus and Dymas, sons of Aegimius, fall in the fight
Masters of the Peloponnese, the Heraclids set up three altars of Paternal Zeus and sacrifice on them
The Heraclids cast lots for the cities: first Argos, then Lacedaemon, then Messene
The Heraclids bring a pitcher of water and agree that each should cast in a lot
Temenus and the sons of Aristodemus throw in stones, but Cresphontes, wanting Messene, throws in a clod of earth
The clod dissolves, the lots of Temenus and then of the sons of Aristodemus come out, and Cresphontes gets Messene
On the altars they find signs: a toad for those who drew Argos, a serpent for Lacedaemon, a fox for Messene
The seers interpret the signs
Temenus passes over his sons and favors his daughter Hyrnetho and her husband Deiphontes
Temenus's sons hire men to murder their father
Temenus is murdered
The army decides that the kingdom belongs to Hyrnetho and Deiphontes
Cresphontes, not long king of Messene, is murdered with two of his sons
Polyphontes, a true Heraclid, takes the throne
Polyphontes takes Merope, the murdered king's wife, as his wife against her will
(Told back) Merope had given her third son, Aepytus, to her own father to bring up
Grown to manhood, Aepytus secretly returns
Aepytus kills Polyphontes
Aepytus recovers his fathers' kingdom
Zeus falls in love with Europa
Zeus turns himself into a tame bull
Zeus mounts Europa on his back
Zeus carries her through the sea to Crete
Zeus beds with Europa in Crete
On Europa's disappearance Agenor sends his sons to search for her, telling them not to return until they find her
Telephassa and Thasus go forth with them in search of her
After a diligent search they cannot find Europa
They give up the thought of returning home
Phoenix settles in Phoenicia
Cilix settles near Phoenicia, in the country by the river Pyramus
Cadmus and Telephassa take up their abode in Thrace
Thasus founds the city of Thasus on an island off Thrace and dwells there
Asterius brings up Europa's children
The grown brothers fall in love with the boy Miletus
The brothers quarrel with each other over him
Because the boy favours Sarpedon, Minos goes to war
Minos has the better of it
The others flee
Miletus lands in Caria and founds a city named after himself
Sarpedon allies himself with Cilix, who is at war with the Lycians, on terms of a share of the land
Sarpedon becomes king of Lycia
Zeus grants Sarpedon to live for three generations
The brothers fall in love with Atymnius
The brothers quarrel over Atymnius
Rhadamanthys makes laws for the islanders
Rhadamanthys flees to Boeotia
After leaving the world Rhadamanthys acts as a judge in Hades with Minos
Minos, living in Crete, makes laws
Asterius dies childless
Minos wishes to reign over Crete
Minos's claim is opposed
Minos alleges that he received the kingdom from the gods
As proof Minos says that whatever he prays for will be done
Sacrificing to Poseidon, Minos prays that a bull may appear from the depths
Minos promises to sacrifice the bull when it appears
Poseidon sends up a fine bull
Minos obtains the kingdom
Minos sends the bull to his herds
Minos sacrifices another bull instead
Minos extends his rule over almost all the islands (bracketed sentence)
Poseidon, angry at Minos for not sacrificing the bull, makes the animal savage
Poseidon causes Pasiphae to conceive a passion for the bull
Pasiphae finds an accomplice in Daedalus
Daedalus had been banished from Athens for murder (told in passing)
Daedalus builds a hollow wooden cow on wheels and sews it into the hide of a skinned cow
Daedalus sets the cow in the meadow where the bull grazes
Daedalus puts Pasiphae inside it
The bull comes and couples with it as if it were a real cow
Pasiphae gives birth to Asterius, the bull-faced Minotaur
Following certain oracles, Minos shuts the Minotaur up in the Labyrinth
Minos keeps the Minotaur guarded there
Daedalus had built the Labyrinth, a chamber of tangled windings (told in passing)
Catreus asks the oracle how his life will end
The god says he will die by the hand of one of his children
Catreus hides the oracles
Althaemenes hears of the oracles
Althaemenes fears to become his father's murderer
Althaemenes sets out from Crete with his sister Apemosyne
Althaemenes puts in at a place in Rhodes
Althaemenes takes possession of the place
Althaemenes climbs Mount Atabyrium
Althaemenes looks out over the islands and makes out Crete
Remembering the gods of his fathers, Althaemenes founds an altar of Atabyrian Zeus
Hermes falls in love with Apemosyne
Apemosyne flees from Hermes
Hermes cannot catch her, for she is faster on foot
Hermes spreads fresh hides on the path
Returning from the spring, Apemosyne slips on the hides
Apemosyne is deflowered
Apemosyne tells her brother what has happened
Althaemenes, thinking the god a mere pretext, kicks her to death
Catreus gives Aerope and Clymene to Nauplius to sell into foreign lands
In old age Catreus longs to hand the kingdom to his son Althaemenes
Catreus goes to Rhodes for that purpose
Catreus lands with the heroes at a deserted spot on the island
The cowherds, taking them for raiding pirates, chase Catreus
Catreus tells them the truth
The cowherds cannot hear him for the barking of the dogs
The cowherds pelt him
Althaemenes arrives
Althaemenes kills Catreus with a javelin, not knowing who he is
Althaemenes learns the truth
Althaemenes prays
Althaemenes disappears into a chasm
The child Glaucus chases a mouse
Glaucus falls into a jar of honey
Glaucus drowns
On his disappearance Minos makes a great search
Minos consults diviners on how to find him
The Curetes tell Minos that whoever best describes his three-coloured cow will restore his son alive
When the diviners are assembled, Polyidus compares the cow's colour to the fruit of the bramble
Compelled to seek the child, Polyidus finds him by a kind of divination
Minos declares that Polyidus must recover the child alive
Polyidus is shut up with the dead body
In his perplexity Polyidus sees a serpent going towards the corpse
Fearing for his own life, Polyidus kills the serpent with a stone
A second serpent comes, sees the first one dead, and goes away
The second serpent returns with a herb and lays it on the dead one's body
The dead serpent comes to life
Surprised, Polyidus applies the same herb to Glaucus's body
Polyidus raises Glaucus from the dead
Minos gets his son back
Minos will not let Polyidus leave for Argos until he teaches Glaucus divination
Polyidus teaches Glaucus under compulsion
As he sails away, Polyidus tells Glaucus to spit into his mouth
Glaucus spits into his mouth
Glaucus forgets the art of divination
On Telephassa's death Cadmus buries her
The Thracians receive Cadmus hospitably
Cadmus comes to Delphi to ask about Europa
The god tells him not to trouble about Europa but to follow a cow and found a city where it falls down from weariness
Cadmus journeys through Phocis
Cadmus falls in with a cow among the herds of Pelagon and follows it
Having crossed Boeotia, the cow sinks down where Thebes now stands
Wishing to sacrifice the cow to Athena, Cadmus sends companions to draw water from the spring of Ares
A dragon guarding the spring kills most of those sent
In anger Cadmus kills the dragon
On Athena's advice Cadmus sows the dragon's teeth
Armed men, the Sparti, rise from the ground
The Sparti kill each other, some in a chance brawl and some in ignorance
Five of the Sparti survive
To atone for the slaughter Cadmus serves Ares for an eternal year of eight years
After his servitude Athena obtains the kingdom for him
Zeus gives him Harmonia as wife
All the gods leave the sky and feast in the Cadmea, celebrating the marriage with hymns
Cadmus gives Harmonia a robe and the necklace made by Hephaestus
Cadmus sees armed men growing out of the ground
Cadmus throws stones at them
Thinking they are pelted by one another, the armed men come to blows
Hephaestus gives the necklace to Cadmus
Zeus gives the necklace to Europa
Europa gives the necklace to Cadmus
Zeus falls in love with Semele
Zeus beds with Semele without Hera's knowledge
Zeus agrees to do for Semele whatever she asks
Deceived by Hera, Semele asks Zeus to come to her as he came when wooing Hera
Unable to refuse, Zeus comes to her chamber in a chariot with lightning and thunder
Zeus launches a thunderbolt
Semele dies of fright
Zeus snatches the six-month child from the fire
Zeus sews the child into his thigh
Semele's sisters spread a report that she had lain with a mortal and falsely blamed Zeus, and was struck by thunder for it
At the proper time Zeus undoes the stitches and gives birth to Dionysus
Zeus entrusts Dionysus to Hermes
Hermes takes Dionysus to Ino and Athamas
Hermes persuades them to rear him as a girl
Hera in anger drives Ino and Athamas mad
Athamas hunts his elder son Learchus as a deer and kills him
Ino throws Melicertes into a boiling cauldron
Carrying the cauldron with the dead child, Ino leaps into the sea
Zeus escapes Hera's anger by turning Dionysus into a kid
Hermes takes the child to the nymphs of Nysa in Asia
Zeus later turns the nymphs into stars, the Hyades
Chiron brings up Actaeon to be a hunter
Actaeon is devoured on Cithaeron by his own dogs
Actaeon had wooed Semele
Zeus is angry at Actaeon for it
Actaeon sees Artemis bathing
Artemis at once turns him into a deer
Artemis drives his fifty dogs mad
The dogs devour him without knowing him
With Actaeon gone, the dogs seek their master, howling
In their search the dogs come to Chiron's cave
Chiron makes an image of Actaeon, which soothes the dogs' grief
Dionysus discovers the vine
Hera drives Dionysus mad
Dionysus roams about Egypt and Syria
Proteus, king of Egypt, receives him
Dionysus arrives at Cybela in Phrygia
Rhea purifies him
Dionysus learns the rites of initiation
Dionysus receives the costume from Rhea
Dionysus hastens through Thrace against the Indians
Lycurgus, king of the Edonians, insults him
Lycurgus drives him out
Dionysus takes refuge in the sea with Thetis
The Bacchanals and the Satyrs who attend him are taken prisoner
The Bacchanals are suddenly released
Dionysus drives Lycurgus mad
Lycurgus kills his son Dryas with an axe, thinking he is lopping a vine branch
Having cut off his son's extremities, Lycurgus comes to his senses
The land stays barren
The god declares by oracle that the land will bear fruit if Lycurgus is put to death
The Edonians lead Lycurgus to Mount Pangaeum and bind him
By the will of Dionysus Lycurgus dies there, destroyed by horses
Dionysus traverses Thrace and all India
Dionysus sets up pillars there
Dionysus comes to Thebes
Dionysus forces the women to leave their houses and rave in Bacchic frenzy on Cithaeron
Pentheus, who has succeeded Cadmus as king, tries to stop these proceedings
Pentheus comes to Cithaeron to spy on the Bacchanals
His mother Agave, in a fit of madness, tears him limb from limb, thinking him a wild beast
Having shown the Thebans that he is a god, Dionysus comes to Argos
Because the Argives do not honour him, Dionysus drives the women mad
On the mountains the women devour the flesh of the infants at their breasts
Wishing to cross from Icaria to Naxos, Dionysus hires a Tyrrhenian pirate ship
The pirates take him on board
The pirates sail past Naxos and make for Asia, meaning to sell him
Dionysus turns the mast and oars into snakes
Dionysus fills the vessel with ivy and the sound of flutes
The pirates go mad
The pirates leap into the sea
The pirates are turned into dolphins
Men perceive that he is a god and honour him
Dionysus brings his mother up from Hades and names her Thyone
Dionysus ascends with her to heaven
Cadmus and Harmonia leave Thebes and go to the Encheleans
The Illyrians attack the Encheleans
The god declares by oracle that the Encheleans will win if they have Cadmus and Harmonia as leaders
Believing him, the Encheleans make Cadmus and Harmonia their leaders against the Illyrians
The Encheleans defeat the Illyrians
Cadmus reigns over the Illyrians
Cadmus and Harmonia are turned into serpents
Zeus sends them away to the Elysian Fields
Polydorus becomes king of Thebes
Labdacus perishes after Pentheus, being of like mind with him
While Laius is a child, Lycus usurps the government
Lycus and Nycteus had killed Phlegyas, son of Ares (told in passing)
Lycus and Nycteus had fled for it
Lycus and Nycteus settled at Hyria
Lycus and Nycteus came to Thebes
Lycus and Nycteus were enrolled as citizens through their friendship with Pentheus
Chosen commander-in-chief by the Thebans, Lycus seizes supreme power
Lycus reigns for twenty years
Zeus has intercourse with Antiope
When she is with child her father Nycteus threatens her
Antiope runs away to Epopeus at Sicyon
Antiope is married to Epopeus
In despondency Nycteus kills himself
Before dying Nycteus charges Lycus to punish Epopeus and Antiope
Lycus marches against Sicyon and subdues it
Lycus kills Epopeus
Lycus leads Antiope away captive
On the way Antiope gives birth to two sons at Eleutherae in Boeotia
The infants are exposed
A neatherd finds and rears them
The neatherd names them Zethus and Amphion
Zethus takes up cattle-breeding
Amphion practises minstrelsy

Throwing a dart at the boar, Peleus accidentally kills Eurytion

Astydamia, wife of Acastus, falls in love with Peleus
Astydamia sends him a proposal for a meeting

Acastus hides Peleus's sword in cow dung
Acastus goes back home

Chiron gives him back his sword, which he had searched for and found

Zeus and Poseidon withdraw

Chiron gives Peleus an ashen spear

Peleus watches her

Achilles's secret is betrayed

Phoenix, son of Amyntor, goes with him

Peleus brought Phoenix to Chiron
Chiron restored his sight
Peleus made Phoenix king of the Dolopians
Patroclus also goes with Achilles

Patroclus had lived in the house of Peleus
Patroclus had become the favourite of Achilles

With a blow of his trident on the acropolis Poseidon brings forth a sea
Athena comes after him
Athena calls on Cecrops to witness her taking possession

Poseidon and Athena strive for possession of the country
Zeus parts them

Zeus appoints Cecrops and Cranaus as arbiters
Zeus appoints Erysichthon as arbiter
Ares catches Halirrhothius, son of Poseidon, trying to violate Alcippe
Ares kills Halirrhothius
Poseidon impeaches Ares
Ares is tried in the Areopagus before the twelve gods
Ares is acquitted
Dawn falls in love with Cephalus

Sandocus passes from Syria to Cilicia
Sandocus founds the city of Celenderis
Cinyras comes with some people to Cyprus

The daughters of Cinyras end their lives in Egypt

Athena comes to Hephaestus, wishing to have arms made

The sisters see a serpent coiled about the babe

Erichthonius institutes the festival of the Panathenaea

Demeter and Dionysus come to Attica
Celeus welcomes Demeter at Eleusis
Icarius welcomes Dionysus
Icarius receives a branch of a vine from Dionysus
Icarius learns how to make wine

Erigone mourns her father
Erigone hangs herself

Tereus hides Procne in the country
Tereus seduces Philomela, saying that Procne is dead
Tereus marries Philomela and beds with her

Procne seeks out her sister
Procne kills her son Itys
Procne boils him
Procne serves him up for supper to the unknowing Tereus

Procne becomes a nightingale

Cephalus finds her out
Procris flees to Minos
Minos falls in love with her
Minos tries to seduce her

As Orithyia plays by the river Ilissus, Boreas carries her off
Boreas has intercourse with her
Zetes and Calais sail with Jason
Zetes and Calais meet their end chasing the Harpies

When the Argonauts sail past with Boreas, they punish Phineus

Eumolpus tries to force his wife's sister

Eumolpus makes friends with the Eleusinians

In the battle that follows Erechtheus kills Eumolpus
Poseidon destroys Erechtheus and his house

Theseus takes up the sandals and the sword

Drawing the thread after him, Theseus makes his way out

Theseus goes to Lycomedes

Broteas, a hunter, does not honor Artemis

Menelaus entertains Alexander for nine days

Hector challenges the bravest of the Greeks to single combat

Ulysses enters the city unknown, as a beggar
